Project SPRUCE: Formation of an International Consortium of Pediatric Anesthesia Groups to Reduce Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Inhaled Anesthetics
items.abstract: Background: Inhaled anesthetic use contributes to environmental harm through release of potent greenhouse gases (GHG). Emissions can be reduced with the use of safe practice changes, including avoidance of high impact agents like desflurane and nitrous oxide, use of low fresh gas flows, and adoption of total intravenous and regional anesthesia when clinically appropriate. These evidence-based practices have been recommended for years, but actual practice changes have not been widely adopted. Methods: The Project SPRUCE (Saving our Planet by Reducing Carbon Emissions) consortium brought together twelve pediatric anesthesia groups into a partnership working to reduce GHG emissions from pediatric anesthesia care. The consortium implemented quality improvement strategies, including change management methods, to reduce GHG emissions from inhaled anesthetics by at least 50%. Change management and quality improvement strategies were utilized to disseminate strategies, implement emissions reduction techniques, and track emissions in pediatric anesthesia care. Specific interventions included education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams. Results: The consortium facilitated adoption of practice changes among anesthesia groups, and sustained emissions reductions though shifts in culture. Greenhouse gas emissions from inhaled anesthesia decreased by 63% (range 43-91%) During the study period, the incidence of nitrous oxide use was reduced by 62.4%, and the average volume of nitrous oxide used per case decreased by 83.5%. Project SPRUCE prevented a total of 14,381 metric tons of excess carbon dioxide equivalent (CO 2 e) emissions from inhaled anesthetics. Conclusions: Collaborative action within our consortium supported widespread and significant reductions in harmful greenhouse gas emissions from pediatric anesthesia care through education and socialization, practice constraints, and direct data feedback to clinical teams.

items.title: Intraoperative Noise Isolation and Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting after Gynecological Laparoscopic Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background: Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) remain common after gynecological laparoscopic surgery despite guideline-based prophylaxis. Auditory information is still processed during clinically adequate general anesthesia, and operating rooms are persistently noisy, but whether attenuating intraoperative sound exposure alters PONV is unknown. Methods: In this single-center, patient- and assessor-blinded randomized trial, women aged 18 to 65 yr undergoing elective gynecological laparoscopic surgery were randomized 1:1 to wear passive noise-attenuating earmuffs from induction until the end of surgery or to usual care. All patients received dexamethasone and palonosetron. The primary outcome was PONV incidence within 48 h, defined as any episode of nausea, retching, or vomiting, assessed across three prespecified windows (post-anesthesia care unit, to 24 h, and 24 to 48 h). Secondary outcomes included PONV severity, its components, rescue antiemetic use, pain, and quality of recovery. Results: Of 364 patients assessed, 192 were randomized. PONV within 48 h occurred in 34 of 96 patients (35.4%) with noise isolation and 50 of 96 (52.1%) with control (adjusted risk difference, −0.179 [95% CI, −0.318 to −0.040]; P = 0.012). Across the three windows the overall adjusted risk difference was −0.134 (95% CI, −0.215 to −0.053; P = 0.001), with no treatment-by-window interaction ( P = 0.332); window-specific values were −0.162, −0.172, and −0.068. PONV severity, retching, and three post hoc endpoints (the vomiting-or-retching composite, complete response 72.9% versus 56.2%, and total response 64.6% versus 47.9%) favored noise isolation after false discovery rate correction. Adverse events, quality of recovery, and opioid exposure (post hoc) showed no evidence of a difference. Conclusions: Among women receiving dual antiemetic prophylaxis for gynecological laparoscopic surgery, intraoperative noise isolation was associated with a lower incidence and severity of PONV.

items.title: Intravenous Lidocaine in Liver Surgery ‒ A Randomized Double-Blind Trial
items.abstract: Background: Managing postoperative pain is a complex challenge in liver surgery. Perioperative intravenous (IV) lidocaine can reduce postoperative pain, opioid use, bowel recovery time and the length of stay, in various types of surgery. Lidocaine is eliminated via hepatic metabolism, and IV lidocaine is rarely evaluated in liver surgery. This study aimed to evaluate the postoperative analgesic efficacy and safety of IV lidocaine administration in patients undergoing minor liver surgery. Methods: Patients planned for minor liver surgery were randomized 1:1 to receive either perioperative IV lidocaine, administered as a 1.5 mg/kg bolus followed by a continuous infusion of 1.5 mg/kg/h until 1 hour after surgery, or placebo. All patients received postoperative opioid analgesia via a patient-controlled analgesia device. The primary outcome was postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, quality of recovery, adverse events, length of stay, and plasma lidocaine concentrations. Results: In total, 124 subjects were included. Postoperative opioid consumption during the first 24 hours after surgery was 83 (50 – 129) mg oral morphine equivalents (OME) in the lidocaine group, and 97 (60 – 135) mg OME in the placebo group, p=0.429. Patients in the lidocaine group experienced lower pain scores at early postoperative time points, but not from postoperative day 1 onward. The Quality of recovery-40 score did not differ, and adverse events were similar between groups. In two cases, plasma concentrations of lidocaine were transiently above 5 µg/ml after bolus administration, without clinical signs of toxicity. All plasma concentrations after resection and at end of infusion were safely below toxic levels. Conclusions: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine did not reduce postoperative opioid consumption after minor liver surgery but conferred transient early analgesic benefits and was found to be safe.

items.title: Individualized mean arterial pressure during cardiac surgery The OPTIPAM Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: Background: Whether targeting an individualized mean arterial pressure (MAP) during cardiac surgery improves outcomes remains uncertain. The balance between improved perfusion and vasopressor-driven blood pressure augmentation is unclear. Methods: In this single-blind, multicenter randomized clinical trial conducted in 10 tertiary centers in France, adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were assigned to either individualized MAP management (target within ±10% of preoperative baseline during surgery and for 24 h postoperatively) or standard management (target MAP ≥65 mm Hg). The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, acute kidney injury, or prespecified neurologic complications within 7 days. Safety outcomes included hemorrhagic complications and transfusion requirements. Results: A total of 172 patients were enrolled before the trial was stopped early by the data and safety monitoring board because of increased bleeding in the individualized group. Mean intraoperative MAP was higher with individualized management (80.6 vs 75.6 mm Hg; P<0.001), despite limited target adherence (33% of intraoperative time) and greater vasopressor use. The primary outcome occurred in 27 of 85 patients (32%) in the individualized group and 25 of 87 (29%) in the standard group (relative risk, 1.1; 95% CI, 0.7 to 1.8; P=0.76). Hemorrhagic complications occurred more frequently in the individualized group (18% vs 3%; P=0.003). Conclusions: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, it was not possible to determine whether an individualized MAP strategy reduced major postoperative complications. More bleeding complications were observed in the individualized group. Future studies should further investigate this safety signal when evaluating individualized blood pressure targets.

Postoperative Digital Health Interventions After Non-Cardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Background: Recovery after non-cardiac surgery increasingly occurs at home, where clinical deterioration may go unrecognized. Digital health interventions may extend postoperative surveillance beyond discharge, but vary widely in components and clinician involvement. We evaluated their association with readmission and other outcomes. Methods: Five databases were searched from inception to December 12, 2025, for prospective randomized and observational studies comparing digital health interventions with standard care in adults after non-cardiac surgery. Readmission was the primary outcome; all-cause and major complications, emergency room (ER) visits, length of stay (LOS), and patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) were secondary. Interventions were grouped by whether a clinician reviewed patient-submitted data and had the ability to take action (active clinician involvement). Random-effects models pooled risk ratios (RR), mean differences (MD), and standardized mean differences (SMD). p values were adjusted for multiple comparisons (Benjamini–Hochberg). Results: In 38 studies (30 randomized, 8 observational; 7,494 patients), digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions (17 studies, n=3,944; RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73–0.99, adjusted p=0.045), ER visits (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.63–0.97), and major complications (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60–0.94), but not all-cause complications (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79–1.08) or LOS (MD −0.04 days, 95% CI −0.26 to 0.18). Pain and anxiety were lower and functional status, quality-of-life, and satisfaction scores higher (absolute SMD 0.41–0.69). Readmission risk was lower with active clinician involvement (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.64–0.92) but not without it (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.78–1.18; interaction p=0.029). Heterogeneity in interventions, cohorts, and outcomes was substantial (PROM I² 50–97%). Conclusions: Digital health interventions were associated with fewer readmissions, ER visits, major complications, and better PROMs, but not fewer all-cause complications or shorter LOS. The readmission association was concentrated in studies with active clinician involvement. Heterogeneity was substantial and certainty of evidence low to very low.

items.title: Quality of Recovery After Primary Breast Cancer Surgery: A Randomized, Two-Centre, Triple-Blinded Trial Comparing Erector Spinae Plane Block and Intravenous Lidocaine Infusion Within a Multimodal Analgesia Framework.
items.abstract: Background: The erector spinae plane block (ESPB) is widely used for primary breast cancer surgery (BCS), though its clinical benefits within optimized multimodal analgesia pathways remain uncertain. Intravenous lidocaine infusion (IVLI) offers a simple, reproducible alternative with potential systemic analgesic effects. This randomized, tripleblinded, placebo controlled, twocentre trial compared the quality of recovery after ESPB versus IVLI for BCS. Methods: Eighty adult patients undergoing primary BCS, with or without axillary dissection, were randomized to receive either ultrasoundguided ESPB (n=40) or intraoperative IVLI (n=40), in addition to a standardized multimodal analgesic protocol. The primary outcome was quality of recovery (QoR15) score at 24 hours. Secondary outcomes included postoperative pain scores, opioid consumption, adverse events, and rescue analgesia requirements. Results: Both interventions produced excellent postoperative recovery, with 24hour QoR15 scores approaching preoperative baselines with no significant difference between groups (mean (SD) 24-hour QoR score; ESPB vs. IVLI group, 137.7(17.9) vs. 136.3(8.8), p=0.61). Pain burden and analgesic requirements over the first 24 hours were similarly low, and no ESPB or lidocainerelated adverse events were observed. Conclusions: Within a standardized multimodal analgesic framework, postoperative recovery and analgesic outcomes did not differ significantly between IVLI and ESPB, suggesting that IVLI may offer a pragmatic alternative when regional anesthesia expertise is limited.

Rethinking the Responsible Adult Requirement after Ambulatory Anesthesia: Toward Risk-stratified Discharge
items.abstract: For decades, ambulatory anesthesia pathways have commonly required a “responsible adult” before discharge after sedation or anesthesia. In practice, this requirement may function as a binary eligibility criterion based on a patient’s social circumstances. However, the empirical evidence evaluating discharge without an escort remains limited and derives largely from observational studies. This Focal Point argues that carefully selected low-risk patients should be studied within structured alternative discharge pathways that preserve safe transportation, communication, observation, and rescue capacity. Such pathways should not permit self-driving or unrestricted solo discharge. The aim is to determine whether postanesthesia safeguards can be matched more precisely to patient, anesthetic, procedural, recovery, transport, and postdischarge risk while preserving conventional adult support for patients whose clinical circumstances warrant it.

Actuarial Validity and Financial Implications of Maximum Paid Anesthesia Time Based on Tolerance Limits for Log-Normal Distributions
items.abstract: Background: We investigate the policy implications of statistically valid upper limits on anesthesia durations. We test whether these tolerance limits categorized by claims data (procedure, surgeon, and facility) differ in practical consequence from limits calculated with data pooled among surgeons and facilities. We evaluate whether using valid tolerance limits at typical insurer sample sizes would differ functionally from no limits. Methods: Simulations had 100,000 replicates per configuration with 8 surgeons per hospital: equal n = 10 or 300 cases per-surgeon or unequal (geometric) median n = 10 and 60. The within-surgeon coefficient of variation was 36.2%. The between-surgeon variance accounted for 22.4% of total log-time variance (intraclass correlation). Five tolerance-limit methods (pooled Weibull generalized pivotal quantity, pooled nonparametric, per-surgeon log-normal, per-surgeon 3-sigma, and per-surgeon nonparametric) were evaluated by coverage probability (95% was correct), case-volume-weighted percentage bias (0% best), functional quantile (90 th for 90 th percentile), and payment satisfaction (100% ideal). Results: Pooled mixtures of cases by procedure were best fit by log-normal distributions. The noncentral-t–based log-normal tolerance limit, calculated per combination of procedure, surgeon, and facility, attained nominal 95% coverage in every configuration. Pooled Weibull and pooled nonparametric limits failed often (coverage 70.9%–79.2% and 62.9%–83.8%). The nonparametric method with all claim data attained 95.4%–97.1% coverage but was unavailable for 85% of surgeons at the realistic condition of unequal sample sizes, median n = 10. Applying the exact log-normal-based tolerance limits on 90 th percentiles functionally achieved percentiles ranging from the 92.1-97.4 th , with resulting payment satisfaction rates of 97.9%-100%. Conclusions: The per-surgeon log-normal 95% upper confidence limit for the 90 th percentile on log-transformed durations was the only valid method computable at realistic sample sizes. Applying those actuarially valid tolerance limits would pay ≈99.4% of historical case-time in full, thus functionally equivalent to retaining no paid time limit.

items.title: Prefrontal hemodynamic fluctuations and functional connectivity during propofol and sevoflurane anesthesia: A functional near-infrared spectroscopy study
items.abstract: Background: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measures cortical hemodynamics, yet its ability to characterize anesthesia-related functional changes remains unclear. Methods: This exploratory secondary analysis used prospectively collected data from 120 female patients undergoing gynecologic laparoscopic surgery under propofol or sevoflurane anesthesia (60 per group). Twenty-channel prefrontal fNIRS recordings covered wakefulness, induction, and maintenance. Deoxygenated hemoglobin-derived amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), functional connectivity (FC), network topology, and within- and cross-state FC similarity were assessed. Support vector machine, logistic regression, and random forest classifiers assessed discrimination between states. Results: During induction, ALFF increased by 89.8% to 202.2% with propofol and 75.2% to 242.0% with sevoflurane across five prefrontal regions (all P < 0.001). During maintenance, mean ALFF was below awake levels, with significant reductions of 20.0% to 40.1% in three regions under sevoflurane (all P ≤ 0.019). Induction-related FC changes were limited and regionally heterogeneous. Regional FC, modularity, and global efficiency showed no significant maintenance-versus-awake differences in either group. Within-state between-subject FC similarity was significantly higher during maintenance than during wakefulness only with sevoflurane (mean difference [MD], 0.110; 95% CI, 0.054 to 0.169; P < 0.001). Cross-state between-subject FC similarity was higher for awake–maintenance than awake–induction comparisons with propofol (MD, 0.072; 95% CI, 0.055 to 0.090) and sevoflurane (MD, 0.144; 95% CI, 0.126 to 0.161; both P < 0.001). Support vector machine classification of induction versus wakefulness yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.75 to 0.90) for propofol and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.91) for sevoflurane; maintenance-versus-awake AUCs were 0.67 (95% CI, 0.58 to 0.75) and 0.76 (95% CI, 0.68 to 0.85). Conclusions: Prefrontal fNIRS detected widespread induction-related hemodynamic changes, but the present connectivity measures provided limited discrimination between maintenance of anesthesia and wakefulness.

Effect of remimazolam versus propofol anaesthesia on postoperative delirium in neurovascular surgery: a randomised noninferiority trial
items.abstract: Background Propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (TIVA) is commonly used in neurovascular surgery, in which intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring limits inhalation anaesthetic use. However, propofol causes hypotension, and prolonged infusions can delay emergence. Remimazolam, a benzodiazepine whose effects are reversible with flumazenil, has been associated with less intraoperative hypotension than propofol, but its use raises concerns about postoperative delirium (POD). We tested whether remimazolam-based TIVA is noninferior to propofol-based TIVA for POD. Methods In this single-centre, double-blind, randomised noninferiority trial, adults undergoing elective intracranial aneurysm clipping, arteriovenous malformation resection, microvascular decompression, or superficial temporal artery-middle cerebral artery bypass received remimazolam-based TIVA with flumazenil reversal at emergence, or propofol-based TIVA, both with remifentanil. The primary outcome was the cumulative incidence of POD within 5 days, assessed twice daily with the Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the 3-Minute Diagnostic Interview for CAM-defined delirium (3D-CAM). The prespecified noninferiority margin was 10 percentage points. Results Among 686 patients in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, POD occurred in 44 of 344 (12.8%) with remimazolam and 37 of 342 (10.8%) with propofol (risk difference, 1.97 percentage points; 95% CI, -2.85 to 6.80; one-sided P Conclusions Remimazolam-based TIVA met the prespecified criterion for noninferiority to propofol-based TIVA with respect to postoperative delirium after elective neurovascular surgery. Interpretation should take into account that the observed incidence of postoperative delirium was lower than anticipated when the noninferiority margin was defined. Clinical trial registration NCT06115031 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

items.title: Ultrasound assessment of fluid tolerance in patients undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery: epidemiology of pulmonary and systemic congestion
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fluid accumulation in surgical patients is associated with worse outcomes. Lung ultrasound (LUS) and venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) grading can assess congestion and thereby fluid tolerance. However, evidence regarding epidemiology, feasibility, and associations of reduced fluid tolerance with outcomes in surgical patients is lacking. METHODS: This was a prospective single-centre observational cohort study in patients undergoing major gastrointestinal surgery. LUS and VExUS were performed before surgery and daily for up to 5 days after surgery. Reduced fluid tolerance was defined as pulmonary congestion (B profile on LUS), systemic congestion (VExUS ≥2), or both. The primary outcome was the prevalence of reduced fluid tolerance. Secondary outcomes were feasibility of ultrasound assessments, Clavien-Dindo grade ≥3 complications, and length of stay (LOS). RESULTS: Of the 200 participants included, 73 (37%) exhibited signs of reduced fluid tolerance, most commonly on postoperative day 4 (n=28; 14%). Reduced fluid tolerance was primarily driven by pulmonary congestion (n=69; 95%), whereas systemic congestion was rare. In most affected patients (47 of 73; 64%), reduced fluid tolerance was limited to 1 day. Of 1200 planned assessments, 146 (12%) were missing: 123 because participants declined, mostly owing to the burden of repeated assessments, and 23 (2%) because of incomplete views. Reduced fluid tolerance was associated with LOS of >7 days (odds ratio 3.29; 95% CI 1.03-10.70), but not with major postoperative complications (hazard ratio 1.18; 95% CI 0.49-2.86). CONCLUSIONS: Reduced fluid tolerance detected by ultrasound is common after major gastrointestinal surgery and associated with increased LOS. Ultrasound assessments were technically feasible, but repeated assessments were perceived as a burden by a substantial proportion of patients. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT06166719 (principal investigator: A.P.J. Vlaar; first registered: 04-12-2023).

Use of perioperative allergy labels appears to be harming, not helping, patients: risks, systems, and research opportunities
items.abstract: Use of perioperative allergy labelling seems to increase the rate of patient complications after surgery, including, paradoxically, the rates of allergic reactions. However, approximately 90% of allergy labels in patient records have been shown to be incorrect when checked using allergy testing, demonstrating the need for system redesign in allergy labelling practices to ensure that they function as intended to reduce the risk of allergy for patients undergoing anaesthesia.

Conceptual model of multidisciplinary shared decision-making for high-risk surgical patients: a Delphi study
items.abstract: High-risk patients need to carefully consider the risks and benefits of surgery. Shared decision-making is a collaborative process that enables patients and clinicians to share information and weigh up options and preferences. There is limited evidence about how best to organise the participation of the full range of healthcare professionals who can contribute to such decision-making processes. We conducted a Delphi study with a panel of experts to clarify how, and for what purposes, different healthcare professionals can contribute to shared decision-making with high-risk surgical patients. Consensus was reached on a conceptual model of multidisciplinary shared decision-making. The model recommends that interactions between patients, supported by family members and informal carers, and healthcare professionals are organised around five areas: options for management and treatment; patient values, goals, and preferences; comprehensive needs assessment; social context and home environment; and perioperative preparations. Experts agreed that achieving multidisciplinary shared decision-making in practice requires four key facilitators: early identification of patients with complex decision-making needs, availability of specialist expertise and support, sufficient time for discussion and decision-making, and coordination and information sharing between interactions. This model organises multidisciplinary involvement in high-risk surgical shared decision-making into five conceptually distinct and operationally interdependent areas. The model has the potential to inform practice and enhance opportunities for shared decision-making for high-risk surgical patients and their multidisciplinary teams.

Counting reactions, not just variants: what malignant hyperthermia can teach precision medicine
items.abstract: Susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia is generally considered to follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with incomplete penetrance. In a recent study in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, Aboelsaod and colleagues integrate national epidemiological data, anaesthetic exposure histories, population genomics, contracture test phenotyping, and Bayesian modelling to estimate the prevalence of individuals capable of developing clinical malignant hyperthermia. Their findings support a threshold model in which variants contribute different degrees of biological liability, potentially modified by other genetic and environmental factors, whereas the probability of reacting during a triggering exposure seems relatively similar once an individual has crossed this threshold. The study also illustrates how combining complementary sources of imperfect evidence can improve risk estimation for rare, exposure-dependent disorders. Ultimately, malignant hyperthermia genetics needs to move beyond categorical variant classification towards variant-specific penetrance estimates that incorporate genetic background, ancestry, exposure history, and other determinants of clinical expression.

Cardiac output monitoring using an automatic arm cuff device in surgical patients
items.abstract: Background Pulse contour devices estimate cardiac output (CO) from an invasive arterial blood pressure waveform. However, arterial catheters are generally used only in higher-risk patients. By contrast, automatic arm cuff devices are used for noninvasive BP monitoring in almost all hospital patients. Furthermore, these devices measure cuff pressure oscillations, which are directly related to pulsatile blood volume rather than BP. We hypothesised that automatic arm cuff devices can offer an effective means to monitor CO. Methods A custom-built cuff device was used to measure cuff pressure and make a unique measurement of the volume of air pumped into and out of the cuff during linear deflation. Cuff device measurements, an invasive BP waveform from a radial artery catheter, and reference CO from pulmonary artery catheter bolus thermodilution were obtained during interventions from 24 liver transplant and 10 cardiac surgery patients (191 measurement sets). A basic analysis was applied to estimate CO in L min −1 as the product of heart rate, the maximum cuff pressure oscillation amplitude, the cuff–arm system compliance (derived from the cuff pressure–volume relationship), and the body-to-arm surface area ratio (derived from anthropometric information). Results The arm cuff–based method yielded a correlation of 0.61 (95% confidence interval 0.37–0.79) and a concordance rate of 83% (75%–91%) against the reference CO. For comparison, classic pulse contour analysis of the invasive BP waveform produced a correlation of 0.59 (0.37–0.75) and a concordance rate of 81% (72%–90%). Conclusions These initial findings suggest potential for convenient CO monitoring using an automatic arm cuff device in surgical patients.

Silencing the fire alarm: responding to intraoperative blood pressure targets
items.abstract: A meta-analysis in a recent issue of the British Journal of Anaesthesia pools randomised evidence on intraoperative arterial blood pressure targets in nine trials in noncardiac surgery. With a total of 14 658 patients included in the analysis, the authors show that higher mean arterial pressure targets do not reduce 30-day mortality, acute kidney injury, or myocardial injury. These findings reinforce the distinction between low blood pressure as a marker of perioperative vulnerability and low blood pressure as a modifiable therapeutic target. Correcting arterial pressure might normalise a number without removing the underlying physiological vulnerability that drives adverse postoperative outcomes. Therefore, this meta-analysis supports a shift from reflexive increases in blood pressure targets towards attention to the underlying cause of haemodynamic instability.

items.title: Chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and perioperative outcomes: a scoping review
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Expert clinical guidelines discourage routine benzodiazepine premedication in older adults because of associations with adverse postoperative outcomes, including delirium and prolonged length of stay. However, these recommendations primarily address acute administration, whereas chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use for non-surgical indications remains incompletely understood, and the relevant evidence has not been comprehensively synthesised. This scoping review characterised the literature on chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and perioperative outcomes by mapping study characteristics, definitions of chronic use, and associated outcome domains and trends. METHODS: Published and grey literature were searched across MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, Scopus, and thesis databases. Screening and full-text review were performed independently in duplicate. Eligible studies included adults undergoing surgery with chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use and excluded studies in which benzodiazepines were administered exclusively within 24 h of surgery. This scoping review was preregistered with the Open Science Framework (10.17605/OSF.IO/573JG). RESULTS: A total of 130 studies were included. Most were observational cohorts (n=109, 83.8%) and examined benzodiazepines as a secondary variable (n=100, 77.0%). Definitions of chronic use were heterogeneous, ranging from 1 month to >1 yr before surgery; duration was not systematically defined in 62 studies (47.7%). Postoperative opioid use (n=53, 40.8%) and delirium or cognitive impairment (n=19, 14.6%) were the most frequently examined outcome domains, with most studies reporting adverse associations with chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use. CONCLUSIONS: Chronic preoperative benzodiazepine use is an inconsistently defined but clinically relevant perioperative exposure. As this scoping review did not include a risk-of-bias assessment, its findings map the evidence but cannot support causal inference. Standardised definitions and prospective studies are needed to inform perioperative medication optimisation.

items.title: Reference values and web-based tool for intraoperative heart rate and blood pressure in paediatric patients undergoing general anaesthesia for noncardiac procedures
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Heart rate (HR) and arterial blood pressure (BP) monitoring is standard of care during paediatric anaesthesia, yet evidence-based reference values for anaesthetised children remain limited. Existing BP reference values do not account for the combined effects of age, sex, weight, and height, and HR reference values in this population are lacking. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicentre study using data from the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group anaesthesia registry (2016-22). Included patients were aged <18 yr, ASA physical status 1 or 2, and undergoing noncardiac procedures under general anaesthesia. We used quantile regression to model the 2.3rd, 16th, 50th, 84th, and 97.7th centiles for HR, mean arterial pressure (MAP), systolic BP, and diastolic BP at two time points: the preparation phase (end of induction) and surgical phase (15-35 min after procedure start). Model covariates included age, sex, weight, and height. We selected the best model for each outcome using cross-validation with pinball loss. RESULTS: A total of 284 385 patients from 57 institutions were analysed. Optimal model complexity varied by outcome: a two-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for preparation phase HR and surgical phase MAP. A three-way interaction model was selected as the best-performing model for the remaining outcomes. Comprehensive prediction tables and an interactive web-based tool were developed for all outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: This study provides integrated HR and BP reference values for healthy paediatric patients undergoing general anaesthesia, incorporating age, sex, weight, and height simultaneously. These reference values with an interactive website can support clinical decision-making and haemodynamic monitoring.

Patient-reported disability has insufficient clinical accuracy for predicting physical function in survivors of critical illness: a secondary analysis of a cluster-randomised trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-ICU care often misses patients unable to attend in-person clinic visits. Remote assessments of physical function might increase access to ICU aftercare. We investigated whether patient-reported disability predicts handgrip strength (HGS) and the 2-Minute Walk Test (2MWT) distance with sufficient clinical accuracy. METHODS: This secondary analysis of the stepped-wedge cluster-randomised Enhanced Recovery after Intensive Care trial included patients from 10 German ICU clusters who completed the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS) 2.0 plus either HGS, the 2MWT, or both, 6 months after ICU discharge. Relationships between WHODAS 2.0, HGS, and 2MWT were analysed using scatter plots, correlation coefficients, linear regressions, and Bland-Altman plots. Predictions of HGS and the 2MWT were compared with the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for both measures. RESULTS: Of 1463 enrolled patients, 620 were analysed. The median WHODAS 2.0 sum score was 11 (Q1, Q3: 3, 22). The median HGS, expressed as a percentage of the expected value (%exp), was 70.6%exp (Q1, Q3: 54.4, 85.6), and the median 2MWT distance was 73.7%exp (Q1, Q3: 61.5, 85.8). The 2MWT was not completed by 59% of patients. Higher disability was moderately correlated with lower HGS (Spearman %exp: -0.41) and shorter 2MWT distance (Spearman %exp: -0.47). In multivariable regression models, the WHODAS 2.0 sum score predicted HGS in kg (β: -0.27 [95% CI: -0.33 to -0.22]; P<0.001) and 2MWT distance in m (β: -1.94 [95% CI: -2.37 to -1.51]; P<0.001), but the limits of agreement exceeded the MCIDs. CONCLUSIONS: With increasing disability, HGS and 2MWT performance declined, although correlations were moderate and uncertainty of predictions exceeded MCIDs of both instruments. Remote WHODAS 2.0 assessments cannot replace in-person physical function testing. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT03671447.

Differential effects of prone positioning and PEEP on ventilation/perfusion distribution across inflammatory ARDS subphenotypes: a porcine experimental study
items.abstract: Background ARDS comprises distinct inflammatory subphenotypes, including hyper- and hypo-inflammatory forms. Whether these differ in ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and response to ventilatory strategies remains unclear. Dual-energy CT enables regional assessment of aeration and perfusion. This experimental study aimed to compare V/Q mismatch between hyper- and hypo-inflammatory subphenotypes, and respective responses to PEEP and prone positioning. Methods In 10 pigs, hypo-inflammatory ARDS was induced by lung lavage followed by injurious ventilation. Hyper-inflammatory ARDS was produced by i.v. endotoxin infusion and fluid loading. Pigs were randomised to hypo- or hyperinflammatory ARDS, with similar oxygenation impairment. Dual-energy CT scans were obtained at individualised low, optimal, and high PEEP settings, in supine and prone positions. V/Q was derived from regional gas and blood volume and classified as low (<0.5), normal, or high (>2). Linear mixed-effects models included injury group, PEEP, and posture as fixed effects, and subject as a random effect. Results Hyper-inflammatory injury showed more severe V/Q mismatch than hypo-inflammatory injury (normal V/Q: 35% [sd=10] vs 51% [8] at low PEEP, supine position; P <0.01). Both PEEP optimisation and prone positioning improved V/Q. Prone positioning reduced high V/Q and dead space in hypo-inflammatory injury (group×posture interaction: F 1,50 =4.32, P =0.04), whereas PEEP reduced low V/Q and shunt in the supine position independent of ARDS subphenotype. Conclusions In porcine models of hyper- and hypo-inflammatory ARDS, hyper-inflammatory injury was associated with more severe V/Q mismatch despite similar oxygenation. Distinct responses to PEEP and prone positioning support a subphenotype-tailored approach to ventilatory management.

Electroencephalography-derived spectral edge frequency 95 targets in toddlers under propofol anaesthesia✰
items.abstract: Background Proprietary processed EEG indices are less accurate in young children. We evaluated spectral edge frequency 95 (SEF95), a nonproprietary EEG index representing the frequency below which 95% of total EEG power resides, to establish target thresholds for varying anaesthetic depths during propofol anaesthesia in toddlers. Secondary objectives were to assess the relationship between SEF95 and plasma propofol concentration, and to evaluate airway reactivity during laryngoscopy. Methods In this prospective study of toddlers aged 13 to 24 months, Dixon's up-and-down method and centred isotonic regression were used to determine the SEF95 targets for 50% (ED 50 ) and 90% (ED 90 ) probability of nonresponse to three clinical stimuli: pacifier placement (assessing consciousness), electrical nerve stimulation (nociception), and laryngoscopy (intubation readiness). Linear mixed-effects regression was used to analyse the association between plasma propofol concentration and SEF95. Results Among 51 toddlers, SEF95 ED 50 and ED 90 targets (Hz) were 21.8 (90% CI 20.8-23.4) and 20.3 (19.1-20.7) Hz for pacifier placement, 12.0 (10.8-18.3) and 10.4 (8.7-11.3) Hz for electrical stimulation, and 10.3 (4.6-11.8) and 4.4 (1.5-5.4) Hz for laryngoscopy. Each 1 Hz increase in SEF95 corresponded to a 0.21 μg ml -1 decrease in plasma propofol (r=0.46, P -1 )=5.80-0.21×SEF95 (Hz). Conclusions This study defined EEG SEF95 targets for loss of consciousness, response to noxious stimuli, and intubation readiness in toddlers aged 13 to 24 months. When combined with existing infant data, these age-specific SEF95 targets can optimise propofol titration and dosing accuracy during EEG-guided propofol anaesthesia in patients aged Clinical trial registration NCT05701748. The effects of ephedrine, phenylephrine, and norepinephrine on pregnant human myometrial contractility: an ex vivo study✰
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The choice of vasopressor during Caesarean delivery to prevent maternal hypotension remains debated. This study aimed to determine the concentration-dependent effects of vasopressors on pregnant myometrium, with and without oxytocin. METHODS: In this prospective ex vivo study, myometrial samples were obtained from full-term pregnant women during elective Caesarean delivery. Myometrial contractility to vasopressors was recorded in the absence/presence of oxytocin compared with controls. Concentration-response testing was done with ephedrine, phenylephrine, and norepinephrine. The primary outcome was the motility index (amplitude×frequency). Isolated primary myometrial cells were also used for calcium mobilisation assays. RESULTS: Myometrial samples were obtained from 32 females. The mean motility index increased with ephedrine (+39.9%; 95% CI 20.6-62.5; P<0.001) and phenylephrine (+36.2%; 95% CI 19.3-55.4; P<0.001), but norepinephrine had no effect (+12.0%; 95% CI -0.7 to 26.1; P=0.066) compared with control. Similar changes in motility index were observed in the presence of oxytocin. Calcium mobilisation recordings on primary myometrial cells supported the contractility findings, with increases in intracellular calcium ions after ephedrine and phenylephrine, but not with norepinephrine compared with control. CONCLUSIONS: Ephedrine and phenylephrine increased ex vivo human myometrial contractility, both independently and in combination with oxytocin, consistent with improving uterine tone during Caesarean delivery. Norepinephrine does not affect myometrial contractility, suggesting that it is safe to use before delivery.

items.title: Beyond difficult: matching airway risk to intervention
Rapid sequence induction: a narrative review
items.abstract: Introduction Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi‐element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. Methods We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. Results Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. Discussion There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision‐making; and practical conduct of the technique.

items.title: Causes of bias in Delphi studies and consensus statements: a methodological review
items.abstract: Introduction The Delphi methodology is a widely‐used tool for achieving expert consensus in healthcare, particularly in areas where empirical evidence is limited or uncertain. Despite its structured design, the Delphi process remains vulnerable to implicit cognitive biases that may influence judgement and group decision‐making. Such biases may inadvertently affect the quality of the consensus process, allow louder voices to influence outcomes, restrict inclusivity and undermine the validity, transparency and evidence‐based nature of recommendations. Methods We conducted a methodological review synthesising literature from cognitive psychology, behavioural science and methodological research on consensus development and Delphi processes. Using a concept‐mapping approach, established cognitive biases were mapped to different stages of the Delphi process, including study design; panel selection; survey development; iterative scoring; and consensus interpretation. Results Ten cognitive biases were organised into four domains reflecting different levels of influence within consensus development: steering‐group and design‐level biases, panel composition and contextual biases, social influence and conformity biases; and individual cognitive heuristic biases. A conceptual framework was developed to systematically identify these biases within Delphi‐based consensus studies. Examples illustrating how these biases may arise in healthcare Delphi processes are presented, alongside potential mitigation strategies. Discussion Recognition and mitigation of cognitive biases are essential for strengthening the methodological rigour and credibility of Delphi studies. Strategies to reduce bias include diversifying expert panels; using neutral language in survey statements; maintaining anonymity during voting; involving methodological expertise in Delphi design; and ensuring transparent iterative feedback. The framework needs prospective validation before its widespread use and may assist journal editors and peer reviewers in critically appraising Delphi studies and improving reporting standards in consensus research.

items.title: Videolaryngoscopy vs. direct laryngoscopy for tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors ( VILARE ): a pragmatic multicentre randomised trial
items.abstract: Introduction Videolaryngoscopy has been associated with improved glottic visualisation and higher first‐attempt tracheal intubation success compared with direct laryngoscopy. However, multicentre evidence evaluating its effectiveness when tracheal intubation is performed by anaesthesia resident doctors in routine practice is limited. Methods Adult patients undergoing surgery requiring tracheal intubation were assigned to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy for the initial attempt. All tracheal intubations were performed by anaesthesia residents under consultant supervision. The primary outcome was successful tracheal intubation on the first attempt. Secondary outcomes included glottic visualisation; number of tracheal intubation attempts; need for adjunct airway devices; procedural difficulty; and procedural complications. Results We enrolled 1001 patients and assigned 501 to videolaryngoscopy and 500 patients to direct laryngoscopy. Successful first‐attempt tracheal intubation was achieved in 397 (79.2%) patients allocated to the videolaryngoscopy group and 351 (70.2%) patients allocated to the direct laryngoscopy group (absolute risk difference 9.0%, 95%CI 3.7–14.4%, p < 0.001). Videolaryngoscopy improved glottic visualisation, with more patients having a modified Cormack–Lehane grade 2 or 2a view (467/501 (93.3%) vs. 404/500 (80.8%); p < 0.001); decreased operator‐reported tracheal intubation difficulty (168/501 (33.5%) vs. 236/500 (47.2%); p < 0.001) and reduced procedural complications (39/501 (7.7%) vs. 91/500 (18.2%); p < 0.001), without a clinically meaningful difference in tracheal intubation time or the need for adjunct airway devices. Discussion In adult patients undergoing tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors, videolaryngoscopy increased first‐attempt success and improved overall procedural performance compared with direct laryngoscopy.

items.title: Complications in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation: an analysis of the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry
items.abstract: Introduction Difficult tracheal intubation is associated with serious complications, including hypoxia, bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Neonates have increased physiologic vulnerability compared with older children, yet detailed data on management strategies and outcomes in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation remain limited. We hypothesised that clinicians have lower first‐attempt tracheal intubation success and higher complication rates for neonates compared with older children with difficult tracheal intubation. Methods We analysed the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry to determine tracheal intubation first attempt success and incidence of complications. We used logistic regression to identify variables associated with complications in neonates. Results During the study period, 6283 paediatric difficult tracheal intubations were recorded, including 420 neonates. First attempt success was lower for neonates (139/420, 33.1%) than older children (2394/4683, 51.1%). Complications occurred more frequently in neonates (123/420, 29.3%) than older children (637/4683, 13.6%). Hypoxia occurred in 92/420 (21.9%) neonates and 269/4683 (5.7%) older children. Severe complications were more frequent in neonates vs. older children (12/420, 2.9% vs. 30/4683, 0.6%, respectively), with cardiac arrests occurring in 4/420 (1.0%) neonates and 11/4683 (0.2%) older children. Difficult mask ventilation occurred more frequently in neonates (60/420, 14.3%) than older children (353/4681, 7.5%). In neonates, increased number of tracheal intubation attempts (aOR 1.61 per attempt, 95%CI 1.30–2.00, p < 0.001) and difficult facemask ventilation (aOR 3.17, 95%CI 1.38–7.30, p = 0.007) were associated with complications. Anticipated difficulty with airway management had a protective effect (aOR 0.37, 95%CI 0.16–0.88, p = 0.025). Discussion Neonates with difficult tracheal intubation experience a substantially higher rate of complications than older children. Early recognition of risk is critical in order to enable careful planning to minimise tracheal intubation attempts in this vulnerable population.

Sugammadex versus neostigmine for neuromuscular blockade reversal in adults
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Reversal of neuromuscular blockade (NMB) is a routine component of general anaesthesia with important implications for recovery quality and peri-operative safety. Recent changes in the cost of sugammadex, together with its efficacy and adverse effect profile relative to neostigmine, may influence its broader clinical use. OBJECTIVES To evaluate the efficacy and safety of sugammadex compared with neostigmine in adult patients. DESIGN Systematic review of randomised controlled trials with meta-analyses and trial sequential analyses. Certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grades of Recommendation, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework. This is an update of a 2017 Cochrane review. DATA SOURCES Online databases were searched up to December 2025. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA Randomised trials enrolling adults receiving rocuronium or vecuronium for elective procedures and comparing sugammadex with neostigmine were included. The outcomes included NMB recovery time and risk of various adverse events. RESULTS We included 165 trials with 19 124 participants. Risk of bias was generally unclear or high. NMB monitoring technique was reported in 113 trials, mostly acceleromyography. Time to reversal of NMB from second twitch to a train-of-four ratio more than 0.9 was shorter with sugammadex 2 mg kg -1 versus neostigmine 0.05 mg kg -1 (mean difference = -10.49 min (95% confidence interval, -11.90 to -9.08), GRADE: moderate). Sugammadex probably reduces the number of patients with at least one adverse event compared with neostigmine (risk ratio = 0.72 (95% confidence interval, 0.61 to 0.84), GRADE: moderate). When looking at specific adverse events, sugammadex probably reduces the risk of residual NMB, inadequate NMB reversal, desaturation, atelectasis, increased upper airway secretion, airway obstruction, bradycardia, dry mouth and urinary retention (GRADE: moderate). CONCLUSIONS Sugammadex probably reverses NMB more rapidly and with fewer adverse events than neostigmine. Broader use of sugammadex has the potential to improve peri-operative outcomes.

Postreperfusion venovenous bypass for hemodynamic stabilization in liver transplantation with hepatic outflow obstruction: a case report
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Chronic inferior vena cava (IVC) stenosis is an uncommon yet serious vascular complication that can significantly impact the success of liver transplantation. We report a case in which postreperfusion venovenous bypass (VVB) was used as a temporizing strategy to achieve hemodynamic stabilization in the setting of severe hepatic venous congestion caused by a fixed suprahepatic IVC obstruction. Clinical features A 58-yr-old male with a history of orthotopic liver transplantation complicated by recurrent IVC stenosis and end-stage kidney disease underwent a simultaneous liver and kidney transplant. Intraoperatively, dense fibrosis was encountered proximal to the suprahepatic IVC, preventing resection of the stenotic segment. Although the liver graft was successfully implanted and reperfused, severe hepatic congestion and refractory hemodynamic instability developed. Venovenous bypass was initiated to augment venous return and stabilize systemic hemodynamics. The kidney transplant was aborted owing to the patient's instability. Postoperatively, the patient initially tolerated the procedure, however, he ultimately died in the intensive care unit. Conclusions This case illustrates an unconventional postreperfusion application of VVB as a rescue measure for refractory hemodynamic instability. Given the presence of a fixed suprahepatic IVC obstruction, VVB only provided temporary hemodynamic support and did not result in graft recovery. This underscores the physiologic limitations of VVB in the presence of irreversible mechanical outflow obstruction and highlights the importance of early recognition and surgical adaptability in anatomically complex cases.

items.title: Types of adult intensive care units and admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023: a nationwide cohort study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Türkiye has one of the highest intensive care unit (ICU) bed capacities among middle-income countries but also globally. Nevertheless, little is known about the characteristics of ICUs in Türkiye, their temporal trends, and ICU admissions and readmissions. We sought to analyze the structural characteristics of all adult ICUs and the clinical profiles of ICU admissions across Türkiye. Methods We conducted a retrospective nationwide cohort study using data from the Turkish Ministry of Health National Electronic Database. We analyzed adult ICU admissions across all levels and types over 6 years (2018-2023) and documented patient demographics, comorbidities, admission diagnoses, and ICU outcomes. Results We retrieved data on 3,362,539 ICU admissions. Among 22 ICU types, mixed ICUs accounted for the highest proportion of admissions (31.4%), followed by coronary (23.7%), anesthesiology (14.3%), medical (6.1%), and surgical (6.0%) ICUs. The proportion of mixed ICU beds decreased from 44.0% in 2018 to 25.1% in 2023. Most ICU beds were in state (public) hospitals (50.8%), followed by private hospitals (34.8%). The number of ICU beds increased from 2019, with a notable rise in state hospitals after 2020. The average number of ICU admissions was 659 per 100,000 population annually. The median patient age was 65 [interquartile range, 39-91] yr, and the ICU mortality was 15.5%. The leading admission diagnoses were respiratory failure (10.1%), cerebrovascular disease (7.1%), and acute kidney injury (5.2%). Hypertension (67.5%) and coronary artery disease (44.8%) were common comorbidities, particularly in nonsurvivors. The 7-day ICU readmission rate was 3.0%. Conclusions The present comprehensive analysis of ICU admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023 highlights a shift toward specialization with a decrease in mixed ICUs. The impact of ICU diversity on resource use and patient outcomes requires further evaluation.

items.title: The relationship between early warning scores at intensive care unit discharge and risk of intensive care unit readmission in adult and pediatric populations: a scoping review
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Readmission after discharge from the intensive care unit (ICU) occurs globally at a rate of approximately 1-12% and is associated with adverse patient outcomes. Despite these findings, there is no internationally accepted tool to guide or standardize decisions regarding ICU discharge. In this scoping review, we aimed to evaluate the use of early warning scores (EWSs) measured at or around the time of ICU discharge as predictors of subsequent ICU readmission in adult and pediatric populations. Source With support from a medical librarian, we searched MEDLINE®, Embase®, and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature from database inception to December 14, 2025. We included quantitative observational and interventional studies that evaluated any EWS (e.g., National EWS [NEWS]/NEWS2, Modified EWS [MEWS], Pediatric EWS [PEWS], Rothman Index, Risk Scoring Index, or related tools) at ICU discharge, immediately prior to transfer, or immediately upon ward admission and reported unplanned ICU readmission following transfer to a hospital ward. Unplanned ICU readmissions were defined as any unplanned return to an ICU after discharge to the ward. We excluded studies in which patients were discharged to locations other than a ward (e.g., home, long-term care) or that focused solely on interfacility transfer. Screening and data extraction were performed in duplicate using a standardized template, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Principal findings The search identified 7,977 records, of which 4,824 remained after removal of duplicates. Of the articles, 58 underwent full-text review, and 20 studies met inclusion criteria. The studies were conducted across North America, Europe, and Asia and included both adult (n = 14) and pediatric (n = 6) populations. All were observational (retrospective or prospective) or pre-post intervention designs; no randomized controlled trials were identified. A range of tools were evaluated, including NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS, PEWS, the Rothman Index, the Risk Scoring Index, and several machine-learning-based EWS models. Of the 20 studies, 17 reported a significant association between higher EWS values at or near ICU discharge and increased risk of unplanned ICU readmission, while three found no significant association. Across studies, readmission rates and EWS thresholds varied, and there was considerable heterogeneity in populations, settings, and outcome time frames. The risk of bias was generally low to moderate across QUADAS-2 domains, although several studies had high or unclear risk in key areas-most commonly patient selection and index test blinding-limiting causal inference. Conclusions Most available studies report that higher EWS values at ICU discharge are associated with an increased likelihood of ICU readmission. Early warning scores may therefore serve as useful adjuncts to clinical judgement when assessing discharge readiness. Nevertheless, the current evidence base is limited by the absence of randomized or robust interventional trials, and substantial heterogeneity, which limits causal inference and the ability to determine whether EWS-guided discharge protocols improve outcomes. Further multicentre prospective studies are needed to determine whether EWS-guided discharge protocols improve patient outcomes, reduce readmissions, and optimize use of ICU resources.

items.title: Public perception of who is responsible for anesthesia-related care: a cross-sectional survey in Japan
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: PURPOSE: We aimed to assess the public perception of who is responsible for anesthesia-related hospital care tasks in Japan and examine associated factors. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional, nationwide, quota-based web survey of adults in Japan in July 2025. Of the 1,944 respondents who initiated the survey, 1,844 completed (94.9%) it, and 1,000 responses were analyzed after quota completion (ages 20-69 yr). The outcomes were attribution (yes/no) of four anesthesia-related hospital care tasks to anesthesiologists: intraoperative anesthesia, postoperative pain management, procedural sedation/analgesia (PSA), and labour neuraxial analgesia (LNA). For each outcome, we fitted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, the Health Interest Scale (HIS), Communicative and Critical Health Literacy (CCHL), board-certified anesthesiologist density, information sources, and task-matched experience, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) control. RESULTS: Attribution was highest for intraoperative anesthesia (84.7%), followed by LNA (65.2%), PSA (37.4%), and postoperative pain management (13.5%). After FDR control, university education or higher was associated with greater attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.30 to 3.32), PSA (aOR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.15 to 2.30), and LNA (aOR, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.30 to 2.55). Task-matched prior experience attributed to anesthesiologists was associated with higher attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (aOR, 3.75; 95% CI, 1.76 to 8.80) and PSA (aOR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.34 to 4.43). Fictional media was the only information-source factor that remained significant after FDR control (intraoperative anesthesia: aOR, 2.73; 95% CI, 1.79 to 4.25; PSA: aOR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.42 to 2.56). No factor met the FDR threshold for postoperative pain management. HIS, CCHL, and anesthesiologist density showed no consistent adjusted associations. CONCLUSIONS: Public attribution of anesthesiologists' roles in Japan varied by task. Educational attainment, task-matched experience, and information sources were more consistently associated with attribution than general health traits or workforce context, supporting the value of role-explicit, task-specific communication strategies.

items.title: Effect-site concentrations of remifentanil to suppress coughing during emergence from general anesthesia in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Remifentanil infusion titrated to effect-site concentration (Ce) is commonly used to suppress coughing during emergence from general anesthesia; nevertheless, the optimal Ce range remains unclear. We aimed to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize the existing evidence on the optimal Ce values of remifentanil for cough suppression during emergence. Source We performed a comprehensive literature search using PubMed®, Embase®, Web of Science™, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar on 27 February 2025. We included prospective studies that used the up-and-down method to estimate the effective concentrations of remifentanil in 50% of patients (EC 50 ) and 95% of patients (EC 95 ) for suppressing coughing during emergence from general anesthesia with tracheal intubation in adult patients. We excluded studies in children or patients undergoing cardiac surgery, as well as those that only compared predefined Ce targets of remifentanil to determine optimal dosing. We obtained pooled estimates using a random-effects model with inverse-variance method, and heterogeneity was quantified using the I 2 statistic. We assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool for randomized trials and the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies for nonrandomized comparative or single-arm studies. The primary outcome was EC 50 estimated using the up-and-down method, with secondary outcomes including model-based EC 50 and EC 95 estimates. Principal findings We included 22 prospective studies comprising 857 adult participants, and none were assessed as being at a high risk of bias or of low methodologic quality. Based on 28 groups and 653 participants across 17 studies, the pooled mean EC 50 from the up-and-down method was 2.0 ng·mL -1 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.8 to 2.3), with considerable heterogeneity (I 2 = 74.5%). Based on 29 groups and 693 participants across 18 studies, the model-based EC 50 was 1.9 ng·mL -1 (95% CI, 1.6 to 2.1), with considerable heterogeneity (I 2 = 96.1%). Based on 31 groups and 809 participants across 20 studies, the model-based EC 95 was 2.7 ng·mL -1 (95% CI, 2.5 to 3.0), with considerable heterogeneity (I 2 = 99.5%). Subgroup analyses revealed higher mean EC 50 values in male individuals (2.6 ng·mL -1 ) and the highest mean EC 50 in patients undergoing video-assisted thoracic surgery (2.6 ng·mL -1 ). Using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation framework, the certainty of evidence was rated as very low for all outcomes. Conclusions The identified EC 50 and EC 95 values of remifentanil for suppressing coughing during emergence from general anesthesia in adults were 2.0 and 2.7 ng·mL -1 , respectively. Patient sex and surgical type may influence the required Ce. Careful dose adjustment is recommended to avoid delayed awakening and hypoventilation, especially in cases requiring higher concentrations. Study registration PROSPERO ( CRD42024623581 ); first submitted 20 December 2024.

items.title: Video double-lumen tube intubation in a modified lateral position for unilateral video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: a randomized controlled trial
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: PURPOSE: We aimed to evaluate and report a protocol for video double-lumen tube (VDLT) intubation in a modified lateral position and evaluate whether it shortens in-room to cut time (IRCT; defined as the time from patient entry to incision) compared with conventional supine intubation in patients undergoing elective unilateral video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). METHODS: , mouth opening < 3 cm, Mallampati class 3-4, or anticipated difficult airway. Participants were randomized 1:1 to modified-lateral-position (Group L) or supine-position (Group S) VDLT intubation using a computer-generated sequence with sealed-envelope allocation concealment. Operators were unblinded; nonoperator staff collecting postoperative data and the outcome analyst were blinded to allocation. The primary outcome was IRCT. RESULTS: Sixty-two patients were randomized (Group L, N = 31; Group S, N = 31), and all were analyzed for the primary outcome. Mean (standard deviation [SD]) IRCT was shorter in Group L (18.1 [2.0] min) than in Group S (31.1 [3.3] min), with a mean difference (L-S) of -13.0 min (95% confidence interval [CI], -14.4 to -11.6; P < 0.001). Intubation time was similar (mean [SD], 103 [15] sec vs 97 [15] sec; P = 0.10). Video double-lumen tube malpositioning occurred in 1/31 (3%) cases in Group L vs 15/31 (48%) cases in Group S (relative risk [RR], 0.067; 95% CI, 0.009 to 0.474; P < 0.001). Sore throat within 48 h occurred in 9/31 (29%) patients in Group L vs 18/31 (58%) patients in Group S (RR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.94; P = 0.02). CONCLUSIONS: In patients undergoing unilateral VATS, VDLT intubation in a modified lateral position shortened IRCT. In exploratory analyses, several secondary outcomes favoured this approach. Intubation in a modified lateral position may be a feasible alternative to conventional supine position intubation in these patients. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ChiCTR.org.cn ( ChiCTR2500112254 ); first posted 21 October 2025.

items.title: Paratracheal air cysts and their associations with postoperative pulmonary complications in patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia: a retrospective propensity-score-matched study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Paratracheal air cysts are rare benign anatomical variants. Although case reports suggest that paratracheal air cysts may lead to complications such as difficult ventilation and pneumothorax in patients whose lungs are mechanically ventilated, their association with postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) remains unclear. We hypothesized that the presence of cysts is associated with an increased incidence of PPCs. Methods In the context of COVID-19, we conducted a retrospective study of all patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia in 2020. On the basis of the presence of paratracheal air cysts, we divided patients into two groups: the paratracheal air cyst group and the paratracheal-air-cyst‑free group. The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs. We used propensity score matching to adjust for confounding and performed multivariable logistic regression analysis in the matched cohort to assess the association. Results Among 7,208 patients, the prevalence of paratracheal air cysts was 2.0% (141/7,208). The incidence of PPCs was 22% (31/141) in the paratracheal air cyst group and 15% (43/280) in the paratracheal-air-cyst-free group. Multivariable regression analysis showed that, after adjusting for confounders, the presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs (adjusted odds ratio, 1.85; 95% confidence interval, 1.03 to 3.33; P = 0.04). Conclusions The presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs. Although this association warrants cautious interpretation due to possible residual confounding and lack of data on intraoperative ventilatory settings, anesthesiologists should consider the potential perioperative implications of this anatomical abnormality during preoperative assessment.

items.title: Development and implementation of an objective framework for measuring clinician faculty research contributions in a Canadian anesthesiology department
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Given the fiduciary responsibility of an academic clinical department to ensure appropriate use of funds to support research, the Department of Anesthesia, Pain Management and Perioperative Medicine at Dalhousie University (Halifax, NS, Canada) aimed to create a framework to support the allocation of remunerated protected research time to clinician faculty members within the department. Methods A departmental Research Accountability Project (RAP) was undertaken in the context of a quality improvement initiative. The RAP initially engaged clinician faculty members in the form of a survey, interviews, and a questionnaire to provide feedback regarding current practices for evaluating protected time for research. On the basis of this feedback, a working group created a list of 151 research outputs encompassing the breadth of research-related activities and assigned scores based on their relative merit. Clinicians with protected research time completed their academic profile, and individual point allocations were calculated. Scores were then weighted by different categories (e.g., publications, grant capture, presentations), and a RAP dashboard was developed to capture research outputs, assign scores, and generate a reporting/feedback mechanism for further analysis. Results Faculty members acknowledged the importance of clinicians having remunerated protected time to carry out research; nevertheless, there was scepticism with respect to how protected research time was managed. These data were then assessed by the working group, and using the RAP metric, individual researcher reports consisting of scores and recommendations were sent to the department head for final evaluation. These reports formed the basis of the researchers' annual academic performance review and consideration for continuance. Conclusions The RAP scoring system provides an objective measure of remunerated protected research time for clinicians to assist in researcher accountability.

items.title: Evaluation of deep learning for the modified Cormack–Lehane classification in videolaryngoscopic images: a prospective observational study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Predicting difficult intubation is still challenging, even with videolaryngoscopy. Videolaryngoscopy (VL) shows the larynx during intubation. The modified Cormack-Lehane (CL) classification grades laryngeal visibility but can vary between observers. Deep learning uses neural networks for objective, real-time airway image evaluation. We aimed to evaluate a YOLOv8-based model for object detection to automate modified CL grade classification from VL images in patients undergoing elective surgery. Methods In this prospective observational study, we developed a deep learning model using 346 VL images from 151 patients undergoing elective surgery. Two anesthesiologists classified images according to the modified CL system, and interobserver agreement was analysed using Cohen's kappa and weighted kappa. We split the data into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, with imbalance corrected via Albumentations augmentation. We evaluated the model results using sensitivity, specificity, and mean average precision with a 95% confidence interval (CI) and validated the model on 60 images not included in the training set. Results Interobserver agreement ranged from moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.66) to good (weighted kappa = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.84). In the test set, the overall recall rate was 0.87, and the specificity was 0.83. In the difficult intubation grades, recall and specificity were observed to be 0.79 (95% CI, 0.52 to 0.92) and 0.93 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.98), respectively, for CL grade 2b, and 0.60 and 1.00, respectively, for CL grade 3. In the external validation data set (n = 60), the model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.767 with a recognition rate of 0.925 for clinically relevant CL grades 2b and 3. Conclusions The YOLOv8-based model showed promising performance in classifying modified CL grades, particularly for clinically relevant difficult views (CL grades 2b-3). Nevertheless, wide CIs and limited external validation indicate uncertainty. The model may be considered an auxiliary tool rather than an independent decision system and requires further validation in larger, multicentre data sets.

items.title: Voluntariness of same-day versus advance consent in low-risk clinical research: a randomized controlled trial
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose The solicitation of same-day consent for participation in clinical research is commonly prohibited by research ethics boards because of concerns about limited decision-making time and patient vulnerability. However, these concerns lack empirical support and restrict both research efforts and patient participation opportunities, particularly in medical specialties such as emergency medicine, critical care, and anesthesiology, in which clinicians and patients interact for the first time on the day of a procedure. We aimed to assess the voluntariness of research consent solicited on the day of surgery compared with consent obtained in advance. Methods We performed a prospective, noninferiority randomized controlled trial examining the voluntariness of informed consent to participate in a low-risk clinical research trial at Women's College Hospital in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The trial design included active deception (invitation to participate in a fabricated research trial) to capture authentic measurements of participants' perceptions of any perceived coercion. Results We randomized 114 patients scheduled to undergo anterior cruciate ligament repair for recruitment into a fabricated low-risk perioperative research trial at one of two time points: at a virtual preanesthesia clinic appointment in advance of the day of surgery, or on the day of surgery. Regardless of their decision, all participants received the (same) standard of care. Overall, 71/114 patients (62%) either consented to participate in the fabricated trial or declined participation but consented to a feedback session during which perceptions of coercion were assessed. Greater participation was observed among patients approached on the day of surgery (fabricated trial, 26/58 [45%]; feedback session only, 18/58 [31%]) than in advance (fabricated trial, 17/56 [30%]; feedback session only, 10/56 [18%]). Perceived coercion, measured using two validated psychometric instruments, did not differ between patients recruited on the day of surgery and those recruited in advance. A subset of patients in each group reported modest perceptions of undue influence, but regardless of recruitment time point, these patients demonstrated their agency to decline participation. Conclusions Our findings suggest that restrictive same-day consent policies, when based on concerns regarding undue influence, may represent a structural barrier to participation in low-risk trials that lacks empirical justification. Study registrations 1) Open Science Framework ( 46twc ); first submitted 17 March 2023; 2) ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT07380035 ); first submitted 16 January 2026.
