Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy in adult intensive care: An ANZICS consensus statement
items.abstract: Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy (PDT) is a commonly performed procedure in intensive care units; However, the high-quality evidence base guiding many aspects of its practice remains limited, resulting in variation across clinicians and institutions. This statement was drafted by a panel of experts, later reviewed by an expert working group comprising representatives from the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society and the College of Intensive Care Medicine, and endorsed by the boards of both organisations. The recommendations presented are based on the best available evidence and, where evidence is scarce, on structured expert consensus. The scope of this statement is confined to PDT in adult intensive care patients. This document reflects current practice at the time of publication and is intended to be a living document, subject to regular review to include emerging evidence and evolving standards of care. In summary, this consensus statement provides evidence-informed, expert-guided recommendations to standardise PDT practice in adult ICUs across Australia and New Zealand, while acknowledging current variability and gaps in the evidence base.

items.title: Outcomes of SGLT2-inhibitor-induced euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis in a North Queensland intensive care unit: A retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Evidence on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i)-associated euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (EuDKA) in the intensive care unit (ICU) and its comparison with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is limited. This study aims to describe ICU characteristics, management and outcomes of SGLT2i-associated EuDKA, identify predictors of poorer outcomes and compare findings with T1DM-DKA. Single-centre retrospective cohort (2017–2023) of adults admitted to a Northern Queensland ICU. EuDKA was defined by plasma glucose <13.9 mmol/L plus ⩾1 of acidaemia, low bicarbonate, raised anion gap or ketonaemia, in patients with T2DM on SGLT2i. A comparator cohort comprised ICU admissions with T1DM-DKA. Demographics, precipitants, biochemistry, insulin therapy, and outcomes were extracted and analysed with non-parametric tests. Fourteen EuDKA and 31 T1DM-DKA admissions were included. EuDKA patients were older with more frequent comorbidities; First Nations Australians were over-represented. Presenting features were heterogeneous, with overlapping precipitants (commonly caloric restriction/fasting or intercurrent illness). Compared with T1DM-DKA, EuDKA had milder biochemical derangement and lower 24-h insulin dose but required longer insulin therapy and longer ICU length of stay; time to acidosis resolution was similar. In exploratory analyses, end-organ complications in type 2 diabetes were associated with longer ICU stay, while obesity and pre-admission insulin therapy were associated with prolonged acidosis duration. ICU-admitted SGLT2i-associated EuDKA differs clinically and in management from classical T1DM-DKA. Findings highlight diagnostic challenges, potential high-risk subgroups, and the need for prospective, multicentre studies to inform risk-based management in critical care.

items.title: Boerhaave’s syndrome complicated by pneumorrhachis and chemical meningitis
items.abstract: Boerhaave’s syndrome is a life-threatening condition characterised by oesophageal perforation. This report presents a case of Boerhaave’s syndrome complicated by pneumorrhachis (air in the spinal canal) and chemical meningitis. A 26-year-old male developed meningism and an agitated delirium following oesophageal rupture, with imaging confirming pneumorrhachis and cerebrospinal fluid analysis consistent with chemical meningitis. Despite a prolonged Intensive Care Unit stay complicated by encephalopathy and severe agitation, the patient made a full neurological recovery with supportive care. This case illustrates a unique pathophysiological progression and underscores the importance of early recognition, exclusion of bacterial meningitis, appropriate prognostication and multidisciplinary management of pneumorrhachis complicating Boerhaave’s syndrome.

items.title: Anaesthetic scavenging: a brief history
items.abstract: Anaesthesia and Intensive CareThe odour from a single drop of ether can be distinctly perceived all over the operating theatre. . . the surgeon, and others who have been about the patient, also smell of the ether to a lesser degree. 1 John Snow.On chloroform and other anaesthetics, 1858While John Snow recognised that ether anaesthesia resulted in detectable levels of ether in the operating room, he stopped short of attributing harm to this phenomenon.It was not until the 1920s that surgeons began expressing concerns that exposure to anaesthetic vapours was influencing their performance, causing headaches and worsening fatigue.2,3 Given all the other stressors that surgeons experienced, no direct link could be established, but air sampling revealed that low levels of ether vapour in operating rooms were ameliorated to a certain extent by improving ventilation in the theatre.4 More immediate and obvious was the risk of fires from ether permeating the theatre.These were often due to static electricity which was difficult to avoid without complex grounding measures.5 Consequently fires were frequent-usually transient, but not without risk to both patient and theatre staff.The fire risk, and the pungent smell of ether drew everyone's attention to ether pollution in the operating theatre.

items.title: Quantitative investigation of airway lumen and area changes before and after surgical tracheostomy using CT imaging: A multicentre retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Post-tracheostomy airway narrowing may be observed after decannulation, but its persistence and clinical significance remain uncertain; quantitative evidence describing post-tracheostomy tracheal changes remains limited. This multicentre retrospective cohort study aimed to quantify computed tomography (CT)-based changes in tracheal area and minimal diameter before tracheostomy and after decannulation and to characterise the longitudinal anatomical variability of post-tracheostomy airway changes. Adult patients who underwent surgical tracheostomy between 2014 and 2024 across five affiliated hospitals were reviewed. Inclusion required both pre-tracheostomy and post-decannulation CT imaging. The tracheal area and minimal diameter were measured at the narrowest axial slice between C6 and T2. Among 4660 tracheostomy patients, 300 met eligibility. Post-decannulation CT demonstrated a mean 13.6% reduction in tracheal area (−52.8 mm 2 ) and 11.2% reduction in diameter (−2.2 mm). Airway narrowing tended to be greater in patients undergoing tracheostomy for head and neck surgery. Tube sizes showed no clear pattern with airway reduction. Of 123 patients later re-intubated, 47.2% required a smaller endotracheal tube, and 12.2% needed multiple tube size attempts. Longitudinal analysis showed substantial inter-individual variability, with no clear temporal trend in recovery. In this multicentre cohort, surgical tracheostomy was followed by modest but measurable decreases in tracheal area and diameter after decannulation. These findings provide descriptive CT-based data on post-tracheostomy airway narrowing and highlight the need for further studies linking anatomical changes with functional airway outcomes.

items.title: The incidence of postoperative hypotension among non-cardiac surgical specialties: A single-centre retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Postoperative hypotension is associated with increased risk of postoperative complications and mortality. There are limited studies quantifying the incidence of this potentially life-threatening condition among different surgical cohorts. We aimed to describe and compare the incidence of postoperative hypotension in the first 48 h after leaving the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) across different surgical specialties after non-cardiac surgery. We conducted a single-centre retrospective study at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. The primary outcome was postoperative hypotension (systolic blood pressure (SBP) <90 mmHg) within 48 h after surgery and discharge from PACU, noted on routine blood pressure monitoring or a requirement for postoperative vasopressor or inotropic support. We estimated odds ratios (OR) using mixed-effects logistic regression models to account for multiple surgical procedures within the same patient. We identified 11,634 surgeries from 17 specialties, of which 47.3% were emergency operations. The median age was 53 years (interquartile range 35–68), with 42.2% being female and 42.5% of patients on regular antihypertensive medication. The overall incidence of ward hypotension was 4.4%. Trauma had the highest rate of postoperative hypotension (27.3%), followed by thoracic surgery (11.6%). Surgical specialties that had a higher risk of hypotension included trauma surgery (OR 13.0, 95% confidence interval (CI) 3.7–46.0) and thoracic surgery (OR 3.6, 95% CI 2.3–5.5). Specialties with a lower risk of hypotension included breast and endocrine surgery (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2–0.7) and plastic surgery (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.3–0.6). Postoperative hypotension is relatively common with substantial variation in incidence between surgical specialties. These findings highlight the need for heightened vigilance for hypotension in certain patients.

items.title: Translating evidence into practice: Deimplementation of routine chest radiography after cardiothoracic drain removal
A case of massive gamma-hydroxybutyrate overdose mimicking brain death
items.abstract: A 36-year-old female was brought into hospital following a massive overdose of 100 ml of gamma-hydroxybutyrate. Unlike prior case reports where ethanol was a co-ingestant with gamma-hydroxybutyrate or its precursor, gamma-hydroxybutyrate was believed to have been the only substance ingested in this case. The patient developed a severe and persistent high anion gap metabolic acidosis and required continuous renal replacement therapy. The patient developed fixed and dilated pupils early on in her clinical course and was found to have a transient loss of most brainstem reflexes on clinical examination, thus mimicking brain death. She also developed generalised tonic-clonic seizures and received midazolam and levetiracetam for seizure control. She was successfully extubated after 5 days on mechanical ventilation and was discharged home on day 11 with no neurological deficits.

items.title: A sympathetic solution: Brachial plexus blockade for suspected adrenaline-induced vasospasm
items.abstract: Vasospasm threatens perfusion across recently reconstructed vessels. Systemic adrenaline, (epinephrine) the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, is a potent vasoconstrictor, and therefore represents a potential, albeit necessary, threat to newly reconstructed vessels. Brachial plexus blockade may dampen localised vasoconstriction, allowing for improved vascular perfusion and reduced risk of vasospasm. An adult male sustained a workplace injury resulting in an open fracture-dislocation of the distal radius and fracture and accompanying radial and ulnar artery transections, requiring a vein graft repair to both vessels and external fixation of the radius and ulna. At 36 h post-operatively, the patient developed anaphylaxis to intravenous amoxicillin–clavulanic acid, requiring boluses and subsequent infusion of adrenaline for anaphylaxis management. Within minutes, the affected limb distal to the arterial repair became pale, cold, pulseless and painful. Adrenaline-induced vasospasm was presumed after multidisciplinary discussion. An ultrasound-guided supraclavicular brachial plexus block using 20 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine was performed as a salvage measure while surgical re-exploration was being considered. Perfusion and pain improved within minutes and had a sustained effect in the setting of adrenaline infusion. The infusion was ceased after 8 h, and the block resolved after approximately 12 h without recurrence of vasospasm. Re-exploration was not required, given the clinical suspicion and subsequent improvement post-block. Brachial plexus block performed for presumed adrenaline-induced vasospasm restored vascular perfusion, by presumed selective blockade of sympathetic ganglion that is responsible for local vasoconstriction, while not counteracting the systemic effects of IV adrenaline administration.

items.title: Association between prior epidural labour analgesia and increased incidence of hypotension after spinal anaesthesia for caesarean section: A retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study
items.abstract: The administration of spinal anaesthesia after epidural labour analgesia may increase the risk of block failure or high spinal block, particularly when the intrathecal local anaesthetic dose is reduced. This retrospective, propensity score-matched cohort study evaluated the feasibility of using a standard spinal dose in partients (i.e. women who are in labour) with epidural labour analgesia undergoing caesarean section. Women who underwent caesarean delivery between April 2016 and March 2020 were analysed. The primary outcome was the rate of conversion to general anaesthesia. After 161 patients had been matched in the epidural labour analgesia-to-spinal anaesthesia and spinal anaesthesia groups, general anaesthesia conversion rates were comparable (3.3% vs 2.5%, P = 0.544); all conversions resulted from block failure. However, the epidural labour analgesia-to-spinal anaesthesia group experienced significantly more frequent hypotension (55.9% vs 30.4%, P < 0.001) and required higher doses of ephedrine (mean 8.3, standard deviation 9.8 mg vs mean 5.9, standard deviation 11.1 mg, P = 0.036). Although epidural labour analgesia did not increase the rates of block failure or high spinal block when preventive strategies were utilised, it was associated with a higher incidence of hypotension and increased vasopressor requirements.

items.title: Perioperative methadone: Clinical use and knowledge among Australian anaesthetists
items.abstract: Intravenous methadone has re-emerged as a perioperative analgesic, yet uncertainty persists regarding its optimal use. Variation in clinician practice and interpretation of pharmacological principles may influence its safe and effective application. We conducted a mixed-methods survey-based study within a national anaesthesia educational programme (ADVANCE). A voluntary, anonymous pre-presentation clinician survey was distributed to predominantly Australian anaesthetists to characterise methadone use, dosing strategies, adjunct prescribing and patient selection. Real-time audience polling during the educational session assessed clinician responses to pharmacology-based and clinical decision-making scenarios. Survey and polling datasets were analysed independently using descriptive statistics. A total of 726 clinicians completed the survey. Overall, 50.6% ( n = 367) of respondents reported using methadone. Among users ( n = 367), practice varied widely across surgical contexts and dosing strategies, including weight-based, fixed and procedure-dependent approaches. Concurrent administration of additional opioids and central nervous system depressants was common (86.1%). Clinicians reported avoiding methadone in specific patient groups, most frequently frail patients, those with prolonged QT interval, or obstructive sleep apnoea. Polling responses demonstrated variability in clinician interpretation of pharmacological principles, particularly regarding timing of central effects. Perioperative methadone use is characterised by substantial variation in uptake, dosing and adjunct prescribing. Variability in clinician responses relative to pharmacological reference data, combined with frequent co-administration of additional opioids and sedatives, highlights potential areas for targeted education and institutional safeguards to support safe implementation.

items.title: Freshwater drowning with profound hypofibrinogenaemia and refractory vasoplegic shock
items.abstract: We present a challenging case of freshwater drowning complicated by profound hypofibrinogenaemia and refractory vasoplegic shock in a 39-year-old male admitted following an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The constellation of physiological and laboratory abnormalities initially precluded a unifying diagnosis. The haemolysis, hyper-fibrinolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation observed in our patient were likely sequelae of freshwater drowning and cardiac arrest. The refractory vasoplegic shock necessitated rescue off-label administration of hydroxocobalamin, resulting in restoration of haemodynamic stability.

items.title: Audit of procedural sedation in a remote Australian hospital 2010 – 2021
items.abstract: Procedural sedation is commonly provided in rural hospitals; however, there is little published safety data. The authors conducted a retrospective audit of anaesthetic records from 2010 to 2021 of procedural sedation in a remote hospital in South Australia. The data were collected from 1912 cases, which were provided mainly for gastroenterology procedures in day case theatre and emergency department settings. Sedation was provided by a general practitioner anaesthetist giving boluses of fentanyl, midazolam and propofol. All patients were low risk (American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status 1–3). There were few anaesthetic problems and no mortality during sedation or in the recovery area. The most common problem was desaturation requiring airway support and oxygen, and occurred in 2% of cases. Procedural sedation was practiced safely in this remote setting.

items.title: Comment on: Postoperative management after oesophagectomy – An evidence-based approach

Diagnostic agreement between the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition criteria and Subjective Global Assessment for preoperative malnutrition in adults undergoing elective surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Protein-energy malnutrition remains frequently unrecognised, under-reported, and undertreated in surgical populations despite being associated with a higher risk of postoperative complications. This systematic review evaluated the diagnostic agreement between the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) operational criteria and the Subjective Global Assessment for identifying adults at risk of preoperative protein-energy malnutrition undergoing elective surgery. MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 5 May 2025. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across eight included studies ( n =5834) in the definitions, cut-offs, and measurement methods for GLIM phenotypic and aetiologic criteria. In six noncardiac surgical studies ( n =3999), pooled sensitivity and specificity were 76% (95% confidence interval [CI] 69–81%) and 88% (95% CI 77–94%), respectively, using a random-effects bivariate model (very low certainty of evidence). Overall diagnostic agreement was fair; thus, the GLIM criteria alone may be insufficient to make the diagnosis of malnutrition and to guide nutritional interventions without additional clinical or dietetic assessment.

items.title: Practice patterns of midazolam administration in patients undergoing cardiac-related non-operating room procedures: analysis of a US anaesthesia database
items.abstract: Background Midazolam can be administered as an anxiolytic, a cardio-stable sedative, or an anaesthetic agent during non-operating room anaesthesia (NORA) procedures. Guidelines suggest avoidance in older or frail patients, and current practices are unknown. We hypothesised that there would be significant variation in midazolam administration for cardiac-related NORA procedures by attending and institutional characteristics, in addition to patient characteristics. Methods This is a retrospective observational analysis of a multi-institution US-centric electronic health record dataset including all adult patients undergoing cardiac-related NORA procedures in the Multicenter Perioperative Outcomes Group database from 2015 to 2022. The primary aim of the study was to identify the proportion of total variance in midazolam administration attributable to patient-, attending-, and institutional-level factors. The secondary aim was to identify practice pattern variations in the dosage and timing of midazolam administration. The primary outcome was any midazolam administration ≤1 h before anaesthesia start to 1 h after anaesthesia end. Secondary outcomes included total dose and timing of midazolam administration. Variance in midazolam administration attributable to patient, attending, and institutional factors was calculated with intraclass correlation coefficients following multilevel mixed-effects generalised linear models, in which a three-level nesting structure was assumed: patients nested within attendings and attendings nested within institutions. For the primary outcome, a binomial distribution and logit link function was specified. For the secondary outcome of total midazolam, the same three-level nesting structure was used, and covariates were modelled using a multilevel mixed-effects model specifying a Gaussian distribution and identity link function. Results A total of 246 918 cardiac-related NORA procedures with care provided by 5212 unique anaesthesia attendings across 63 institutions with a median case volume of 9 (inter-quartile range [IQR] 2–37) were included in the analysis. Midazolam was administered in 33.0% of patients ( n =81 602), including 25.5% of patients aged ≥65 yr ( n =40 469). Midazolam administration declined from 50.7% of patients in 2015 to 29.0% in 2022 ( P <0.001). The median dose was 2 mg (IQR 2–2), with 89.9% administered before procedure start. For transoesophageal echocardiography procedures, it was estimated that 37.0% of midazolam administration (30.4–44.3) was attributable to attending variation and 26.4% (19.2–35.2) to the institution, assuming that 36.6% of the variation was attributable to known patient factors. For transcatheter/endovascular procedures, attending, institution, and patient factors accounted for 45.7% (39.0–52.6), 27.7% (19.7–37.4), and 26.6%, respectively. Conclusions Although patient-level factors accounted for a meaningful proportion of variability, substantial variation in midazolam administration was also attributable to attending- and institution-level factors. Further studies on clinical outcomes and patient experience associated with this type of midazolam administration have the potential to inform future practice.

items.title: Daily debriefings, burnout, and impostor phenomenon in anaesthesiology trainees and supervisors: a controlled feasibility study
items.abstract: Burnout is a growing concern in anaesthesiology. In the UK, one in four consultants has considered leaving the National Health Service within 5 yr, citing mental health deterioration.1 Anaesthesiologists work under sustained time, legal, and economic pressure, which can drive the emotional exhaustion (EE), depersonalisation (DP), and reduced accomplishment that constitute burnout.2 In academic hospitals, board-certified anaesthesiologists fulfil their clinical duties while supervising and teaching trainees, who are themselves highly exposed: burnout symptoms affect 38–85% of trainees in published surveys.

items.title: Effects of propofol- or sevoflurane-containing anaesthesia on auditory brainstem responses in children: a systematic review
items.abstract: Background Auditory brainstem response (ABR) provides objective hearing assessment in children who cannot undergo reliable behavioural audiometry. Sedation or general anaesthesia may facilitate recording but can alter electrophysiological measurements and potentially influence diagnostic interpretation. The primary aim of this systematic review was to explore electrophysiological and diagnostic outcomes of paediatric ABR testing when at least one study condition included propofol or sevoflurane. Methods This Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 systematic review was prospectively registered in International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261324873). PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from inception, with searches updated on 17 August 2026. Two reviewers independently screened the original search; one reviewer screened the later update. Because of clinical and methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. Results The database searches identified 2386 records and yielded six eligible studies. Citation checking identified one additional study, giving seven in total. Four studies reported longer wave V latency under anaesthesia than under their respective comparators, but co-administered agents and differing populations preclude drug-specific attribution. In a within-participant comparison, hearing-loss classification differed between sevoflurane and propofol; a later observational cohort found no significant adjusted association for its distinct exposure groups. Conclusions Four of seven studies reported longer ABR electrophysiological wave V latency under anaesthesia, but five studies had a high risk of bias. A single study with within-participant comparison found different diagnostic classifications under sevoflurane and propofol. Heterogeneous designs and exposures do not establish which anaesthesia technique best preserves paediatric ABR findings.

items.title: Prognostic value of growth differentiation factor 15 in older patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery: a prospective observational study at a tertiary hospital
items.abstract: Background Emergency abdominal surgery in frail older patients carries a high risk of mortality and cardiovascular complications. Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF-15) is a strong prognostic marker across different patient populations and may improve perioperative risk stratification. We assessed associations between preoperative GDF-15 concentrations and postoperative outcomes in older patients undergoing emergency abdominal surgery. Methods This preplanned secondary biomarker substudy of the ProPEL cohort included 142 patients aged ≥75 yr undergoing emergency abdominal surgery between January 2020 and April 2021. The primary endpoint was 30-day all-cause mortality. Secondary endpoints were 90-day mortality and 30-day mortality or major adverse cardiac events (MACEs). Intraoperative blood transfusion was added as a post hoc exploratory analysis. Results Overall, 30-day all-cause mortality was 12% (17/142). Mortality was 31% (11/36) in the highest GDF-15 quartile compared with 6% (2/35 or 2/36) in each of the lower quartiles. Each doubling of GDF-15 was associated with increased 30-day mortality (hazard ratio: 1.75, 95% confidence interval: 1.15–2.66, P =0.009) independent of age, sex, and Clinical Frailty Scale, and in a model adjusted for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T hazard ratio 1.65 (1.03–2.65), P=0.037. GDF-15 predicted 30-day death or MACE, adjusted for age, sex, and Clinical Frailty Scale, but not after adjusting for high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T. Associations with 90-day mortality were attenuated after adjustment. A doubling of GDF-15 concentrations was associated with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.90 (95% confidence interval 1.29–2.78, P =0.001) for intraoperative blood transfusion. Conclusions GDF-15 was associated with 30-day mortality and the need for blood transfusion in older adults undergoing acute abdominal surgery.

items.title: Glutamate infusion and the incidence of acute kidney injury after coronary artery bypass grafting in relation to preoperative risk and baseline kidney function
items.abstract: Background Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and serious complication after cardiac surgery, with limited preventive strategies. Glutamate supplementation may reduce AKI indirectly by enhancing recovery of post-ischaemic myocardial metabolism and function; however, its metabolic effects appear attenuated in diabetic hearts. We investigated the association between glutamate infusion and postoperative AKI in patients without diabetes mellitus undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), according to preoperative risk and kidney function. Methods This post hoc analysis pooled data from two randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled GLUTAMICS trials. Patients without diabetes mellitus undergoing CABG with or without concomitant valve surgery were allocated to i.v. 0.125 M L-glutamic acid or saline. AKI was defined as a postoperative increase in plasma creatinine ≥50% from baseline (RIFLE risk stage or higher) and analysed according to European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II (EuroSCORE II) quartiles and estimated creatinine clearance. Results Among 791 patients, 391 received glutamate and 400 received placebo. In the combined two highest EuroSCORE II quartiles, AKI incidence was lower with glutamate (8.0% vs 16.8%; relative risk [RR] 0.47; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.27–0.84; P =0.011). Among patients with an estimated creatinine clearance of ≥50 ml min −1 , AKI occurred in 2.7% vs 9.6% (RR 0.28; 95% CI 0.14–0.58; P <0.001). No benefit was observed with severe preoperative kidney dysfunction (estimated creatinine clearance <50 ml min −1 ). Significant interactions were observed between glutamate allocation and preoperative risk ( P =0.025) and severe preoperative kidney dysfunction ( P =0.027). Conclusions Glutamate infusion was associated with a lower incidence of AKI in higher-risk patients without diabetes mellitus, particularly those without severe preoperative kidney dysfunction. These exploratory findings require prospective confirmation. Trial registration number ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT00489827 and NCT02592824).

Decision support and automation in goal-directed fluid therapy: current evidence and remaining questions
items.abstract: Goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) individualizes perioperative fluid administration according to dynamic hemodynamic variables, but its implementation remains inconsistent and its impact on patient-centered outcomes is still debated. Decision-support and automated systems have been developed to improve adherence, identify fluid responsiveness more efficiently, and reduce the workload of protocolized hemodynamic management. This structured narrative review summarizes the evidence across four outcome levels: process, surrogate hemodynamic, intermediate physiological, and patient-centered clinical. The most consistent evidence concerns process improvement: decision support increases protocol adherence and improves the proportion of fluid challenges that achieve a predefined stroke volume response, largely on non-randomized evidence. Improvements in surrogate hemodynamic control have also been reported, and selected randomized trials suggest favorable effects on microcirculatory flow and lactate. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical benefit. Fluid responsiveness does not necessarily indicate a need for fluid administration, and most available studies remain small, single-center, or focused on surrogate outcomes. Evidence that these systems improve postoperative complications, acute kidney injury, length of stay, or mortality is currently lacking. Ongoing multicenter trials should address this gap. Decision support appears to improve how perioperative fluids are administered, but whether it improves what ultimately happens to patients remains unresolved.

items.title: Factors associated with the ionized-to-total magnesium ratio in major hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgery: a single-center prospective observational study
items.abstract: Purpose To identify perioperative factors associated with the ionized-to-total magnesium (iMg/tMg) ratio at intensive care unit (ICU) admission and on postoperative day (POD) 1 after major open hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgery. Methods This single-center prospective observational study enrolled adults undergoing elective surgery. Paired iMg and tMg measurements were obtained at ICU admission and on POD 1. The primary analyses evaluated perioperative factors associated with the iMg/tMg ratio at each time point using univariable linear regression and multivariable linear regression with backward elimination. Exploratory analyses assessed temporal changes using paired t tests. Results Of 150 enrolled patients, 141 were analyzed. At ICU admission, the ratio was positively associated with iMg immediately after anesthesia induction (P = 0.007) and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (P = 0.041), and negatively associated with anesthesia time (P = 0.005) and total cholesterol (P = 0.018). On POD 1, the ratio was positively associated with intraoperative non-Mg-containing fluid volume (P = 0.016), and negatively associated with operation time (P < 0.001), hypertension (P = 0.013), and albumin (P = 0.007). Model R 2 values were 0.10 and 0.20 at ICU admission and on POD 1, respectively. In exploratory analyses, the mean ratio increased between postoperative measurements (0.659 to 0.713; P < 0.001). Mean iMg decreased from 0.589 mmol/L after induction to 0.545 at ICU admission, then increased to 0.640 on POD 1 (all P < 0.001). Conclusion Perioperative factors associated with the iMg/tMg ratio differed between ICU admission and POD 1 after major open hepatobiliary-pancreatic surgery. Both models had limited explanatory power. These findings should be interpreted in relation to sampling time and require independent validation before informing clinical management.

items.title: Right- versus left-sided double-lumen tubes and hypoxemia during anesthesia in patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors
items.abstract: Purpose Right-sided double-lumen endobronchial tubes (DLTs) are often avoided because of technical difficulties and concerns about respiratory complications, although evidence that they increase hypoxemia during anesthesia remains limited and inconsistent. We evaluated the association between DLT side and hypoxemia during anesthesia in patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors. Methods This single-center retrospective cohort study included adult patients undergoing unilateral surgery for left-sided lung tumors between October 2008 and May 2023. The primary outcome was hypoxemia during anesthesia, defined as SpO 2 ≤ 90% for at least 3 consecutive min during the anesthetic period. Propensity score overlap weighting was used to adjust for measured differences between patients receiving right-sided and left-sided DLTs. Odds ratios (ORs) and absolute risk differences (RDs) were estimated. Results Among 1,280 patients, 842 received right-sided DLTs and 438 received left-sided DLTs. After overlap weighting, measured covariates were well balanced. The incidence of hypoxemia during anesthesia was 20.0% with right-sided DLTs and 18.5% with left-sided DLTs (OR, 1.10; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.68-1.79; P = 0.70). The RD was 1.51 percentage points (95% CI - 3.86-6.87). No clear between-group differences were observed in exploratory secondary respiratory outcomes. Conclusion We found no clear evidence that right-sided DLT use was associated with a higher incidence of hypoxemia during anesthesia than left-sided DLT use. However, equivalence between the two devices was not established, and further studies are needed to determine whether clinically important differences in hypoxemia risk exist.

Comparison of gasping breaths induced by three commonly used volatile anesthetics in mice
items.abstract: Background Previous studies showed that administration of inhaled 2-MAC sevoflurane induces gasping in mice by activating a persistent sodium current in the brainstem, an effect blocked by riluzole. However, whether other commonly used volatile anesthetics elicit a similar gasping response in mice has not previously been investigated. This study compared respiratory responses to high doses of three volatile anesthetics. Methods Seven spontaneously breathing adult mice each inhaled one of three anesthetics (sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane) on separate days, and eventually inhaled all three anesthetics. Each anesthetic concentration was increased from 1 MAC to inhaled 2-MAC, while breathing patterns and suprahyoid muscle electromyographic activity (EMG SH ) were measured. The effects of riluzole (18 mg/kg, i.p.) on gasping were also tested in five additional mice anesthetized with desflurane and/or isoflurane. Results All three inhaled anesthetics altered the respiratory pattern from eupnea in 1 MAC to gasping in inhaled 2-MAC in seven mice. However, the time course of ventilation and EMG SH responses to volatile anesthetics at inhaled 2-MAC differed significantly among the three agents: desflurane had the strongest inhibitory effect on inspiratory and EMG SH activities, isoflurane had the weakest inhibitory effects and promoted stable gasping, and sevoflurane showed an intermediate effect. In addition, riluzole administration eliminated isoflurane- and desflurane-induced gasping in five mice. Conclusion All three anesthetics produced a similar gasping response at inhaled 2-MAC; however, the response's time course and the mechanism by which stable gasping was maintained depend heavily on the volatile anesthetic used.

items.title: Perioperative factors associated with postoperative continuation of mechanical ventilation after initial burn surgery: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Purpose Early surgical intervention, including debridement and grafting, is crucial in acute burn injury management. Although early extubation in operating rooms (ORs) reduces intensive care unit length of stay and ventilator-associated complications, extubation feasibility following initial burn surgery remains uncertain. We investigated perioperative factors associated with postoperative continuation of mechanical ventilation (MV) after initial burn surgery. Methods This retrospective study analyzed patients with burns who underwent acute-phase debridement between 2018 and 2024. Patients requiring postoperative MV were compared with those extubated in ORs. Factors independently associated with postoperative MV were identified using multivariate logistic regression analysis. Results Among 418 patients, 75 required postoperative MV. Age (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.00-1.06), percentage of total body surface area (%TBSA) burned (aOR = 1.08, 95% CI 1.03-1.12), preoperative intubation (aOR = 11.8, 95% CI 3.02-46.4), intraoperative fluid administration volume (ml/kg) (aOR = 1.04, 95% CI 1.01-1.06), and intraoperative maximum vasoactive-inotropic score (VIS) (aOR = 1.18, 95% CI 1.10-1.26) were independently associated with postoperative MV continuation. This association between the intraoperative maximum VIS and postoperative MV continuation was maintained in the sensitivity analysis excluding preoperatively intubated patients (aOR = 1.16, 95% CI 1.08-1.25). Conclusion Age, %TBSA burned, preoperative intubation, intraoperative fluid administration volume, and maximum intraoperative VIS were independently associated with postoperative continuation of MV after initial burn surgery. Maximum intraoperative VIS may provide additional information regarding the hemodynamic component of perioperative severity by quantifying the intensity of vasoactive and inotropic support required during surgery.

items.title: Intraoperative bedside lung-ultrasound use to optimize positive end-expiratory pressure for elective robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy or cystectomy: a randomized clinical trial
items.abstract: Purpose This study evaluated efficacy and safety of intraoperative individualized stepwise positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) titration guided by lung ultrasound (LUS) in reducing pulmonary atelectasis and complications in patients undergoing robotic-assisted radical prostatectomy or cystectomy (RARPC). Methods This randomized trial included 88 patients undergoing elective RARPC. Patients were assigned to either standard ventilation (PEEP 4 cmH₂O; group C) or LUS-guided stepwise PEEP titration up to 12 cmH₂O (group R). Patients, outcome assessors, and the data analyst were blinded. The primary outcome was analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model, estimating the between-group difference in LUS score at 2 h after surgery. Results Group R showed significantly lower total LUS scores at 2 h after surgery (adjusted difference: -1.68, 95%CI: -2.89 to -0.47; p = 0.007) compared to group C. Likewise, significantly lower LUS scores were observed in Group R from the end of surgery onward. PEEP titration progressively reduced post-pneumoperitoneum atelectasis rates from 50% to 9.1%, at a highest PEEP level of 12 cmH₂O. Dynamic lung compliance in group R was significantly greater at Top compared with the control group (58.93 ± 3.48 vs. 49.91 ± 5.74 mL/cmH₂O; p Conclusion Intraoperative LUS-guided individualized PEEP optimization significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative atelectasis and improved dynamic lung compliance without compromising hemodynamic stability in patients undergoing RARPC. Lung ultrasound offers a practical, effective, and non-invasive bedside tool for optimizing ventilation in high-risk surgical settings. Trial registration and protocol This study was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov in March 2024 (ID: NCT06307704). The trial protocol is available through the ClinicalTrials.gov registry at https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06307704 .

items.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.containerTitle: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
items.abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is widely used to evaluate emergency department (ED) patients with headache, increasing costs, radiation exposure, and workload. Non-invasive intracranial pressure waveform (ICPW) monitoring has been proposed as an adjunctive triage tool. We assessed its diagnostic performance for identifying abnormal head CT findings in ED patients with red-flag headaches and explored potential resource implications. This retrospective study included 84 patients with red-flag headaches at Hospital Leforte Morumbi, Brazil (June–September 2023). All underwent non-invasive ICPW monitoring (brain4care System) and head CT during the same ED encounter. ICPW was abnormal if P2/P1 ≥ 1.2 or time-to-peak (TTP) ≥ 0.3. Sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPV, NPV) were calculated against abnormal CT. CT expenditure and ED length of stay were assessed as exploratory outcomes. ICPW showed 90.0% sensitivity, 66.2% specificity, 98.0% NPV, and 26.5% PPV for abnormal CT. Median P2/P1 ratio yielded an ROC AUC of 0.778 (95% CI 0.640–0.900). Forty-nine patients (58.3%) had both normal ICPW and normal CT; their median ED stay was 3.5 h shorter than that of the overall cohort, though causality cannot be inferred. One patient had normal ICPW despite abnormal CT. Hypothetically, the normal examinations represented a projected gross CT expenditure of US$34,300. The high NPV supports further investigation of ICPW as an adjunctive risk-stratification tool, but the retrospective single-center design, small sample, and few abnormal CTs preclude definitive conclusions. ICPW should not replace clinical assessment or neuroimaging; resource implications remain exploratory hypotheses requiring prospective, multicenter validation.

items.title: Macroscopic dye distribution after classical versus extrafascial interscalene block: an exploratory comparative cadaveric pilot study
items.abstract: Background: Extrafascial injection has been proposed as a phrenic nerve-sparing alternative for interscalene brachial plexus block (ISB), but the anatomical basis for the reported reduction in phrenic nerve involvement remains incompletely characterized. We compared macroscopic dye distribution patterns between classical ISB and extrafascial injection in paired cadaveric specimens. Methods: In five formalin-fixed cadavers, bilateral ultrasound-guided injections with indigo carmine (20 ml per side) were performed. A classical ISB and extrafascial injection were applied to contralateral sides. Three blinded anatomists independently assessed staining intensity (deep, light, none) in real time during dissection. Results: Both techniques produced deep staining of C5-6 roots, upper trunk, and suprascapular nerve in 5/5 specimens. The phrenic nerve was stained in all 10 specimens (5/5 in each group); deep staining occurred in 4/5 (80%) classical ISB specimens and 0/5 extrafascial specimens, though all 5 extrafascial specimens showed only light staining. Spread to infraclavicular cords was limited with both techniques. Conclusions: Dye reached the C5-6 roots, upper trunk, suprascapular nerve, and phrenic nerve in all 5 specimens of both groups. Phrenic nerve staining intensity was lower with the extrafascial technique than with classical ISB in 4 of 5 paired cadavers, identical in 1 of 5, and never higher. The functional and clinical implications of this intensity difference cannot be determined from the present anatomical model and require prospective validation.

items.title: Commentary: from enhanced recovery toward patient-centered recovery—the role of ERAS in robotic gynecological surgery
Weight- and age-dependent bias in remimazolam pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic models during bispectral index-guided anesthesia: a retrospective analysis
items.abstract: Background The Schüttler pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PKPD) model for remimazolam was derived from healthy male volunteers (20-38 years; 64-99 kg). This study examined how body weight and age modify the relationship between effect-site concentration (Ce) and bispectral index (BIS) in Korean surgical patients. Methods This retrospective study analyzed Schüttler-predicted remimazolam Ce and observed BIS from 52 adult patients under remimazolam-remifentanil total intravenous anesthesia. A linear mixed-effects model examined demographic modifiers of the Ce-BIS relationship, including Ce × weight and Ce × age interaction terms. Patients were stratified by body weight ( Results Body weight significantly modified the Ce-BIS relationship (Ce × weight interaction, P = 0.029), with lower body weight and older age each independently associated with lower observed BIS than model-predicted values. In patients weighing Conclusions Body weight and age significantly modify the Ce-BIS relationship in remimazolam-based anesthesia, with negative bias observed across all four PKPD models in low-body-weight older patients. These findings warrant prospective validation in larger and more diverse cohorts and remimazolam PKPD model refinement that adequately incorporates body size and age.

items.title: Association between serial perioperative oxygen reserve index measurements and postoperative pulmonary complications in patients at increased pulmonary risk undergoing non-thoracic surgery
NeuroPOCUS: what every intensivist should know
items.abstract: Ultrasound has become a paramount tool in critical care. Nowadays, it is common for intensivists to use ultrasound to evaluate cardiac function, pulmonary alterations, guide vascular access, and monitor systemic venous congestion through ultrasound-based techniques. However, the brain remains often overlooked in the point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) practice. NeuroPOCUS encompasses cerebral hemodynamic assessment, mainly at the level of the middle cerebral artery, as well as evaluation of hydrocephalus, hematoma size, midline shift and intracranial pressure. Most of these are basic or basic-plus skills. In this manuscript, we present a concise guide on what every intensivist should know about NeuroPOCUS, including basic key concepts, technique and several real illustrative figures.

items.title: From failed to failing epidural: an evolution of concepts around the management of labor epidural analgesia for a better maternal comfort and safety
items.abstract: Labor epidural analgesia has markedly improved in quality and safety over the past two decades. However, maintaining consistent analgesic efficacy throughout labor remains challenging, and inadequate blocks continue to be encountered in routine practice. In this Experts' opinion, we examine the spectrum of failed and failing epidural analgesia and identify critical periods during labor associated with an increased risk of block inadequacy. We propose pragmatic definitions for onset failure, breakthrough pain, failing epidural, and failed conversion to surgical anesthesia, based on the most recent evidence. We contend that a clear conceptual framework is essential for obstetric anesthesia teams to anticipate, recognize, and manage inadequate epidural analgesia effectively. We therefore outline practical, evidence-informed strategies for prevention and treatment. A structured and anticipatory approach to epidural management may improve maternal comfort and safety, while supporting a more patient-centered model of care.

items.title: Nutritional support in immunosuppressed critically ill patients
items.abstract: Immunosuppressed patients now make up a growing share of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, largely as a result of advances in cancer treatment, organ transplantation, and immunomodulatory therapies. While their short-term ICU mortality may be similar to that of immunocompetent patients when illness severity is taken into account, these individuals often face longer ICU stays, more complications, and poorer long-term outcomes. In this context, artificial nutrition plays a central role in ICU management and represents a potentially modifiable intervention. Beyond meeting energy requirements, nutritional support may help sustain immune function, preserve gut integrity, and reduce the risk of infectious complications. Whenever possible, enteral nutrition should be favored, as it supports the intestinal barrier and gut-associated lymphoid tissue, even when delivered at low, trophic doses. Parenteral nutrition remains indispensable in the presence of intestinal failure but should be used cautiously, given its association with complications such as catheter-related bloodstream infections. Critical illness profoundly alters gut-immune interactions, promoting dysbiosis, increased intestinal permeability, and immune dysfunction - processes that may be further amplified by immunosuppressive therapies. This has fueled interest in immunonutrition strategies, including arginine, ω-3 fatty acids, glutamine, and nucleotides. However, evidence in immunosuppressed critically ill patients remains limited and inconsistent, preventing firm recommendations. Looking ahead, the integration of body composition assessment, immune-metabolic phenotyping, multi-omics technologies, and artificial intelligence may enable more personalized nutritional strategies. Future studies should focus on phenotype-specific randomized trials to better define the optimal route, composition, timing, and dosing of nutritional support in this complex population.

items.title: Histology of the parietal peritoneum: a scoping review of microanatomy and potential relevance to preperitoneal analgesia
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The abdominal preperitoneal plane beneath the posterior rectus sheath has been recently described as a potential target for regional analgesia. Techniques such as ultrasound-guided preperitoneal or deep rectus sheath blocks aim to deposit local anesthetic adjacent to the abdominal parietal peritoneum, a structure traditionally regarded as a serosal membrane. Some anatomical and clinical evidence suggests that the parietal peritoneum may represent a more complex neurovascular interface relevant to pain transmission. METHODS: A systematic scoping review of the literature was conducted to synthesize available histological evidence on the abdominal parietal peritoneum. Studies investigating its microanatomy, vascularization, and innervation were included. Given the heterogeneity of study designs and outcomes, a descriptive mapping approach was adopted without quantitative synthesis. RESULTS: The included studies show that the parietal peritoneum is composed of a mesothelial layer supported by a submesothelial connective tissue matrix. The matrix contains collagen fibers, microvasculature, immune cells, and both myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibers. Neuroanatomical findings indicate sensory afferents originating from the thoracolumbar nerves, as well as mechanoreceptive and nociceptive fibers within the submesothelial layer. CONCLUSIONS: While conclusive evidence of visceral afferent innervation is still scarce, these experimental observations imply a more complex sensory organization. Overall, these results may support the notion of the parietal peritoneum as a biologically active fascial interface. This perspective may provide a conceptual framework for considering the preperitoneal plane as a potential target in abdominal pain. Further translational and human-based studies are needed to clarify its role in regional analgesia.

items.title: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome: what the intensivist needs to know
items.abstract: Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) is a significant complication of chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy, a revolutionary treatment for hematologic malignancies. This syndrome, which might affect approximately 30% of CAR-T therapy recipients, presents a wide spectrum of neurological symptoms, ranging from mild confusion to life-threatening cerebral edema. In the intensive care unit (ICU), managing ICANS is critical due to its potential severity. Pathophysiology of ICANS is driven by immune-mediated inflammation disrupting the blood-brain barrier, resulting in cerebral cytokine infiltration and glial cell activation. Its severity is associated with elevated cytokine levels in cerebrospinal fluid and serum, which points to the need for specific biomarkers and predictive tools. Standardized assessments, including the Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy (ICE) Score, together with brain imaging and adjunctive diagnostic tests, provide clinicians with essential baseline information for the assessment and monitoring of neurological complications. ICU management focuses on supportive care and pharmacologic strategies. Corticosteroids represent the cornerstone of treatment, effectively targeting neuroinflammation while preserving the antitumor efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy. Anticonvulsants, hyperosmolar agents and advanced neurocritical care measures are also pivotal. Recent advances suggest potential benefits of alternative therapies, such as anti-cytokine agents and innovative immune cell products with reduced neurotoxic risks. Despite advancements, challenges persist, including diagnostic ambiguities, resource allocation, and variability in care protocols. This review highlighted challenges in ICANS management for ICU physicians, intending to underline the importance of early detection, rigorous monitoring, and tailored interventions to improve patient outcomes.

Implementing an NT-proBNP-guided preoperative cardiac risk assessment algorithm in noncardiac surgery: a before-and-after cohort study
items.abstract: Several algorithms guide perioperative cardiovascular (CV) evaluation, and recent evidence supports more objective functional-capacity assessment and selective biomarker testing. We developed and implemented an updated evidence-based preoperative CV algorithm for patients undergoing noncardiac surgery. The goal was to identify patients at elevated risk for major adverse cardiovascular events and guide appropriate management without overutilizing cardiac testing or specialist consultation. We conducted a retrospective before-and-after cohort study at a university-affiliated hospital, comparing baseline care (March 2017-February 2020) with post-implementation period 1 (PI1; January-December 2021; NT-proBNP threshold 300 pg/mL) and post-implementation period 2 (PI2; January-August 2022; threshold 200 pg/mL). The algorithm combined clinical risk calculation, the Duke Activity Status Index, and selective NT-proBNP measurement or stress testing for asymptomatic adults with estimated perioperative CV event risk greater than 1%. Outcomes included NT-proBNP testing, cardiology referral, postoperative troponin measurement, elevated postoperative troponin/perioperative myocardial injury (PMI), 30-day myocardial infarction (MI), and mortality. Among 66,695 patients (34,990 baseline, 11,606 PI1, and 20,099 PI2), NT-proBNP testing increased from 220 (0.7%) at baseline to 174 (1.5%) in PI1 and 301 (1.6%) in PI2 ( p < 0.001 for each comparison). Among tested patients, the proportion with NT-proBNP greater than 300 pg/mL did not differ between baseline and PI1 (42.7% vs. 34.5%, p = 0.096); in PI2, 31.9% exceeded the protocol threshold of 200 pg/mL. Cardiology referrals decreased from 0.7% to 0.2% in PI1 and 0.5% in PI2 ( p < 0.001 for each; relative reductions 76.4% and 34.7%, respectively). Postoperative troponin measurement decreased from 1,343 (3.8%) to 322 (2.8%) and 550 (2.7%) ( p < 0.001 for each), whereas the proportion of monitored patients with elevated troponin/PMI increased from 13.7% to 25.5% and 19.8% ( p < 0.001 for each). Overall PMI rates were 0.5%, 0.7%, and 0.5%, respectively. Thirty-day MI and mortality did not differ. The algorithm increased selective NT-proBNP testing and reduced cardiology referrals and postoperative troponin testing without increasing stress testing or short-term adverse outcomes.

items.title: Intraoperative continuous glucose monitor accuracy compared with point of care glucose testing and assessment of preoperative medication hold parameters on glycemic control during orthopedic procedures: a observational study
items.abstract: Perioperative glycemic control includes a multitude of variables which are patient specific and may not distill to a one size fits all patient approach. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems present the opportunity to improve care by constantly monitoring patient glucose control perioperatively. The primary objectives of this observational study were to evaluate the performance of a CGM during the perioperative period while also assessing the glycemic control results from following preoperative medication hold times recommended by the American Diabetes Association Standards of Care (ADA SOC). CGM systems were applied prior to admission in this single center study using recommendations from the ADA SOC for medication hold times. Point of care (POC) glucose measurements were taken every 30 min intraoperatively for comparison to CGM glucose values. Phase I focused solely on CGM performance, phase II added a calibration step preoperatively to determine if performance could be further improved. Accuracy was assessed with mean absolute relative difference (MARD) between POC and CGM glucose values and error grid analysis (EGA). Glycemic control was evaluated via preoperative POC and CGM glucose values and intraoperative time below range (TBR), time in range (TIR), and time above range (TAR). Sixty patients completed the study with combined preoperative glucose values of mean (± SD) 131.1 (± 26.1) mg/dL for POC glucose and 150.7 (± 35.2) mg/dL for CGM. Intraoperative MARD in phase I was 18.1% (± 17.2) with 64.7% of CGM-POC pairs in zone A, 33.6% in zone B, and 1.7% in zone C on EGA. Phase II intraoperative MARD was 9.8% (± 6.9) with 93.6% of CGM-POC pairs in zone A, 6.4% in zone B. Combined phase I/II intraoperative TBR was 0.7%, TIR 91.5%, TAR 7.8%. One intraoperative hypoglycemic event (69 mg/dL) occurred in phase II. Postoperative (12 h) MARD for phase I was 11.4% (± 9.1), phase II 7.1 (± 5.4). CGM performance was within acceptable limits of agreement with POC glucose testing during the intraoperative period which improved following the addition of a preoperative calibration step. Glycemic control values obtained both pre and intraoperatively were within target range providing support for use of current recommended hold times.

items.title: Non-reassuring fetal status and neonatal outcome after non-elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia: a mediating effect of post-spinal hypotension
items.abstract: To examine both the direct and mediating effects of post-spinal hypotension in the relationship between non-reassuring fetal status (NRFS) and adverse neonatal outcomes. This secondary analysis of a previously conducted prospective observational study included term pregnant women in labor who underwent non-elective emergency caesarean sections under spinal anaesthesia. The indication for caesarean section was categorized as either NRFS or non-NRFS. The primary outcome measure for this study was adverse neonatal outcome, defined as a composite of neonatal resuscitation required immediately after delivery, a 1-minute Apgar score < 7, a 5-minute Apgar score < 7, neonatal intensive care unit admission, or in-hospital death within 7 days. Causal mediation analysis was used to investigate the relationships between NRFS, post-spinal hypotension, and adverse neonatal outcomes. Out of the 335 parturients, post-spinal hypotension occurred in 155 (46%), and adverse neonatal events were observed in 56 newborns (16%). Causal mediation analysis showed that both total and direct associations between NRFS and adverse neonatal outcomes remained significant after adjusting for confounders. However, the indirect effect through post-spinal maternal hypotension was not significant. In multivariable logistic regression analysis, NRFS and post-spinal hypotension were independently associated with adverse neonatal outcomes, with odds ratios of 10.26 (95% CI, 4.13 to 25.48; P < 0.001) and 2.03 (95% CI, 1.01 to 4.07; P = 0.044), respectively. We found no evidence that post-spinal hypotension mediated the association between NRFS and composite adverse neonatal outcomes in non-elective cesarean section, although NRFS and post-spinal hypotension were each independently associated with these outcomes.

items.title: Counting caesarean sections is not enough: a framework for measuring obstetric anaesthesia readiness in resource-constrained settings
items.abstract: Availability of caesarean delivery is not equivalent to access to safe and effective operative obstetric care. Caesarean-section rates, procedure volumes, geographical-access measures, and facility designations are essential for identifying underuse, overuse, and inequalities, and they are often used because they are more readily available than detailed measures of perioperative quality. However, these indicators do not establish whether a facility has the personnel, monitoring, oxygen, suction, medicines, blood access, postoperative observation, and escalation systems required to provide anaesthesia safely and respond effectively when complications occur. We propose an evidence-informed Obstetric Anaesthesia Readiness Framework that makes these capabilities an explicit component of maternal-health performance rather than an assumed feature of caesarean capability. The framework was developed through a focused, non-systematic synthesis of international anaesthesia standards, emergency obstetric-care guidance, obstetric anaesthesia literature, facility-readiness evidence, and evidence from Somalia and comparable resource-constrained settings. Candidate readiness components were organised by clinical function and mapped across structure, clinical processes, rescue capacity, and organisational learning. Five interconnected domains emerged: workforce and clinical competency; infrastructure, monitoring, and documentation; airway management, resuscitation, and essential medicines; haemorrhage response and referral capacity; and recovery, surveillance, and safety governance. Somalia is used as an illustrative fragile health-system context in which workforce concentration, uneven facility readiness, and limitations in emergency and critical-care capacity make the distinction between nominal access and effective safe access particularly important. The framework is intended to complement, rather than replace, caesarean monitoring, comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care indicators, international anaesthesia standards, and maternal and perinatal death surveillance. The proposed framework is an evidence-informed measurement model that has not yet undergone formal consensus development or empirical validation. Its candidate domains and indicators require expert consensus, feasibility assessment, inter-rater reliability testing, and evaluation against meaningful measures of maternal safety before routine, accreditation, or regulatory use. Maternal-health systems should measure not only whether caesarean delivery is available, but whether the personnel, monitoring, rescue capacity, haemorrhage response, postoperative care, team preparedness, and governance processes required to provide it safely are reliably available and functioning when needed.

items.title: Perioperative hemodynamic management in elderly hypertensive patients: a systematic review of monitoring-guided strategies and postoperative outcomes
items.abstract: Background Older adults receiving long-term antihypertensive therapy represent a rapidly growing surgical population in whom intraoperative blood pressure management remains contentious. Observational evidence consistently links intraoperative hypotension with adverse postoperative outcomes, but whether specific blood pressure targets or hemodynamic management strategies improve clinical outcomes remains uncertain. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov from 1 January 2013 to 15 January 2026 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and prospective or retrospective cohort studies of haemodynamic monitoring-guided management in patients with a mean or median age of at least 65 years receiving chronic antihypertensive therapy or with documented chronic hypertension undergoing non-cardiac surgery. Two reviewers independently screened records, extracted data using a piloted form capturing design, setting, population, hypertension status, intervention, comparator, and raw outcome events, and assessed risk of bias (RoB 2 for RCTs; ROBINS-I for cohort studies). Quantitative pooling was prespecified only for comparisons with three or more studies sharing design, intervention class, and outcome definition; otherwise, a structured narrative synthesis with fully tabulated study-level effect data was performed. Certainty was rated with GRADE. Reporting follows PRISMA 2020. Results Nineteen studies (7 randomized controlled trials reported in 9 publications; 12 cohort studies) comprising 1,074,313 patients were included. In RCTs, higher or individualized intraoperative blood pressure targets did not reduce major vascular or organ-injury composites compared with routine targets (POISE − 3: risk ratio [RR] 0.99, 95% CI 0.89–1.11; IMPROVE-multi: RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.93–1.30), although one small trial favoured individualized systolic targets (INPRESS: RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.57–0.95); certainty was low because of inconsistency and indirectness. Observational cohorts consistently reported duration-dependent associations between intraoperative hypotension and acute kidney injury or myocardial injury (moderate certainty for the association, not for a causal effect of any specific target). Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy was neutral in the largest contemporary trial (OPTIMISE II: postoperative infection RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.88–1.18) but beneficial in smaller earlier trials (low certainty). Continuing renin–angiotensin-system inhibitors increased intraoperative hypotension (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.19–1.44) without increasing major complications (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.19; moderate certainty). A hypotension-avoidance strategy did not reduce postoperative delirium in randomized data (cogPOISE − 3: RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.79–1.38), and observational findings were inconsistent (low certainty). Conclusions Intraoperative hypotension is consistently and duration-dependently associated with organ injury in observational surgical cohorts, although much of this evidence is derived from broader non-cardiac surgical populations rather than exclusively elderly hypertensive patients. Randomized evidence specific to elderly hypertensive populations remains limited and does not demonstrate consistent benefit from higher blood pressure targets, goal-directed haemodynamic therapy, or specific antihypertensive withholding strategies.Recommendations for this population should rest on guidelines and individualized judgment rather than on claims of moderate-certainty trial evidence that the current literature does not provide. Renal denervation and other device-based therapies are outside the scope of this review and are identified as future research priorities only.

items.title: Effect of cardiac-index guided intraoperative haemodynamic therapy on postoperative outcome in non-cardiac surgery patients – a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Background Optimal perioperative haemodynamic management is essential to reduce postoperative complications. While multiple technologies allow for advanced monitoring, clear evidence on the effectiveness of Cardiac Index-guided goal-directed therapy (CI-GDT) compared to standard care in non-cardiac surgery is lacking. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to investigate the impact of CI-GDT on postoperative outcome. Methods A systematic search using PubMed and Web of Science (2010–2025) identified randomised controlled trials (RCT) comparing CI-GDT to standard care in adult non-cardiac surgery. Study selection and data extraction were conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered under PROSPERO (CRD420251058399). Odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and 95% prediction intervals (PI) were calculated using a random-effects model. Risk of bias was assessed via the RoB 2 tool. Heterogeneity was quantified with I 2 , τ 2 , and Cochran’s Q. Reporting bias was evaluated by funnel plots, Egger’s test, and trim-and-fill method. Sensitivity was assessed by leave-one-out analysis. Results Twenty-one RCTs were included, of which 20 contributed data to the meta-analysis of postoperative complications. CI-GDT significantly reduced the incidence of postoperative complications (OR .59 [.45–.78]; PI .20–1.74; I 2 = 62.9%). Mortality did not differ significantly between groups (OR 0.77 [.57–1.05]; I 2 = 0%). Funnel plot and Egger’s test indicated no significant publication bias ( p =.15). Leave-one-out analysis confirmed robustness of findings. Trim-and-fill did not suggest missing studies. Certainty of evidence was graded high. Discussion/conclusion CI-GDT was associated with a lower incidence of patients experiencing at least one postoperative complication, whereas mortality did not differ significantly. However, substantial heterogeneity and a prediction interval crossing the null indicate that the benefit may not be consistent across clinical settings. These findings do not establish an independent advantage of CI targeting over other GDT strategies.
items.limitations: This review has several limitations. The included evidence was derived from multiple relatively small trials involving clinically heterogeneous patient populations undergoing a wide range of surgical procedures. The haemodynamic interventions also varied substantially with respect to the predefined CI thresholds, additional target variables, monitoring technologies, and protocol-specified use of fluids, vasopressors, and inotropic drugs. Furthermore, definitions and observation periods for postoperative complications and mortality were not uniform across studies. These sources of clinical and methodological heterogeneity probably contributed to the observed statistical heterogeneity and the wide prediction interval.

items.title: Intraoperative fluid infusion rate during major pulmonary resection within an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathway: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background Intraoperative fluid management remains a debated component of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways in thoracic surgery, with current guidelines recommending intraoperative infusion rates of 2–6 mL/kg/h despite limited high-quality evidence. We assessed whether the intraoperative fluid infusion rate was associated with prolonged length of stay (LOS) after major pulmonary resection. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 540 consecutive patients undergoing lobectomy, bi-lobectomy, or segmentectomy within a structured ERAS pathway, stratified by intraoperative infusion rate: G1 <4 mL/kg/h ( n= 76), G2 4–8 mL/kg/h ( n= 328, reference), and G3 >8 mL/kg/h ( n= 136). Multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify risk factors for prolonged LOS (>3 nights), before we conducted a generalised (multinomial) propensity score matching on four covariates (FEV1, blood loss, operating time, open surgical approach), yielding 59 matched triplets (177 patients). Results Prolonged LOS occurred in 206 patients (38.1%) and was independently associated with high intraoperative infusion rate (OR 2.86 [1.70–4.81]; p< 0.001). Propensity score matching confirmed a statistically significant association between prolonged LOS and infusion rate with 62.7% of G3 patients experiencing prolonged LOS compared to 42.4% in G2 and 39.0% in G1 ( p= 0.020). Conclusions Within a structured ERAS programme, high intraoperative fluid infusion rates (>8 mL/kg/h) were independently associated with prolonged length of stay after major pulmonary resection, in both multivariable and propensity-matched analyses. These findings suggest that high fluid infusion rates may be associated with longer hospital stay. Future efforts should prioritise prospective evaluation of individualised fluid strategies.

items.title: Impact of liberalised preoperative water intake and intravenous-to-oral transition on patient experience and system efficiency in thoracic surgery: a before-and-after study
items.abstract: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) protocols aim to improve perioperative care by enhancing patient experience, workflow efficiency, and cost-effectiveness; however, quantitative evidence for their system-level impact in thoracic surgery remains limited. We evaluated patient-reported experience and system efficiency following implementation of an ERAS-based perioperative hydration/medication protocol. We conducted a single-centre comparative before-and-after study and included consecutive patients undergoing pulmonary resection or thymectomy (January–September 2025). The protocol permitted water intake until 3 h before surgery, reduced routine preoperative intravenous hydration, and replaced routine intravenous medications with oral alternatives when appropriate. Primary outcomes were postimplementation patient-reported measures (fasting-related discomfort, satisfaction, and actual preoperative water intake). Secondary outcomes included nursing time for medication-related tasks, perioperative outcomes, and direct institutional costs. We included 461 patients. Protocol implementation was not associated with increased postoperative complications. Within the postimplementation period, reported preoperative water intake was higher after the educational refinement (55.0% vs. 74.7%; relative risk 1.36). Intake was less frequent in men (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.38; P = 0.002) and more frequent among patients scheduled later in operative order (aOR, 1.90; P = 0.044). Discomfort was higher after wedge resection (aOR, 2.13; P = 0.027) and thymectomy (aOR, 2.47; P = 0.011) than after lobectomy, while satisfaction remained high. Transitioning routine medications from IV to oral reduced nursing task time by 71.8% per patient (median, 2.4–8.5 min) and was associated with estimated direct savings of ~ USD 18,700 per 1,000 surgeries. This ERAS-based protocol was associated with high patient-reported satisfaction, improved nursing workflow efficiency, and reduced institutional costs, with no observed safety signal.

Healthcare professionals' experiences of an intensive weight loss programme as prehabilitation before cancer surgery: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Background Healthcare professionals (HCPs) are gatekeepers to recruitment in cancer trials. We aimed to explore HCPs views on recruiting to and delivering a trial of an intensive weight loss programme with dietetic support as prehabilitation before cancer surgery. Methods This was a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with dietitians, nurses, and surgeons delivering the trial. Data were analysed descriptively, followed by a framework approach to chart the findings against the RE-AIM framework (reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, maintenance) to evaluate the scalability of the intervention. Results We interviewed six research nurses, four nurse specialists, and two surgeons from eight NHS recruiting hospitals in England and the three dietitians delivering the intervention. HCPs reported approaching most eligible patients but did not approach those thought to be emotionally burdened by their diagnosis (Reach). HCPs also described the programme as a simple way for people to lose weight, potentially improving their postoperative outcomes and allowing them to take control during an uncertain time, though this view compromised equipoise (Effectiveness). While HCPs found it straightforward to deliver the trial and had limited safety concerns, some questioned if the minimum body mass index eligibility of 28 kg/m 2 was too low (Adoption). Dietitians experienced a positive feedback loop when participants adhered to the programme, supporting their perception that the intervention was effective and worthwhile (Implementation). HCPs viewed the programme as filling a gap in prehabilitation but raised concerns about scalability due to limited dietetic workforce capacity (Maintenance). Conclusions HCPs involved in delivering the programme mostly supported introducing it as prehabilitation before cancer surgery. Scaling the programme may require improvements, particularly to its reach and maintenance. This could include exploring how other trained individuals with appropriate clinical and dietetic oversight could support the delivery of behavioural support. Trial Registration ISRCTN39207707, prospectively registered 13/03/2023.
