The primary outcome was survival to discharge; secondary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) at hospital arrival, survival to admission, and favorable outcome (cerebral performance category score ≤ 2). We used mixed effects logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, arrest location, witness status, initial rhythm, bystander interventions, timing elements (call to EMS arrival, 1st defibrillation, 1st epinephrine, 1st amiodarone, and 7th defibrillation), and clustering by county. Sensitivity analyses included restricting post-implementation cases to those receiving esmolol (as-treated), exclusion of COVID-era controls (2020-2021), and using propensity score matching for cases receiving esmolol to controls. Results: A total of 227 patients met criteria (147 pre- and 80 post-esmolol implementation [65% received esmolol]), unadjusted outcomes were similar: ROSC 15.0% vs 17.5% (p=0.62), survival to admission 26.5% vs 33.8% (p=0.25), survival to discharge 10.9% vs 11.2% (p=0.93), and favorable outcome 10.9% vs 11.2% (p=0.93) for controls and esmolol periods, respectively. Adjusted analyses showed no significant association with ROSC (aOR 1.95, 95% CI 0.80-4.77), survival to admission (aOR 1.71, 95% CI 0.89-3.29), survival to discharge (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 0.47-3.31), or favorable outcomes (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 0.47-3.31). The as-treated analyses, the analyses excluding COVID-era controls, and propensity matched analyses for cases receiving esmolol (n=46) matched to controls (n=46) were similarly not significant. Conclusions: The addition of esmolol for the management of shock-refractory OHCA after failure of standard therapy in this EMS system was not associated with differences in patient outcomes.

items.title: Myocardial Responses to Eplontersen in Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: The CARDIO-TTRansform CMR study
items.abstract: Background: Transthyretin-lowering therapies target the underlying cause of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), but their effects on myocardial amyloid burden and cardiac remodelling remain incompletely characterized. We evaluated the myocardial effects of sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen using serial multiparametric cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR). Methods: This CMR study was a pre-specified, international, prospective study embedded within the randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 CARDIO-TTRansform trial. Participants underwent CMR at baseline and planned assessments at weeks 25, 49, 97, and 140. The primary imaging analysis evaluated longitudinal changes in CMR parameters using mixed models for repeated measures. Myocardial amyloid regression and progression were defined as ≥5 percentage-point decreases and increases in extracellular volume (ECV), respectively. All other patients were considered stable. Results: We enrolled 120 participants with baseline and ≥1 follow-up CMR assessment (eplontersen, n=58; placebo, n=62; mean age, 76.7±6.5 years; 95% male; baseline stabilizer, 12.5%). At week 140 eplontersen resulted in lower ECV, compared with placebo (least-squares mean difference [95% CI], –6.7 percentage points [ –8.7 to –4.7]; P<0.001) and lower native T1 ( –25.9ms [–41.7 to –10.2 ]; P=0.002) and left ventricular mass (–19.1g [–28.0 to –10.2]; P<0.001). Eplontersen also increased left ventricular ejection fraction (+5.1% [1.8–8.3]; P=0.002), right ventricular ejection fraction (+4.6% [0.6–8.7]; P=0.03), and left ventricular global longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain and right ventricular longitudinal strain (all P<0.05), compared to placebo. At week-140, myocardial amyloid regression occurred in 12.5% receiving eplontersen versus 0% receiving placebo, whereas progression occurred in 12.5% versus 76%, respectively. Conclusions: Sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen resulted in substantially lower myocardial ECV and favorable changes in cardiac structure, biventricular systolic function, and myocardial deformation compared with placebo in a cohort of patients mostly not on background stabilizer at baseline. These findings provide randomized evidence that lowering circulating transthyretin modifies myocardial disease progression in ATTR-CM and support serial multiparametric CMR for characterizing myocardial treatment response.

Off-Pump Versus On-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting in Prefrail and Frail Patients: 30-Day and 1-Year Outcomes From the FRAGILE Randomized Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Frailty is associated with worse outcomes after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). However, the comparative effectiveness of off-pump CABG (OPCAB) versus on-pump CABG (ONCAB) in prefrail and frail patients remains uncertain. METHODS: This multicenter, randomized, open-label trial enrolled patients ≥60 years of age classified as prefrail or frail, randomized 1:1, between January 2018 and December 2024. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or reoperation for bleeding. Secondary outcomes included ventilation time, intensive care unit and hospital stay, transfusion requirements, completeness of revascularization, surgical wound infection at 30 days, and neurocognitive function preoperatively and at 1 year. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle; relative risks with 95% CIs were estimated. RESULTS: A total of 508 patients were included (OPCAB, n=258; ONCAB, n=250; median age, 68 years [interquartile range, 65.0–73]; 30.5% female). The primary composite outcome occurred in 28 patients receiving OPCAB (10.9%) and 40 patients receiving ONCAB (16.0%; relative risk, 1.47 [95% CI, 0.94–2.31]; P =0.09). Surgical wound infection was more frequent with ONCAB (20 [8.0%] versus 9 [3.5%]; P =0.04). No significant differences were observed in neurocognitive or quality of life outcomes at 1 year. Estimated 1-year survival probabilities were 96.1% and 92.8% in the OPCAB and ONCAB groups, respectively ( P =0.099). CONCLUSIONS: In prefrail and frail patients undergoing CABG, OPCAB and ONCAB resulted in similar rates of the primary composite outcome. No significant differences between OPCAB and ONCAB were found in neurocognitive outcomes. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02338947.

items.title: Generation of Human Cardiomyocytes With Adult-Like Metabolism by a Chemically Defined Medium for Mitochondrial Disease Modeling
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC cardiomyocytes) as a model for cardiac disease have become increasingly important, bolstered by the Food and Drug Administration’s initiative to promote novel alternative methods for biomedical research. A key limitation of metabolically immature iPSC cardiomyocytes is their limited ability to accurately recapitulate mitochondria-dependent pathologies, such as Friedreich ataxia–associated cardiomyopathy. Adult cardiomyocytes are characterized by a high density of interfibrillar mitochondria, abundant respiratory complexes (I–V) that form supercomplexes, and efficient utilization of fatty acids to drive mitochondrial respiration. These unique metabolic structures and functions are largely missing in iPSC cardiomyocytes. Further, whether iPSC cardiomyocytes can efficiently utilize fatty acids for respiration in the presence of glucose, a unique adult feature, remains unclear. METHODS: We developed a chemically defined, 11-component maturation medium (MM11) designed using a bioinformatics-guided strategy that identified high-fidelity transcriptional markers of adult cardiac metabolic maturity. Human iPSC cardiomyocytes were treated with MM11 for 2 weeks and evaluated at the molecular, structural, and functional levels, with an emphasis on mitochondrial maturity. We benchmarked our results with isolated primary adult human cardiomyocytes. Last, we tested whether this method could enable us to more accurately model Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy. RESULTS: MM11 treatment increased expression of metabolic pathways, including mitochondrial respiration and fatty acid metabolism, at the transcript and protein levels. Ultrastructural analyses revealed the formation of interfibrillar mitochondria and mitochondrial respiratory supercomplexes, a feature never shown in previous reports. Functionally, MM11-treated iPSC cardiomyocytes exhibited substantially increased oxidative phosphorylation and a metabolic preference for fatty acid utilization in the presence of physiologic substrates, as determined by oxygen consumption assays and 13 C isotope tracing. CONCLUSIONS: MM11 promotes robust metabolic maturation of human iPSC cardiomyocytes, enabling sophisticated mitochondrial architecture and substrate utilization. These metabolically matured cardiomyocytes more faithfully model mitochondria-dependent cardiac pathologies, including ischemia-reperfusion injury and Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy, improving the use of iPSC cardiomyocytes for mechanistic studies of human heart disease.

items.title: Cardiovascular Health Promotion for US Veterans: Current State, Gaps, and Strategies: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
items.abstract: US veterans represent a large and diverse population with distinctive demographic characteristics, comorbidity profiles, and social determinants of health shaped by military service. These factors contribute to a high burden of cardiovascular risk and low attainment of ideal cardiovascular health. At the same time, the Department of Veterans Affairs, which operates the nation’s largest integrated healthcare system, provides a unique infrastructure for delivering population-level cardiovascular disease prevention for veterans. Understanding its successes and ongoing challenges can inform broader strategies across all health systems for promoting health among veterans. This scientific statement applies the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 framework, expanded to include mental health and substance use, to evaluate veteran cardiovascular health. For each domain, we review guideline recommendations, barriers to achieving optimal health, and major Veterans Affairs programs such as Patient Aligned Care Teams, the MOVE! Weight Management Program for Veterans, Whole Health, telehealth-based interventions, and integrated mental health and substance use disorder services. Across domains, veterans receiving Veterans Affairs care often achieve outcomes that are equal to or better than those of their non–Veterans Affairs counterparts, reflecting the strengths of the system in coordinated, team-based care and research-driven implementation. Despite substantial progress, opportunities remain to improve veteran lifestyle behaviors, metabolic health, lipid and blood pressure control, engagement in mental health and substance use care, and detection and management of sleep disorders. Addressing these challenges at the Veterans Affairs will require continuing to expand care access, enhancing digital data integration, tailoring interventions to high-risk subgroups, and strengthening implementation strategies to improve uptake and engagement across Veterans Affairs services.

items.title: Abstract P1060A: CPR Training Perception and Willingness to Act: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Pre-Medical Students
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is critical step for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survival. Pre-medical students represent an unstudied and high-potential bystander population, yet predictors of post-training CPR willingness remain poorly characterized. Hypothesis: Pre-medical students from a public university in Argentina perceiving CPR training as highly important would demonstrate greater willingness to perform CPR after course completion. Methods: Prospective, cross-sectional study post mandated CPR-course survey of all pre-medical students (full cohort 2026) at Universidad Nacional de La Matanza, Argentina. The educational program comprised a 3-hour, theoretical-practical course led by university instructors in accordance with the 2025 AHA guidelines. Variables included demographics, prior CPR exposure (awareness, prior formal course, real-life CPR performance), perceived training importance (Likert 1-5), post-course CPR willingness (Likert 1-5; high=4-5). Real-life CPR performance was operationally defined as the delivery of chest compressions with or without the use of an automated external defibrillator (AED). Bivariate analyses used chi-square and crude odds ratios (OR, 95%CI). Two multivariable logistic regression models identified independent factors associated to: Model 1: high post-course CPR willingness and model 2: prior real-life CPR performance. Results: 448 students responded (mean age 21.9±5.5 years; 70.8% female). Prior awareness of CPR was high (94.9%); 32.1% had completed a prior formal CPR course; only 6.5% had performed CPR in a real-life emergency. Perceived importance was: 96.2% rated 5/5. High post-course CPR willingness was reported by 67.2%. In bivariate analysis, maximum importance perception was associated with high willingness to render CPR in real life (OR=3.07, 95%CI:1.14-8.23, p=0.020), as was prior formal CPR course (OR=1.82, 95%CI:1.16-2.84, p=0.008). In multivariable analysis (Model 1), maximum importance perception independently predicted high willingness (adjusted OR=2.96, 95%CI:1.07-8.22, p=0.037). For real-life CPR performance (Model 2), prior formal CPR course (adjusted OR=5.24, 95%CI:2.06-13.36, p<0.001) and older age (adjusted OR=2.18 per SD, 95%CI:1.63-2.92, p<0.001) were the sole independent predictors. Gender was not associated with either outcome. Conclusions: Perceiving CPR training as maximally important independently predicted greater willingness to perform CPR post-course. Prior formal CPR training was the strongest predictor of real-life CPR performance. These findings support early, repeated CPR training in medical curricula and emphasize framing instruction within clinical relevance to enhance motivation and real-world application. These cross-sectional associations warrant confirmation in longitudinal studies.

items.title: Peripheral Artery Disease in Acute Care Settings: Diagnosis and Management of Common Presentations and Emergencies: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
items.abstract: People with peripheral artery disease (PAD) are often misdiagnosed or diagnosed late and, even after diagnosis, are undertreated with both pharmacologic and invasive therapies. The disease is associated with an increased risk of mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, other vascular disease, limb loss, and reduced quality of life. Although the risks and long-term management of PAD are well documented, these risks are acutely magnified when PAD exists as a comorbidity in patients hospitalized for other cardiovascular or medical conditions. Procedures requiring vascular access for the treatment of acute myocardial infarction, cardiogenic shock, or valvular heart disease, as well as procedures for the treatment of the patient’s underlying PAD, require special consideration in patients with PAD. Familiarity with the use and placement of mechanical circulatory support in patients with PAD, as well as the management of recent endovascular or surgical vascular interventions, is essential for providing appropriate care in the acute care setting.

items.title: Correction to: Infective Endocarditis: Diagnosis, Antibiotic Therapy, and Management: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
Transapical Beating-Heart Septal Myectomy for Obstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
items.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a prevalent heterogenous genetic cardiac disorder. In the cardiac myosin inhibitor era, the guideline-directed management of HCM remains an emerging frontier worldwide. Septal myectomy has been the gold standard treatment option for obstructive HCM over the past 60 years. However, the complexity of this procedure and required expertise (and lack of qualified training) have limited its success and availability beyond high-volume HCM centers. Transapical beating-heart septal myectomy (TA-BSM), a newly developed innovative technique, simplifies conventional septal myectomy by eliminating the need for sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass, and aortotomy. Most important, the inclusion of real-time intraoperative echocardiographic guidance and evaluation makes TA-BSM safer, more precise, cost-effective, and reproducible. The apparent advantages of TA-BSM, including substantial reductions in surgical trauma and operating times and much faster postoperative recovery in patients with obstructive HCM, are encouraging. TA-BSM is particularly feasible in patients with long-segment obstruction, or small aortic valve annulus, or in those who had undergone previous cardiac operations. The frequent resolution of systolic anterior motion and associated mitral regurgitation after TA-BSM, without concomitant mitral valve intervention, highlights the central role of intraoperative echocardiography and close surgeon-echocardiographer collaboration in achieving optimal procedural outcomes. Further multicenter evaluation of TA-BSM will help define its role among septal reduction strategies for patients with obstructive HCM.

items.title: Mitral Valve Surgery in the Developing World
Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair: Preference Versus Evidence
Ischemic Mitral Regurgitation: A Changing Paradigm
Degenerative Mitral Regurgitation: From Prolapse to Precision Therapy
items.abstract: Degenerative mitral valve regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse affects ≈15 million people globally and is the commonest indication for mitral intervention in high-income countries, but its biology, natural history, and lifetime management are ill defined. This review summarizes current knowledge of the epidemiology, pathophysiology, diagnosis, risk stratification, and lifetime management of degenerative mitral regurgitation, with a focus on areas of uncertainty, recent advances, and emerging research directions. These include translational research focused on determining genetic and cellular drivers of disease progression and mechanistic studies geared to improve detection and prevention of downstream myocardial dysfunction, particularly in high-risk phenotypes, including arrhythmic mitral prolapse. The current landscape of randomized trials and large registries comparing contemporary surgical and transcatheter treatment and strategies to improve patient access to care and outcomes across all patient risk profiles and populations are also discussed.

items.title: Immersive Reality in Cardiothoracic Surgical Education
items.abstract: Immersive reality technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality, mixed reality, and related extended reality platforms, are reforming how surgeons learn complex anatomy, rehearse procedures, develop technical skills, and manage unexpected or rare intraoperative crises. Cardiothoracic surgery is particularly well suited to these tools because postgraduate training occurs in a high-stakes environment characterized by complex 3-dimensional anatomy, limited operative exposure, minimally invasive/robotic approaches, open communication, and the need for synchronized team performance. Immersive platforms facilitate anatomy education and procedural planning and enable deliberate practice and nontechnical skills training. Although most studies remain small, heterogeneous, and focused on surrogate outcomes rather than patient outcomes, evidence from surgical education and cardiothoracic surgery literature demonstrates that these tools impart improvement in knowledge, confidence, procedural accuracy, and simulator performance. This article defines immersive reality technologies, reviews their educational rationale and emerging applications in cardiothoracic surgery, proposes an implementation framework for training programs, and highlights limitations related to haptics, validation, privacy, equity, and regulatory oversight. The next phase should focus on validation of outcome-linked curricula that integrate immersive simulation into competency-based surgical education.

items.title: Transapical Beating-Heart Septal Myectomy for Symptomatic Nonobstructive Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Initial Clinical Experience
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (nHCM), defined as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy without left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, remains challenging to treat because of its heterogeneous pathophysiology. This study evaluated the safety and efficacy of transapical beating-heart septal myectomy in patients with symptomatic nHCM. METHODS: Patients with symptomatic, drug-refractory nHCM were prospectively enrolled to undergo transapical beating-heart septal myectomy through a left minithoracotomy. Under real-time transesophageal echocardiographic guidance, septal myectomy was tailored to relieve systolic cavity obliteration and mid-to-apical ventricular obstruction and to enlarge the left ventricular cavity. The primary end point was procedural success at 6 to 12 months postoperatively, defined as fulfillment of all prespecified criteria compared with baseline: ≥1-class improvement in New York Heart Association functional class, ≥10-point increase in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score, ≥10-mL increase in stroke volume, and normal or grade I diastolic function. RESULTS: Between January 2023 and January 2025, 97 consecutive eligible patients with nHCM underwent transapical beating-heart septal myectomy at Tongji Hospital. At postoperative 6 to 12 months, procedural success was achieved in 87.6%. Specifically, New York Heart Association functional class I increased from 0% at baseline to 93.8% at follow-up, the median Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire score improved from 64 (interquartile range, 56–69) to 87 (interquartile range, 82–92; P <0.001), the stroke volume increased from 53.5 mL (interquartile range, 41.0–66.6 mL) to 70.8 mL (interquartile range, 61.3–82.3 mL; P <0.001), and normal or grade I diastolic function increased from 65.6% to 97.9%. Among patients who underwent paired cardiopulmonary exercise testing (n=58), peak oxygen uptake increased by 1.1±2.9 mL/kg/min ( P =0.008). In an exploratory, hypothesis-generating analysis of 12 patients with paired 1 3 N-ammonia positron emission tomography, coronary flow reserve increased from 1.8±0.3 to 2.0±0.4 ( P =0.034). Adverse events included mitral valve injury (n=1) and ventricular septal perforation (n=1), the latter resulting in 1 postoperative death. CONCLUSIONS: Transapical beating-heart septal myectomy was associated with favorable left ventricular geometric remodeling and meaningful improvements in symptoms, health status, and functional capacity in selected patients with symptomatic nHCM. Being a potential therapeutic option for a previously difficult-to-treat population, it warrants further evaluation in controlled, multicenter studies. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT05648825.

items.title: Thrombosed Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Pseudoaneurysm After Neonatal Ross-Konno Repair
Biatrial Versus Left Atrial Maze Ablation During Cardiac Valve Surgery for Persistent Atrial Fibrillation: The ABLATION Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Guidelines recommend concomitant surgical ablation during cardiac surgery in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). However, the optimal lesion set remains uncertain, with ongoing debate regarding the relative benefits and risks of biatrial versus left atrial (LA) maze ablation. METHODS: In this multicenter, randomized, single-blind trial, patients with persistent or long-standing persistent AF undergoing rheumatic mitral valve surgery, with or without concomitant cardiac surgical procedures, were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo biatrial or LA maze ablation. The biatrial group underwent a complete Cox-Maze IV procedure; the LA group received a left-sided maze lesion set. To ensure standardization and consistency of the ablation procedures, surgeons underwent pretrial training and certification, and all procedures were videorecorded and centrally reviewed. The primary outcome was freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmias lasting >30 seconds without antiarrhythmic drugs within 12 months. The key secondary end point was freedom from permanent pacemaker implantation. RESULTS: All 323 randomized patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (mean age, 56.5 years; 72.1% women; mean LA diameter, 51.9 mm). At 12 months, 78.7% of patients (129 of 164) in the biatrial group and 68.6% (109 of 159) in the LA group were free from atrial tachyarrhythmias (adjusted difference, 10.7% [1-sided lower 95% CI, 3%]; P =0.01). Freedom from permanent pacemaker implantation was noted in 97.0% (159 of 164) of the biatrial group and 98.1% (156 of 159) of the LA group, meeting the predefined noninferiority criterion with a margin of −5% (adjusted difference, –1.1% [1-sided lower 95% CI, –3.9%]; P noninferiority =0.01). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with persistent or long-standing persistent AF undergoing rheumatic cardiac valve surgery, biatrial maze ablation was superior to LA maze ablation in reducing recurrent atrial tachyarrhythmias, while maintaining noninferiority with respect to permanent pacemaker implantation. These findings provide direct evidence to inform lesion-set selection for surgical ablation during cardiac surgery. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT05021601.

items.title: Surgical Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation
items.abstract: Atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart failure, mortality, and reduced quality of life. Although catheter ablation is the most widely used rhythm control strategy, its efficacy is limited in patients with non-paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and large left atria. To address this therapeutic gap, surgical approaches, including minimally invasive ablation, hybrid epicardial-endocardial strategies, and left atrial appendage exclusion, have continued to evolve. In this review, we focus on recent evidence to guide clinical decision-making on patient selection, advances in minimally invasive surgical and hybrid techniques, left atrial appendage exclusion, and postoperative anticoagulation management. Minimally invasive standalone Cox-Maze IV procedure and hybrid epicardial-endocardial ablation have demonstrated superior long-term freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmias compared with thoracoscopic epicardial surgical ablation or catheter ablation alone. Five-year arrhythmia-free survival has approached 85% to 95% in experienced centers after the Cox-Maze IV procedure and approximately 60% to 70% after hybrid ablation, compared with 35% to 45% after thoracoscopic epicardial ablation and 30% to 35% after single catheter ablation alone. Surgical left atrial appendage exclusion performed at the time of ablation may further reduce thromboembolic risk, although the optimal strategy for postprocedural anticoagulation remains uncertain. Careful patient selection remains essential, with atrial fibrillation type, duration, left atrial size, and previous treatment failure known to be key predictors of procedural success. As surgical techniques and supporting evidence continue to grow, standalone surgical ablation may assume a more important role in the contemporary management of atrial fibrillation, particularly for patients with advanced disease who are unlikely to achieve durable rhythm control with catheter ablation alone.

items.title: Minimally Invasive Mitral Valve Repair: Preference Versus Evidence: A Less Invasive Surgical Approach for Mitral Valve Disease
Introduction to the 2026 Cardiovascular Surgery–Themed Issue of Circulation
Hedgehog Signaling-Dependent Heterochronic Control of Cardiomyocyte Differentiation Establishes Distinct Cardiac Progenitor Fields
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The mammalian heart is formed from distinct cardiac progenitor fields: the first heart field (FHF), second heart field (SHF), and juxta-cardiac field (JCF). How these fields are established remains one of the oldest questions in cardiac biology and is central to understanding congenital heart disease, which differentially affects derivatives of the individual fields. Previous work has demonstrated that the fields emerge and differentiate at distinct times; however, the mechanisms underlying their establishment have remained elusive. Here, we implicate Hedgehog signaling–dependent heterochronic control of cardiac differentiation in the emergence of different heart fields. METHODS: We assessed Hedgehog signaling activity by assembling a cardio-mesodermal single-cell atlas. We analyzed Hedgehog ligand gene expression by confocal imaging in gastrulating mouse embryos. We investigated the necessity of Hedgehog signaling using 2 distinct genetic Hedgehog loss-of-function mouse models, analyzed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing analysis. RESULTS: Our results show that Hedgehog signaling mediates field-specific heterochronic control of differentiation timing that orchestrates the establishment of the SHF and JCF as distinct from the FHF. We identify a common cardiac progenitor transcriptomic state from which all 3 fields emerge. We show that the SHF and JCF are established coincident with Hedgehog signaling reception, whereas the FHF evades Hedgehog pathway activity and rapidly differentiates. We find that Hedgehog ligand expression sandwiches the cardiac mesoderm emerging from the primitive streak, spatially coordinating SHF and JCF establishment. Partial depletion of Hedgehog signaling causes premature activation of the cardiac differentiation program in the SHF and JCF. Complete ablation of Hedgehog signaling results in failed SHF and JCF establishment. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings reveal a Hedgehog signaling-dependent, non–cell-autonomous heterochronic mechanism required for SHF and JCF formation. This heterochronic mechanism provides a new paradigm for understanding the ordered temporal emergence of the cardiac progenitor fields that support the development of the 4-chambered heart, as well as a general model for the emergence of progenitor fields that drive organogenesis across the mammalian body plan.

High Bleeding Risk and Aspirin Omission at the Time of Primary PCI in STEMI
items.abstract: Background Patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) at high bleeding risk (HBR) are also at increased risk of ischemic events, making the optimal antiplatelet therapy challenging. Whether HBR identifies patients who may benefit from upfront aspirin omission at the time of primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains unclear. Objectives In this study, we sought to evaluate whether HBR modifies the effect of aspirin omission in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI. Methods The PREMIUM trial randomized patients with STEMI before primary PCI to low-dose prasugrel monotherapy or dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus prasugrel. In the DAPT group, patients meeting Academic Research Consortium (ARC) for HBR criteria were permitted to discontinue aspirin at 3 months, whereas non-HBR patients were intended to continue DAPT for 12 months. This post hoc analysis assessed the primary outcome of a 12-month composite of all-cause death, stroke, or myocardial infarction and the major secondary outcome of Bleeding Academic Research Consortium type 3 or 5 bleeding according to HBR status. Results Among 2,189 patients, 786 (35.9%) met ARC-HBR criteria. HBR patients had higher rates of the primary outcome (16.2% vs 6.2%; HR: 2.68; 95% CI: 2.05-3.52) and the major secondary outcome (10.9% vs 4.9%; HR: 2.28; 95% CI: 1.65-3.14). The primary outcome occurred with monotherapy vs DAPT in 18.0% vs 14.5% of HBR patients (HR: 1.29; 95% CI: 0.91-1.82) and 7.4% vs 5.0% of non-HBR patients (HR: 1.55; 95% CI: 1.01-2.37; P for interaction = 0.51). The major secondary outcome occurred in 9.2% vs 12.5% of HBR patients (HR: 0.71; 95% CI: 0.46-1.11) and 3.8% vs 6.1% of non-HBR patients (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.38-1.00; P for interaction = 0.67). Conclusions ARC-HBR identified patients with a substantially higher overall risk after primary PCI for STEMI, but did not identify a subgroup with a more favorable treatment effect of upfront aspirin omission. Clinically meaningful treatment-effect modification cannot be excluded, owing to limited precision. These findings do not support using HBR status alone to guide upfront aspirin omission and should be interpreted in the context of the low-dose prasugrel regimen used in Japan. (Prasugrel Monotherapy Following Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction [PREMIUM; NCT05709626]).

items.title: Angiography-Derived vs Wire-Based Fractional Flow Reserve to Guide Revascularization: The Randomized LIPSIA-STRATEGY Trial
items.abstract: Background Wire-based physiological assessment is recommended to guide coronary revascularization but remains underused. Angiography-derived physiology offers a wire-free alternative; however, randomized comparisons with pressure wire fractional flow reserve (FFR) have yielded inconsistent findings. Objectives This study sought to determine whether angiography-derived vessel fractional flow reserve (vFFR)-guided revascularization is noninferior to pressure wire FFR guidance for intermediate coronary stenoses. Methods The multicenter, investigator-initiated, randomized LIPSIA-STRATEGY trial included patients with acute or chronic coronary syndromes and at least 1 intermediate coronary stenosis at 8 German centers. Patients were randomized 1:1 to undergo revascularization based on vFFR or FFR. The primary outcome was major adverse cardiac events, defined as a composite of cardiac death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or unplanned clinically driven revascularization within 1 year, analyzed by modified intention to treat against a noninferiority margin of 3.5 percentage points. Results Between June 2020 and February 2025, 1,053 patients (median age: 69 years) underwent randomization (vFFR, n = 528; FFR, n = 525). At 1 year, major adverse cardiac events occurred in 15 of 493 patients (3.0%) in the vFFR group and in 20 of 493 (4.1%) in the FFR group (risk difference: -1.01 percentage points; P for noninferiority Conclusions In patients with intermediate coronary stenoses requiring physiological assessment, a vFFR-guided revascularization strategy met the prespecified absolute criterion for noninferiority to wire-based FFR at 1 year. Because the observed event rate was lower than anticipated, the margin was less conservative on a relative scale than intended. In a post hoc sensitivity analysis using the relative margin of 1.44 implied by the original assumptions, noninferiority was not met in the primary modified intention-to-treat population. In the corresponding post hoc per-protocol sensitivity analysis, noninferiority was met using this relative margin. Whether that additional revascularization is beneficial is not answered by similar 1-year event rates. (Comparison of Vessel-FFR Versus FFR in Intermediate Coronary Stenoses; NCT03497637; Protocol ID HRC045277.).

items.title: Trial Registration in an Era of Rapidly Evolving Technology
Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features
items.abstract: Background Current guidelines recommend echocardiographic surveillance every 1-2 years for patients with moderate aortic stenosis (AS). Ongoing randomized trials are evaluating transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for patients with moderate AS and at-risk features associated with rapid progression or poor outcomes. The prevalence and prognostic impact of these features in clinical practice are unknown. Objectives To determine the prevalence and prognostic impact of at-risk features in real-world clinical practice among patients with moderate AS. Methods We analyzed deidentified data from 14,859,523 patients at 48 US institutions (egnite Registry; IRB exempt). Patients with moderate or severe AS per echocardiographic assessment (ACC/AHA guidelines) identified on or after January 1 , 2022, were included. At-risk features for moderate AS (PROGRESS trial criteria) included valve-related symptoms, left ventricular ejection fraction <60%, diastolic dysfunction grade ≥2, stroke volume index <35 mL/m , atrial fibrillation, or elevated natriuretic peptide. Outcomes were 2-year mortality, hospitalization with heart failure, aortic valve replacement (AVR), and progression to severe AS (Kaplan-Meier for mortality; Aalen-Johansen with death as a competing event for the others). Results Among 53,994 patients with at least moderate AS, 35,343 (65.5%) were moderate, and 18,651 (34.5%) were severe. Among patients with moderate AS, 27,815 (78.7%) had at least 1 at-risk feature. At 2 years, the cumulative mortality for patients with moderate AS without at-risk features, moderate AS with at-risk features, and severe AS was 9.0% (95% CI, 8.1–9.9), 20.1% (95% CI, 19.5–20.7), and 23.5% (95% CI, 22.7–24.3), and hospitalization with heart failure was 21.9% (95% CI, 20.7–23.2), 44.6% (95% CI, 43.8–45.3), and 54.8% (95% CI, 53.9–55.8), respectively (p value <0.0001 for both). With follow-up censored at AVR, progression to severe AS at 2 years was similar with and without at-risk features (28.2% vs 26.3%). Conclusions In this large real-world cohort, the vast majority of patients with moderate AS had at-risk features and experienced worse clinical outcomes, with 2-fold higher risks of mortality and hospitalization with heart failure than those without at-risk features, despite similar progression to severe AS. These findings support risk-based stratification of moderate AS and investigation of strategies to reduce adverse events in patients with at-risk features.

items.title: 10-Year Outcomes of Initial CTO-PCI vs No CTO-PCI Strategies for Chronic Total Occlusion
items.abstract: Background The long-term clinical effects of percutaneous coronary intervention for chronic total occlusion (CTO-PCI) remain uncertain. Objectives This study aimed to compare 10-year clinical outcomes between initial CTO-PCI and no CTO-PCI strategies in the extended follow-up of the DECISION-CTO trial. Methods The DECISION-CTO trial was an open-label, multicenter, randomized trial conducted at 19 centers in 5 Asian countries. Patients were randomly assigned to an initial strategy of CTO-PCI or no CTO-PCI, with guideline-directed medical therapy in both groups and PCI of obstructive non-CTO lesions encouraged in both groups. The primary endpoint was a composite of death from any cause, myocardial infarction, stroke, or any revascularization at 10 years, analyzed in the modified intention-to-treat group. Results Between March 2010 and October 2016, 834 patients were randomly assigned, and 804 of these patients were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (413 CTO-PCI, 391 no CTO-PCI). Clinical follow-up at 10 years was complete in 688 patients (85.6%), without a significant between-group difference (P = 0.69). At 10 years, the primary endpoint had occurred in 134 patients in the CTO-PCI group and 138 patients in the no CTO-PCI group (Kaplan-Meier estimates: 33.9% vs 37.4%; risk difference: -3.5 percentage points; 95% CI: -10.4 to 3.3 percentage points; P = 0.32). Restricted mean event-free survival time at 10 years was also similar between groups (7.52 vs 7.53 years; difference: -0.01 years; 95% CI: -0.54 to 0.52 years; P = 0.97). Death from any cause did not differ significantly between groups (12.7% vs 16.5%; HR: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.52-1.12; P = 0.16). Conclusions Over 10 years, an initial strategy of CTO-PCI was not associated with a significant difference in the primary endpoint or all-cause mortality compared with an initial strategy of no CTO-PCI. However, the wide CIs preclude definitive conclusions regarding the potential benefit or harm of an initial CTO-PCI strategy. (Drug-Eluting Stent Implantation Versus Optimal Medical Treatment in Patients With Chronic Total Occlusion [DECISION-CTO]; NCT01078051; extended follow-up, NCT06908499).

Single vs Double ProGlide Devices for Access Site Closure after Transfemoral Aortic Valve Replacement
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite advances in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), access-site vascular complications remain an important source of procedural morbidity. The conventional double-ProGlide strategy may increase the risk of access-site stenosis and other vascular complications, particularly in patients with challenging iliofemoral anatomy. Retrospective studies have suggested that a single-ProGlide strategy may offer an effective alternative, but this strategy has not yet been evaluated in a randomized trial. OBJECTIVES: This trial aimed to determine whether a single-ProGlide strategy could offer a simpler alternative to the conventional double-ProGlide strategy without increasing vascular complications. METHODS: The SINGLE-CLOSURE trial was a prospective, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 25 centers in China. Patients aged ≥65 years scheduled for transfemoral TAVR were assigned 1:1 to single-ProGlide or double-ProGlide closure for the main access site. The primary endpoint was the in-hospital composite of Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC)-3-defined access-site or access-related major and minor vascular complications. RESULTS: A total of 876 patients were randomized. In the modified intention-to-treat population, the primary endpoint occurred in 57 of 436 patients (13.1%) in the single-ProGlide group and 65 of 430 patients (15.1%) in the double-ProGlide group, meeting the prespecified criterion for noninferiority (risk difference: -2.2%; 95%: -7.0% to 2.6%; P = 0.013; noninferiority margin: 3.19%). Access-related major vascular complications occurred in 2 patients (0.5%) in the single-ProGlide group and 6 patients (1.4%) in the double-ProGlide group. Among the secondary endpoints, individual components of the primary endpoint, access-related bleeding, time to hemostasis, and all-cause mortality were similar between groups. Access-site stenosis was numerically less frequent with the single-ProGlide strategy (5.0% vs 7.9%), whereas additional closure devices might be used more often (2.5% vs 0.9%). CONCLUSIONS: A single-ProGlide strategy was noninferior to conventional double-ProGlide closure for the composite of VARC-3-defined access-site or access-related vascular complications after transfemoral TAVR. Primary endpoint events were predominantly minor vascular complications.

items.title: Percutaneous Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement for Symptomatic Mitral Regurgitation
items.abstract: Background Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is an approved treatment option for select high-risk patients with symptomatic mitral regurgitation (MR). The main cohort of the ENCIRCLE trial, evaluating fully percutaneous transseptal TMVR with the SAPIEN M3 system, demonstrated 13.9% mortality, significant MR reduction, and improved functional and health status outcomes at 1 year. Objectives We report 2-year outcomes from the main cohort of the ENCIRCLE trial. Methods Eligible symptomatic patients with ≥3+ MR who were not suitable for surgery or transcatheter edge-to-edge repair underwent TMVR with the SAPIEN M3 system. Independent study oversight included an echocardiographic core laboratory and a clinical events committee. Endpoints included the nonhierarchical composite rate of all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization (HFH) as well as clinical, echocardiographic, functional, and health status outcomes. Results A total of 299 patients were treated, with 2-year follow-up data available for 202 of 210 eligible patients (96.2%). Mean age was 75.5 ± 9.3 years, 50.8% were men, and the mean Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality score for mitral valve replacement was 6.6% ± 4.1%. At 2 years, MR reduction was sustained, with MR ≤1+ in 97.0% patients (P Conclusions The 2-year results of the ENCIRCLE trial demonstrated durable near MR elimination with sustained improvements in functional and health status outcomes in surviving patients. These findings support transseptal TMVR as a therapeutic option for carefully selected patients with symptomatic MR. (The ENCIRCLE Trial [ENCIRCLE]; NCT04153292).

items.title: Coming Full Circle
Outcomes of Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement for Aortic Regurgitation in LVAD Patients: The JENA-VAD Study
items.abstract: Background Aortic regurgitation (AR) during left ventricular assist device (LVAD) support causes recurrent heart failure. Surgery is high risk and stenosis-designed valves anchor poorly in noncalcified anatomy. Objectives The goal of this study was to evaluate early outcomes of the AR-specific Trilogy transcatheter heart valve for LVAD-associated AR. Methods JENA-VAD is a prospective, multicenter, single-arm investigational device exemption study. An independent committee adjudicated endpoints using VARC-3 (Valve Academic Research Consortium-3) definitions. The primary efficacy endpoint was the VARC-3 device success composite adapted for LVAD support, and the primary safety endpoint was the VARC-3 early safety composite. Results Fifty patients were treated (mean age 69.2 years; 40% female). Median follow-up was 105 days (range 27 to 577 days). Technical and device success were 96.0% (95% CI: 86.3-99.5). Freedom from any component event of the VARC-3 early safety composite was 90.0% (95% CI: 78.2-96.7). At 30 days, 7 VARC-3 safety events occurred in 5 patients: type 2 to 4 bleeding (n = 2), major vascular complications (n = 2), device-related peripheral interventions (n = 2), and new pacemaker (1 of 7 without prior pacing; 14.3%). There were no strokes or myocardial infarctions. Two transient ischemic attacks occurred in patients without valve abnormalities. Beyond 30 days, cardiovascular death occurred in 1 patient (day 86). Follow-up computed tomography (CT) imaging or transesophageal echocardiography was obtained in 12 patients, and 11 (including 3 within 30 days) had leaflet thickening or thrombosis, including all patients who underwent CT. The remaining 38 patients did not have postprocedure imaging. Two of these events were symptomatic: valve thrombosis and a transient ischemic attack (day 116), and prosthetic AR that required valve-in-valve implantation (day 146) and subsequent heart transplantation. In exploratory analyses, NYHA functional class at 30 days was I or II in 72.3% (34 of 47) and Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire overall summary score rose 11.5 ± 21.5 points (n = 44). Conclusions Transcatheter valve replacement using a dedicated system in LVAD patients was feasible with high technical and device success and without early death, stroke, or moderate or severe residual AR. Leaflet thickening or thrombosis, detected on clinically indicated CT imaging, occurred in 22%, representing a lower bound. Follow-up is ongoing to inform longer-term safety and effectiveness. (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Using the JenaValve Trilogy Heart Valve System for Clinically Significant Aortic Regurgitation in Patients With Left Ventricular Assist Devices [LVAD]; NCT06594705).

items.title: AI-Enabled Echocardiography Identifies Prominent Epicardial Adipose Tissue Associated With an Adverse Cardiometabolic Profile
items.limitations: Certain limitations merit consideration. First, the training label was an expert-reader assignment of a prominent epicardial fat depot extracted from routine clinical reports, which is more specific than sensitive. Report-negative studies were labeled negative, and external cohorts lacked report labels (MIMIC-IV echocardiography reports are not available); we therefore used CT-derived EAT as the quantitative reference standard. Clinical reports flag overt accumulation rather than applying a standardized echocardiographic threshold for epicardial adiposity. The continuous biomarker score nevertheless tracks a graded spectrum of severity, as supported by its correlation with CT-quantified EAT and its graded associations with cardiometabolic biomarkers and newly documented disease.

Right Heart Dysfunction in Valvular Heart Disease
items.abstract: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is an important determinant of clinical outcomes across a wide range of cardiovascular pathologies. As the prevalence of valvular heart disease (VHD) increases with the aging population, the intersection between RV function and VHD will become all the more relevant for proper risk assessment, treatment selection, and prognostication. Even though RV dysfunction may not always be attributed to VHD, we aim to give clinicians, researchers, and regulators a deep understanding of how patients with VHD should be evaluated for RV dysfunction and treated when RV dysfunction coexists with VHD. We begin with a discussion of the epidemiology and diagnostic evaluation of RV dysfunction in patients with a variety of VHD subgroups, including right-side (ie, associated with the tricuspid valve) and left-side (ie, associated with the mitral and aortic valves) VHD. Attention is also given in that section to contemporary methods and evolving techniques for identifying and phenotyping different forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD. No single imaging test practically or comprehensively captures all degrees and forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD; therefore, the discussion emphasizes integrating evidence from different imaging modalities and hemodynamic assessments. The second component of the review discusses how RV dysfunction affects therapeutic options, including medical, transcatheter, and surgical therapies for VHD. The focus of the discussion is on the interplay between RV dysfunction in patients with right-side VHD, namely tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Unlike left-side VHD, where RV dysfunction is a marker of overall disease severity but does not necessarily indicate futility or nonresponse to therapy, right-side VHD and TR-associated RV dysfunction identifies a subset of patients where intervention may precipitate even worse RV function. The nuances of these interactions between ventricular and valvular function are the emphasis of this section, and we aim to provide a framework for understanding RV function in the context of these different forms of VHD. Finally, the review concludes with an eye to the future, discussing the ways in which RV dysfunction can be identified and managed with the use of novel techniques. This discussion is increasingly relevant as RV dysfunction and VHD frequently coexist, and accurate identification is critical to matching the right treatment for the right patient.

items.abstract: Background Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is increasingly used as an alternative to oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. Its comparative effectiveness and safety in patients at a high risk of both stroke and bleeding remain uncertain. Objectives We evaluated the efficacy and safety of LAAC vs contemporary medical therapy in a high-risk population using individual participant data from randomized trials. Methods Bibliographic databases and trial registries through August 5, 2026, were searched for randomized trials comparing percutaneous LAAC with contemporary medical therapy in populations with a trial-level mean CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score ≥4. A 1-stage common-effect analysis used Cox models stratified by trial and adjusted for age, sex, CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score, and HAS-BLED score. Both primary outcomes were time to first stroke, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular/unknown death (efficacy) and time to first major bleeding (safety). A flexible time-varying Cox model was used for major bleeding. The protocol was submitted to PROSPERO (CRD420261335972). Results CLOSURE-AF (Left Atrial Appendage CLOSURE in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Compared to Medical Therapy) and PRAGUE-17 (Left Atrial Appendage Closure vs. Novel Anticoagulation Agents in Atrial Fibrillation) contributed 1,290 participants (647 assigned to LAAC and 643 to control). Median age was 77.3 years (Q1-Q3: 71.4-81.9 years), and 809 participants (62.7%) were men. The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 142 LAAC participants (21.9%) and 133 control subjects (20.7%) (adjusted HR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.77-1.24; P = 0.842). Major bleeding occurred in 86 LAAC participants (13.3%) and 80 control subjects (12.4%) (adjusted HR: 1.03; 95% CI: 0.75-1.39; P = 0.874). The treatment effect on major bleeding varied over time (P for treatment-by-time interaction Conclusions In high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation, no statistically significant difference was detected between LAAC and contemporary medical therapy for the primary efficacy outcome or major bleeding. The major bleeding hazard varied over time, with higher early and lower later conditional hazard estimates; however, a cumulative bleeding benefit was not demonstrated by 3 years. Long-term randomized data are needed to improve the precision of later treatment-effect estimates.

items.title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Anticoagulation for Atrial Fibrillation
items.abstract: Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as an alternative to long-term anticoagulation for preventing stroke or systemic embolism in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) based on several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that collectively enrolled >7,000 participants. In this JACC Evidence Review, we interpret the major RCTs as distinct experiments, clarify what each can and cannot establish, and offer a phenotype-based framework for interpreting the evidence. The most recent RCTs, OPTION, CLOSURE-AF, and CHAMPION-AF, have prompted efforts to pool the evidence into a single summary estimate. However, these trials are not one coherent evidence base; they are distinct clinical experiments that asked different questions. They differ in patient phenotype, comparator, device generation, postprocedure antithrombotic regimen, endpoint construction, and follow-up duration. Study-level meta-analysis of published reports remains methodologically valid for estimating the broad direction of effect of a device class, but when the component trials differ materially in patient phenotype, comparator, and outcome construction, the pooled estimate does not map to a common patient group or treatment decision. Patient eligibility as well as thromboembolic and bleeding risk varied markedly across trials. In addition, device technology has progressed, and comparators have evolved from warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants. Heterogeneity and insufficient details also exist about the antithrombotic therapy regimen in LAAC arms and adjunct antiplatelet therapy in control arms. Methodological issues further complicate interpretation, including the use of bleeding events (ie, the putative ancillary benefit of LAAC compared with anticoagulation) within composite endpoints tested for noninferiority, varying noninferiority margins, analytical approaches that may undermine the interpretation of noninferiority, and exclusion of periprocedural bleeding from primary safety endpoints in some trials. Finally, the standard of care for anticoagulation in AF has evolved, obviating concomitant aspirin use in stable individuals on therapeutic anticoagulation, thereby reducing bleeding risk compared with that of the control arm of LAAC RCTs. For most anticoagulation-eligible patients, anticoagulation remains the preferred first-line strategy. LAAC is a reasonable option when long-term anticoagulation is unsafe or unsustainable provided that procedural risk, adjunct antithrombotic feasibility, surveillance needs, and competing mortality are carefully considered. RCT evidence in this latter population is limited, and RCTs in other populations have features that limit their support for LAAC as an alternative to anticoagulation. Because LAAC and anticoagulation offer different types of risk, aligning the most applicable evidence with patient values through shared decision-making is central to care.

items.title: When and How to Consider Left Atrial Appendage Closure as a Management Option for Patients With Atrial Fibrillation
Antithrombotic Therapy Management After Left Atrial Appendage Closure
items.abstract: Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure is increasingly used for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation, particularly when long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC) is unsuitable. Although postprocedural antithrombotic therapy is necessary to prevent device-related thrombosis (DRT), it may increase bleeding and attenuate the benefit of avoiding long-term OAC. Uncertainty over the optimal antithrombotic strategy persists, with available randomized trials being small and heterogeneous. Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) monotherapy and dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) are 2 common early strategies. In ANDES, DRT was numerically less frequent with DOAC than with DAPT (1.5% vs 4.1%). In ADALA, low-dose apixaban was associated with greater net benefit than DAPT (HR: 0.19; P = 0.02), although enrollment was prematurely stopped. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found significantly lower DRT with DOAC than with DAPT (risk ratio: 0.17). Current guidelines endorse regimens largely based on device-specific trial protocols or low-certainty evidence. During the initial postimplantation period, antithrombotic therapy should primarily aim to support device healing and prevent DRT, with treatment intensity tailored according to risk profile, concomitant indications, patient preferences, and the feasibility of imaging follow-up. Reassessment at 45 to 90 days should guide de-escalation once adequate device healing has been confirmed, with no fixed treatment stop date. In the absence of device-related complications, long-term OAC or DAPT should be continued only for concomitant indications, whereas continuation of single antiplatelet therapy or complete withdrawal of antithrombotic therapy should be individualized according to thrombotic and bleeding risk. Finally, definite or probable DRT generally warrants OAC, when feasible; in contrast, treatment decisions should not be based solely on the presence or size of a peridevice leak. This review critically appraises the available evidence and guideline recommendations and discusses how treatment intensity and duration may be tailored over time according to evolving thrombotic and bleeding risks.

Comparison of Outcomes Between Men and Women Treated With Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Oral Anticoagulation After Catheter Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation
items.abstract: Background Women sex is an established, nonmodifiable risk factor for adverse outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has been proposed as an alternative to oral anticoagulation (OAC) for stroke prevention in patients with AF; however, there are limited data on sex-based outcomes of LAAC following catheter ablation. Objectives This study sought to compare outcomes of LAAC vs OAC after AF ablation in men and women. Methods Patients with AF and CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc ≥2 in men and ≥3 in women were randomized 1:1 to either ablation + LAAC or ablation + OAC. The primary safety endpoint was nonprocedural major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding at 36 months. The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 36 months. Results The study included 1,053 men and 546 women. LAAC and OAC demonstrated comparable primary efficacy events in men (HR: 0.96; 95% CI: 0.56-1.65; P = 0.88) and women (HR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.41-1.62; P = 0.55), with no treatment-by-sex interaction (P interaction = 0.71). Procedural complication rates were similar at 2.3% in men and 3.7% in women with only 1 pericardial effusion in each group, not related to the index LAAC procedure. At 36 months, the primary safety endpoint was significantly lower in the device group among men (HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.23-0.50; P Conclusions In this prespecified analysis of the OPTION (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]) trial, stroke, systemic embolism, and mortality outcomes were not significantly different between LAAC and OAC following AF ablation in either men or women. Compared with OAC, LAAC demonstrated a greater magnitude of major and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding reduction in men as compared with women. (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]; NCT03795298).

items.title: What Counts in a Stroke-Prevention Strategy?

Left Atrial Appendage Closure in Patients Considered Unsuitable for Oral Anticoagulation
items.abstract: Background Oral anticoagulation (OAC) use in atrial fibrillation is suboptimal due to real or perceived bleeding risks. Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an alternative to OAC, but pivotal trials used OAC comparators. Objectives The study sought to assess the long-term safety and effectiveness of LAAC in patients deemed unsuitable for OAC. Methods The ASAP-TOO trial was a multinational randomized trial of patients with atrial fibrillation, CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 years, diabetes mellitus, prior stroke or transient ischemic attack or thromboembolism, vascular disease, age 65-74 years, sex category) score ≥2, and OAC unsuitability; target enrollment was 888 patients. Patients were assigned 2:1 to LAAC with a Watchman device or control treatment-single antiplatelet therapy or no therapy. Device patients received dual antiplatelet therapy for 3 months and aspirin through 12 months. The primary effectiveness endpoint was ischemic stroke or systemic embolism; the primary safety endpoint was death, ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, or 7-day device/procedure-related events requiring major intervention. Results Enrollment stopped early because of slow accrual, accentuated by the COVID-19 pandemic: only 481 patients were randomized (320 LAAC, 161 control treatment) and withdrawal was significant (7.8% LAAC, 24.2% control treatment), with disparate follow-up durations (median 876 days and 440.1 total patient-years of follow-up for control patients; median 1,768 days and 1,154.6 total patient-years of follow-up for LAAC patients), reducing statistical power. Patients were 75 ± 8 years of age, the CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score was 4.6 ± 1.7, and 34% had prior intracranial/subdural hemorrhage. Implantation success was 97.8%. Only 31 of the 101 planned primary effectiveness events occurred, fewer than the 34 events required to trigger the first planned interim analysis. The primary safety endpoint occurred in 1.0% of implant-attempted patients, meeting the prespecified performance goal (P Conclusions In this prematurely terminated and underpowered trial, LAAC implantation was successful, with acceptable safety. Long-term estimates with LAAC were numerically favorable for thromboembolism but imprecise, while early bleeding was increased with the mandated antiplatelet regimen. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory and integrated with contemporary evidence and shared decision making. (Assessment of the WATCHMAN Device in Patients Unsuitable for Oral Anticoagulation [ASAP-TOO]; NCT02928497).

Intravascular Lithotripsy vs Super-High-Pressure Noncompliant Balloons for Treatment of Calcified Coronary Lesions
items.abstract: Background Although calcified coronary lesions are associated with poor outcomes after percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI), randomized data guiding lesion preparation are limited. Small studies suggest potential benefits of super-high-pressure noncompliant balloons (SH-NCB); however, they have not been directly compared with intravascular lithotripsy (IVL). Objectives The goal of this study was to conduct a randomized comparison of SH-NCBs vs IVL in calcified lesions. Methods In this open-label, randomized controlled, noninferiority trial with blinded outcomes assessment (ie, the PROBE design), patients aged ≥18 years with calcified coronary lesions were randomly assigned (1:1) to undergo lesion preparation with SH-NCBs or IVL before PCI with drug-eluting stents. All patients were required to undergo optical coherence tomography (OCT). The primary endpoint was final stent expansion (%) according to OCT. Secondary endpoints included procedural success, strategy success, target vessel failure, stent expansion <80%, and safety outcomes (eg, coronary perforation). Results Between December 21, 2022, and August 11, 2025, a total of 278 patients underwent the randomly assigned study procedure using plaque modification with SH-NCBs or IVL before stent implantation. The majority of patients (68%) had severe calcium based on an OCT Fujino score ≥4. Study procedures involving IVL tended to be longer and require more auxiliary devices compared with SH-NCBs. The median pressure applied with SH-NCBs compared with IVL was 40 atmospheres vs 6 atmospheres. Regarding the primary endpoint of stent expansion, SH-NCBs were noninferior to IVL (85% vs 84%; P noninferiority < 0.0001). The results were consistent across all subgroups, including calcium severity. Use of SH-NCBs, compared with IVL, resulted in similar rates of procedural and strategy success. Safety outcomes, specifically coronary perforations, did not differ between the 2 groups. At 30 days’ follow-up, target vessel failure events (including cardiac death, target vessel revascularization, or myocardial infarction) occurred in 4 (2.8%) patients in the SH-NCB group and in 8 (5.7%) patients in the IVL group (HR: 0.50; 95% CI: 0.15 to 1.66; P = 0.26). Conclusions In calcified coronary lesions, SH-NCBs were noninferior to IVL for stent expansion and exhibited a comparable safety profile in experienced operators using intravascular imaging. (Value of IVL Compared To OPN Non-Compliant Balloons for Treatment of Refractory Coronary Lesions [VICTORY]; NCT05346068 )

items.abstract: Background Contemporary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has improved outcomes in three-vessel disease (3VD). However, the Supraflex Cruz sirolimus-eluting stent (SES) has not been compared with the SYNERGY everolimus-eluting stent (EES) in this setting. Objectives We compared the performance of the Supraflex Cruz SES and the SYNERGY EES in patients with de novo 3VD undergoing contemporary PCI. Methods We randomized 1,548 patients to the Supraflex Cruz SES (n=774) or the SYNERGY EES (n=774). Patients were selected after Heart Team discussion incorporating the SYNTAX Score II. Contemporary PCI included angiography-derived physiology, intravascular imaging optimization, CTO expertise, and short DAPT followed by prasugrel monotherapy. The primary endpoint was the 1-year patient-oriented composite endpoint (POCE: all-cause death, any stroke, any myocardial infarction, or any revascularization), estimated by Kaplan–Meier in the intention-to-treat population. The non-inferiority margin was 4.28%. Results Median follow-up was 367 days (IQR, 362–372). At 1 year, POCE was 15.23% (95% CI, 12.87–17.96) with Supraflex Cruz SES and 14.51% (95% CI, 12.20–17.21) with SYNERGY EES. The risk difference was 0.72 percentage points; the one-sided 95% upper confidence bound was 3.71%, below the margin (P non-inferiority=0.025). Myocardial infarction occurred in 10.07% (95% CI, 8.14–12.43) versus 8.14% (95% CI, 6.41–10.33), revascularization in 6.40% (95% CI, 4.86–8.40) versus 6.81% (95% CI, 5.22–8.87), and stent thrombosis in 1.31% (95% CI, 0.71–2.43) versus 1.08% (95% CI, 0.54–2.14). Conclusions In patients with 3VD undergoing contemporary PCI, the Supraflex Cruz SES was noninferior to the SYNERGY EES for 1-year POCE. Clinical Trial Registration NCT04390672

items.title: Fully Retrievable Self-Expanding Short-Frame Valve for Aortic Regurgitation
Prognostic Impact of Discharge Transprosthetic Tricuspid Gradient After Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement
items.abstract: Background Although transprosthetic gradients are established prognostic markers after left-sided valve interventions, the prognostic significance of discharge tricuspid gradient (dTVG) after transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) remains unclear. Objectives This study sought to evaluate the association between dTVG and clinical outcomes after TTVR and identify high dTVG determinants. Methods TRIPLACE (Global Multicenter Registry on Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement) is an international, multicenter TTVR registry. A discharge landmark analysis was performed, excluding patients with in-hospital mortality, lack of TTVR technical success, missing dTVG, or unavailable follow-up at any time point. Endpoints included all-cause mortality and the composite of all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization. The optimal dTVG cutoff was identified through quartile-based survival analysis and confirmed by log-rank maximization. Multivariable Cox models were developed using cross-validated candidate variable selection. Results Among 526 patients, 474 were included. Median follow-up was 208.5 days (Q1-Q3: 54-474 days). A data-driven dTVG cutoff of 3.5 mm Hg identified 122 of 474 patients (25.7%) with high dTVG. dTVG ≥3.5 mm Hg was associated with higher 1- and 3-year mortality (HR: 2.07; 95% CI: 1.14-3.75; P = 0.017 and HR: 2.07; 95% CI: 1.24-3.48; P = 0.006, respectively) and composite endpoint events (HR: 1.99; 95% CI: 1.31-3.03; P = 0.001 and HR: 1.96; 95% CI: 1.33-2.88; P 2 increase; 95% CI: 0.71-0.88). Conclusions Elevated dTVG after TTVR independently identifies patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes. A 3.5 mm Hg threshold may support postprocedural risk stratification, whereas inner valve diameter represents a potentially modifiable determinant of elevated dTVG. (TRIPLACE [Global Multicenter Registry on Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement]; NCT06033274).

items.title: One Lesion, Two Perspectives
Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve-in-Valve and Valve-in-Ring Implantation: the TRIVIR registry
items.abstract: Background Transcatheter tricuspid valve-in-valve (TViV) and valve-in-ring (TViR) procedures are increasingly used; however, data on clinical outcomes, valve performance, and symptomatic improvement remain limited. Objectives To evaluate a real-world multicenter cohort undergoing transcatheter TViV and TViR procedures. Methods We conducted an international multicenter registry including patients undergoing TViV/TViR procedures. The TRIVIR Registry evaluated all-cause mortality and a composite endpoint (CE), defined as all-cause mortality, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, and tricuspid bioprosthesis degeneration during follow-up. Results Between 2012 and 2025, 75 patients underwent TViV (n=62) or TViR (n=13) across 16 centers using Sapien (88%) or Myval (12%) valves. Median follow up was 1.86 years (IQR 0.10-2.59). Mean age was 62±13 years, and 69% were women. NYHA class III–IV decreased from 72% at baseline to 13% at 1-3 months and remained low during follow-up. No 30-day deaths occurred, while periprocedural complications occurred in 24% of procedures, mostly minor (17.3%). At 3 years, the Kaplan–Meier estimates of all-cause mortality and CE were 35.6% and 42.9%, and the cumulative incidences of HF hospitalization and tricuspid bioprosthesis degeneration were 16.6% and 11.4%, respectively. Patients who died had markers of advanced disease, including higher NT-proBNP levels, greater diuretic requirements, more frequent pacing/CRT implantation, and higher procedural complication rates. Conclusions TViV/TViR represents a viable treatment strategy and provided sustained symptomatic improvement in high-risk patients. Patients who died exhibited a more advanced clinical profile, highlighting the importance of appropriate patient selection, early referral, and treatment in experienced centers.
