items.abstract: BACKGROUND Paravalvular leak (PVL) is a complication of surgical valve replacement and is associated with poor prognosis. Percutaneous device closure offers a less invasive alternative to repeat surgery. OBJECTIVE Evaluate the Amplatzer Valvular Plug III (APVL3) for PVL closure after surgical implant of a mechanical or bioprosthetic valve. METHODS PARADIGM is a prospective, multicenter, single-arm study assessing transcatheter PVL closure. The primary endpoint was a composite of safety and effectiveness measures evaluating the implant success, PVL reduction ≥2 grades on exit from the procedure, procedural mortality, and device-related reinterventions through 30 days. Descriptive safety and performance endpoints were evaluated at 30 days. RESULTS A total of 200 patients were enrolled across 24 sites in the United States, Europe, and Canada. Average age was 67.7+/-11.5 years, 58.5% were male, and 70.0% had a mechanical valve. Median(IQR) logistic EuroSCORE was 5.2(3.2,10.3), median(IQR) STS PROM was 2.9%(1.4,5.4), and 53.1%(104/196) were NYHA class III/IV. Heart failure was the primary indication for PVL closure (89.5%), and 65.0% were treated for mitral PVL. Successful implantation was achieved in 96.0%(192/200), with no procedural mortality. The primary endpoint was met in 94.0%(188/200), exceeding the performance goal(P<0.0001). The 30-day procedural success was 77.3%(140/181). At 30 days, mortality was 2.0%(4/200,95%CI:0.5-5.0), hemolytic anemia occurred in 3.5%(7/200,95% CI:1.42%,7.08%), 95.7%(156/163) had mild or less PVL, 82.7%(143/173) were NYHA class I/II, and KCCQ-OS improved by 15.7(12.6,18.8) points. CONCLUSION PARADIGM met its primary endpoint, with favorable short-term outcomes. The results support this transcatheter device as a promising therapeutic option for PVL closure. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04489823

items.title: Posterior Leaflet Restoration for Secondary Mitral Regurgitation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Secondary mitral regurgitation (MR) contributes to morbidity and mortality in patients with symptomatic valve disease. Although transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is beneficial, many patients remain suboptimal candidates. Posterior leaflet restoration (PLR) provides a prosthetic coaptation surface via an adaptive coaptation element that inflates during systole and deflates during diastole to facilitate leaflet coaptation. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate the safety and feasibility of PLR using the MRace implant (Polares Medical, Inc). METHODS: Early Feasibility Experience of Posterior Leaflet Restoration to Reduce Mitral Regurgitation Using the MRace Implant in Georgia and Brazil (EXPLORE MR) enrolled 78 symptomatic patients with severe secondary MR (≥3+), stratified post hoc by left ventricular end-diastolic volume: nonseverely enlarged left ventricle (NSELV) (N = 46) and severely enlarged left ventricle (SELV) (N = 32). The primary endpoint was 30-day mortality; secondary endpoints were MR reduction and functional outcomes. RESULTS: The implant was successfully deployed in 96.2% of patients. All-cause mortality at 30 days was 6.4%. MR ≤2+ was achieved in 93.8% of patients at 30 days and was sustained in 90.6% at 1 year. Patients with NSELV showed better results in MR ≤1+ at every time point (94.4% at 30 days, 89.5% at 1 year) compared with the SELV group (79.3% and 69.2%, respectively). The NSELV subgroup demonstrated better functional recovery, with NYHA functional class I or II rising from 8.7% to 84.2%, vs a more attenuated response in the SELV group (15.6%-76.9%). The 6-minute walk test improved in the paired NSELV cohort (Δ +93.9 m), but not in paired patients with SELV (Δ -7.8 m). Kaplan-Meier 1-year all-cause mortality was 29.5% overall and was better in patients with NSELV (19.4%) than in SELV (41.7%). CONCLUSIONS: PLR with the MRace implant achieves substantial MR reduction and meaningful functional improvement, most pronounced in patients without severely enlarged left ventricles. (XPLORE MRace [BR]: Early Feasibility Experience of Posterior Leaflet Restoration to Reduce Mitral Regurgitation Using the MRace Implant [EXPLORE MRace]; NCT06113354).

items.title: TECTONIC CAD
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Severe coronary calcification complicates percutaneous coronary intervention by limiting lesion compliance and impairing stent expansion. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the SonicForce Coronary Intravascular Lithotripsy System (Abbott Vascular) in severely calcified de novo coronary lesions. METHODS: TECTONIC CAD intravascular lithotripsy investigational device exemption (NCT06885177) was a prospective, multicenter, single-arm study of 335 patients at 40 U.S. CENTERS: The primary safety endpoint was 30-day target lesion failure, defined as cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or clinically driven target lesion revascularization. The primary effectiveness endpoint was procedural success. Each endpoint was tested against a prespecified performance goal. A prespecified optical coherence tomography (OCT) substudy evaluated calcium modification and stent expansion. RESULTS: , with stent expansion of 95.9% ± 18.6%. Calcium fracture was identified in 62.5% (50 of 80) of lesions after intravascular lithotripsy and 66.3% (53 of 80) after stenting. CONCLUSIONS: TECTONIC CAD met both prespecified coprimary safety and effectiveness endpoints, demonstrating low 30-day target lesion failure and high procedural success. OCT demonstrated calcium fracture and favorable stent expansion at maximum contiguous calcium.

items.title: Rotational Atherectomy Plus Intravascular Lithotripsy Versus Intravascular Lithotripsy Alone for Coronary Calcified Nodules
items.abstract: Background Optimal lesion preparation for coronary calcified nodules (CNs) and intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) pulse delivery for severe calcification remain uncertain. Objectives This study sought to evaluate phenotype-specific calcium modification in severe calcification with and without CNs. Methods In this single-center randomized trial using a new-generation coronary IVL catheter, patients with optical coherence tomography-defined CNs (Cohort A) were assigned 1:1 to rotational atherectomy (RA) plus IVL or IVL alone; patients with severe calcification without CNs (Cohort B) were assigned 1:1 to maximum or operator-determined IVL pulses. Primary endpoints were minimum stent area (MSA) at the CN site in Cohort A and at the maximum calcium arc site in Cohort B. Results Among 120 patients, 66 (55%) were in Cohort A (33 per group) and 54 (45%) in Cohort B (27 per group). MSA at the CN site was 7.41 ± 2.12 mm 2 with RA plus IVL vs 6.23 ± 1.55 mm 2 with IVL alone (mean difference: 1.18 mm 2 ; 95% CI: 0.27-2.09; P = 0.012). In Cohort B, MSA at the maximum calcium arc site was 5.50 ± 1.19 mm 2 with maximum IVL pulses vs 5.56 ± 1.45 mm 2 with operator-determined IVL pulses (mean difference: -0.06 mm 2 ; 95% CI: -0.78 to 0.67; P = 0.873). Conclusions RA plus IVL increased final stent area vs IVL alone in CN lesions, whereas maximum IVL pulses did not significantly increase final stent area compared with operator-determined pulses in severe calcification without CNs. These findings warrant validation in larger multicenter trials with clinical endpoints. (Coronary Calcified Nodule Management With Rotational Atherectomy Plus Shockwave Intravascular Lithotripsy vs Intravascular Lithotripsy Alone: A Prospective, Randomized Trial [NODULE-SHOCK]; ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07000045).

items.title: 1-Year Safety and Effectiveness of a Next-Generation Dual-Seal Left Atrial Appendage Occluder
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is a stroke prevention alternative for patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) intolerant to long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC). The next-generation dual-seal device was designed to improve operator ease of use while maintaining effective LAAO of the predicate device. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this analysis was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a next-generation device through 1 year. METHODS: VERITAS is a single-arm, prospective, global, multicenter study. Patients with nonvalvular AF with an increased thromboembolism risk seeking a nonpharmacologic alternative to OAC were enrolled. One-year descriptive endpoints are provided, including mortality, neurological events, major bleeding, and device-related complications. One-year cardiac imaging was assessed for peridevice leak and device-related thrombus (DRT). RESULTS: Complete left atrial appendage (LAA) closure (0 mm leak) was observed in 91.1% (95% CI: 87.9%-93.7%) of patients by either transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or cardiac computed tomography and 96.3% (95% CI: 93.2%-98.2%) by TEE alone. The cumulative DRT rate was 3.3% (95% CI: 2.0%-5.3%) with only 0.4% (95% CI: 0.1%-1.5%) deemed clinically relevant. One-year key clinical outcome rates are as follows: all-cause mortality: 3.9% (95% CI: 2.4%-6.3%); cardiovascular mortality: 1.9% (95% CI: 0.9%-3.8%); major bleeding: 6.6% (95% CI: 4.5%-9.2%); ischemic stroke or systemic embolism: 1.8% (95% CI: 0.8%-3.3%); pericardial effusion requiring intervention: 0.9% (95% CI: 0.3%-2.1%). No (0%) device embolization occurred. Median follow-up was 365 days (IQR: 349-380 days). CONCLUSIONS: The VERITAS study results support the 1-year safety and effectiveness of the next-generation device. (Abbott Medical-VERITAS Study; NCT06707688).

items.title: 3-Year Comparison of Sirolimus- Versus Paclitaxel-Coated Balloon Angioplasty in Femoropopliteal Artery Disease
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sirolimus-coated balloons (SCBs) have emerged as alternatives to paclitaxel-coated balloons (PCBs), but randomized comparative data beyond 2 years are lacking. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to compare patient-reported outcomes, effectiveness, and safety through 3 years in symptomatic femoropopliteal artery disease. METHODS: SIRONA was a prospective, multicenter, randomized controlled trial comparing SCB angioplasty with a PCB strategy. Patients were randomized 1:1 after successful predilation. Prespecified 3-year outcomes included walking capacity, health-related quality of life, clinically driven target lesion/vessel revascularization (cdTLR/cdTVR), mortality, major amputation, and amputation-free survival. RESULTS: Among 482 randomized patients (SCB, n = 238; PCB, n = 244), 96.3% had intermittent claudication; 3-year follow-up was completed by 76.5% and 79.6%, respectively. Changes in patient-reported walking distances did not differ between-groups. Three-year freedom from cdTLR was 88.2% (95% CI: 83.1%-91.9%) versus 80.2% (95% CI: 74.1%-85.0%; HR: 0.60, 95% CI: 0.36-0.97; nominal log-rank P = 0.03). Post-hoc analysis suggested time-varying treatment effects (treatment-by-period interaction P = 0.006), with separation after the first year. Freedom from cdTVR (HR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.50-1.21; nominal P = 0.27) and amputation-free survival (HR: 1.09, 95% CI 0.57-2.09; nominal P = 0.79) did not differ. CONCLUSIONS: Through 3 years, no between-group differences were observed in walking capacity and health-related quality of life or clinical safety outcomes between SCB angioplasty and the PCB strategy. Three-year freedom from cdTLR was higher with SCB angioplasty, with treatment effect that varied over time. Given the exploratory, nonmultiplicity-adjusted 3-year analysis, the cdTLR difference requires confirmation.

Location Matters
Cardiac Damage and Clinical Outcomes in Symptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The extent of cardiac damage in patients with aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with worse clinical outcomes. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to investigate the clinical impact of cardiac damage using the updated criteria incorporating the echocardiographic probability of pulmonary hypertension. METHODS: This post hoc subanalysis of LANDMARK trial, which randomized 768 patients with severe AS to the Myval transcatheter heart valve (THV) series or to contemporary THVs (Sapien and Evolut series), used updated cardiac damage classification: stage 0, no cardiac damage; stage 1, left ventricular damage; stage 2, left atrial or mitral valve damage; stage 3, pulmonary artery or tricuspid valve damage; and stage 4, right ventricular damage. The impact of cumulative cardiac damage, defined as meeting all criteria for stages 1 to 4, was also assessed. The primary endpoint was 1-year all-cause mortality. RESULTS: Cardiac damage stages were assessed in 596 patients (stage 0, n = 36; stage 1, n = 88; stage 2, n = 284; stage 3, n = 84; stage 4, n = 104), with a mean age of 80.2 (5.7) years and a mean Society of Thoracic Surgeons score of 3.3% (2.4%). One-year mortality was 0%, 1.1%, 4.7%, 7.2%, and 20.4% in stages 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively (log-rank P < 0.001). The area under the curve for predicting 1-year mortality was 0.739. Patients with cumulative cardiac damage had the highest mortality (23.6%). In the multivariable analysis, stage 4 was independently associated with higher 1-year mortality. CONCLUSIONS: The updated cardiac damage staging stratified 1-year mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, highlighting the importance of comprehensive echocardiographic assessment in severe AS. (LANDMARK Trial: a Randomised Controlled Trial of Myval THV [LANDMARK]; NCT04275726).

items.title: Is Bilateral Occlusion Mandatory?
Transcatheter vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement for Isolated Native Aortic Regurgitation
items.abstract: Background Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is well established for aortic stenosis, while its application for isolated native aortic regurgitation (AR) was previously off label and technically challenging. Comparative data between TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are limited. Objectives The aim of this study was to compare patient characteristics and outcomes of off-label TAVR vs SAVR among patients with isolated native AR. Methods Using the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database, patients ≥65 years of age who underwent TAVR or SAVR for isolated native AR (2017-2023) were identified. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to evaluate short- and long-term outcomes. Fine-Gray models accounted for death as a competing risk, reported as subdistribution HRs (SHRs). Results Among 9,859 patients, 1,742 propensity score-matched pairs were included, with balanced baseline characteristics (mean age 75.8 years vs 75.7 years; female sex 517 of 1,742 [29.7%] vs 528 of 1,742 [30.3%]). In the matched cohort, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization (OR: 0.33; 95% CI: 0.28-0.39; P Conclusions In this analysis, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization and comparable 5-year survival as SAVR, although pacemaker and long-term reinterventions rates were higher.

items.title: Prosthesis–Patient Mismatch and Patient-Centered Outcomes After TAVR
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prosthesis-patient mismatch (PPM) after transcatheter aortic valve replacement has been widely studied for its association with clinical outcomes, but its effect on patient-reported health status remains less defined. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to evaluate the association between PPM severity and health status through 3-year follow-up after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. METHODS: This post hoc analysis of the SCOPE I (Safety and Efficacy of the ACURATE Neo/TF Compared to the SAPIEN 3 Bioprosthesis) randomized trial categorized patients according to PPM severity using Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria. Endpoints included survival and patient-reported health status, with an integrated outcome defined as being alive with good health status (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary score ≥75 without a decline of >10 points from baseline). RESULTS: Among 662 patients, moderate and severe PPM occurred in 184 (27.8%) and 69 (10.4%), respectively. All-cause mortality at 1 and 3 years was 7.0% and 20.5%, with no differences across PPM categories. Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary score was similar through 1 year but lower at 3 years in patients with severe vs no PPM (median 71.1 vs 83.9; P = 0.027). Fewer patients with severe PPM were alive with good health status at 3 years (30.6% vs 49.4%; P = 0.021). In multivariable analysis, severe PPM was associated with a lower likelihood of the integrated outcome (OR: 0.51; 95% CI: 0.27-0.96; P = 0.036), but this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for 30-day mitral regurgitation (OR: 0.59; 95% CI: 0.30-1.15; P = 0.121). CONCLUSIONS: Among survivors, severe PPM was associated with a lower likelihood of good health status at 3 years. This association was attenuated after accounting for 30-day residual mitral regurgitation, suggesting a possible contributory role. Given the post hoc design, the findings are hypothesis-generating.

items.title: Mavacamten for Refractory Dynamic Intraventricular Obstruction After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
The Right-Sided Substrate for Sudden Cardiac Death
Prevalence and Consequences of Guideline-Directed Indications for Aortic Valve Replacement in the EARLY TAVR Trial
items.abstract: BackgroundThe current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association valvular heart disease guidelines were published before several recent trials that provide greater support for early intervention in patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AS). ObjectivesThis study sought to investigate the prevalence and clinical impact of American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Class II recommendations for AVR in the EARLY TAVR trial. MethodsThe EARLY TAVR trial randomized patients with asymptomatic severe AS to transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance (CS) with conversion to TAVR based on development of ACC/AHA Class I indications. Patients in the intention-to-treat cohort were stratified by presence of a Class II indication for AVR at randomization. The primary endpoint of the present analysis was the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization. Interaction tests were performed to assess whether the treatment effect differed by level of guideline recommendation. Timing of conversion to AVR in the CS group according to the presence/absence of Class II indications was also assessed. ResultsOf the 901 patients randomized to TAVR (N = 445) and CS (N = 446), 636 (70.6%) patients had no guideline recommendation, and 265 (29.4%) had at least1 1 Class II recommendation for AVR at the time of randomization. At a median follow-up of 3.8 years, patients with a Class II indication for AVR experienced higher rates of the primary endpoint (Class II: 24.5% vs no recommendation: 14.5%; HR = 1.78; 95% CI: 1.30-2.44; P < 0.001) and were more likely to have acute valve syndrome at the time of conversion. Compared with CS, the relative benefit of early TAVR on the primary endpoint was similar regardless of the presence or absence of a Class II guideline recommendation (HR = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.37-1.02 vs 0.61; 95% CI: 0.40-0.92; Pinteraction = 0.96). ConclusionsAmong patients in the EARLY TAVR trial, Class II indications for AVR were present in almost one-third of patients at baseline. The benefit of early TAVR was consistent regardless of the presence or absence of Class II indications. These findings support the strategy of early TAVR over CS in asymptomatic patients with severe AS, independent of guideline indications. Clinical Trial Registration: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03042104; Unique Identifier: NCT03042104

Development of a Quantitative Contrast CT-Based TAVR-Risk Score to Reliably Predict Deformation in Bicuspid Aortic Valves
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) calcification affects clinical outcomes by causing transcatheter heart valve (THV) deformation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, a computed tomography (CT)-based scoring system for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation has not been established. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to develop a cardiac CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation. METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included consecutive patients with BAV who underwent TAVR using contemporary balloon-expandable valves between January 2016 and December 2024 and who had preprocedural and postprocedural CT imaging. The BAV TAVR-risk score integrated calcification severity and distribution across valve leaflets, raphe, annulus, and left ventricular outflow tract, quantified using a fixed HU-850 threshold of detection on contrast-enhanced CT scans. Score thresholds were derived by receiver operating curve analysis with Youden index optimization. Patients were categorized into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk score groups. RESULTS: Among 321 patients (median follow-up: 1,825 days; Q1-Q3: 765-1,825 days), 56 (17.4%) were classified into the high-risk score group. Both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV occurred in 49 of the 321 patients (15.3%) and were predominantly observed in the high-risk score group. However, in the low-risk score group, 149 of 155 patients (96.1%) demonstrated no underexpansion or eccentricity of the THV. A high BAV TAVR-risk score independently predicted both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV (OR: 89.13; 95% CI: 35.02-226.83; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score provides a systematic method to precisely quantify BAV severity which reliably predicts THV deformation for BAV patients with contemporary balloon-expandable valves and may help guide decision-making in this challenging population.

items.title: Prognostic Impact of Paravalvular Regurgitation in Patients With Severe Low-Flow, Low-Gradient Aortic Stenosis Undergoing TAVR
items.abstract: Background Paravalvular regurgitation (PVR) is a frequent complication after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and may influence clinical outcomes in patients with high-gradient aortic stenosis. However, its prognostic relevance in patients with low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis (LFLG-AS) undergoing TAVR remains incompletely elucidated. Objectives This study sought to evaluate the prognostic significance of PVR severity in patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR with current-generation prostheses. Methods This multicenter registry-based cohort study included consecutive patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR from January 2019 to December 2024 at 17 high-volume Italian centers. PVR severity was classified using a 5-class grading scheme and stratified as Results A total of 1,358 patients were included. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower event-free survival among patients with ≥2+ PVR at discharge compared with those with Conclusions In this large, real-world study of patients with LFLG-AS treated with current-generation TAVR devices, PVR ≥2+ was independently associated with worse clinical outcomes after discharge, regardless of LFLG-AS subtype.

items.abstract: This comment refers to ‘Milvexian with Antiplatelet Therapy after Acute Coronary Syndrome Event’, published in the New England Journal of Medicine; https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2608717. FⅪa inhibitors were developed around a very attractive -though not novel- therapeutic proposition: pathological thrombosis might be reduced while largely preserving physiological haemostasis, potentially dissociating efficacy from safety.2,3 LIBREXIA ACS tested this hypothesis in a contemporary ACS setting and prompts consideration of what this strategy of anticoagulation may offer to patients receiving intensive antiplatelet therapy. Moreover, most patients had undergone revascularization during the index hospitalization and were receiving guideline-directed medical therapy. The rationale for adding an oral anticoagulant in this intensively treated population rests on the persistence of high levels of thrombin generation and FⅪ despite effective platelet inhibition. This concept had found clinical support in the results of the ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51 trial, in which low-dose rivaroxaban added to antiplatelet therapy reduced cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke, at the cost of increased major and intracranial bleeding.4 FⅪa inhibition with milvexian offered the theoretical possibility of preserving this antithrombotic benefit with less interference with physiological haemostasis.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-enhanced electrocardiography for detection and prediction of dilated cardiomyopathy
items.abstract: Background and Aims A major challenge in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) care is the identification and management of individuals at risk before disease manifestation. An artificial intelligence (AI) model applied to electrocardiography (ECG) was developed to detect and predict the echocardiographic DCM phenotype (left ventricular dilatation with systolic dysfunction) and was evaluated for its ability to stratify the risk of incident DCM in familial cohorts. Methods A deep learning model was trained to detect the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and to predict its future onset, using more than 330 000 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston. Model performance was validated in cohorts from the UK Biobank, Zhongshan Hospital, and Antwerp University Hospital, and compared with models based on traditional ECG features and echocardiographic traits. To assess performance in familial DCM, genetically predisposed individuals identified through cascade screening at the cardiogenetics clinics of Antwerp University Hospital (n = 166, 18% DCM positive) and Maastricht University Medical Center (n = 177, 18% DCM positive) were evaluated. Results The AI-ECG model achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of .87–.97 for diagnosing the prevalent DCM phenotype, outperforming traditional ECG parameters. AI-ECG was comparable to echocardiography for predicting future DCM (C-index .80–.87 and .80–.90, respectively). In familial cohorts, 5-year negative predictive values were 95.5% (Antwerp) and 91.5% (Maastricht), with corresponding positive predictive values of 42.4% and 39.4%, while high-risk scores were associated with a 5.1–6.4-fold increased risk of incident DCM. Conclusions The explainable AI-ECG model detects the echocardiographic DCM phenotype and predicts future disease, and supports the exclusion of short- to mid-term disease in genetically at-risk individuals. This low-cost tool could help reduce surveillance burden and facilitate earlier intervention.

items.title: AI algorithms and external validation: promises, pitfalls, and a practical blueprint
items.abstract: External validation involving the testing of a frozen AI model on independent data from other sites, populations, time periods, or devices provides the clearest estimate of intended-use setting performance when those external data are deployment-representative of the expected population, measurement processes, and clinical workflow. It yields realistic estimates of discrimination and calibration, exposes shortcut learning and distribution shift, quantifies clinical utility through decision-analytic measures, and reveals subgroup disparities requiring mitigation. Yet common pitfalls undermine credibility: quasi-external splits with hidden relatedness; spectrum and prevalence mismatch; site, workflow, and hardware effects; label noise and reference-standard drift; analytic flexibility and selective reporting; small, underpowered samples; reliance only on the area under the curve; unreported threshold tuning; and leakage. A practical blueprint emphasizes pre-registration; representative, multi-site cohorts spanning geography, time, and acquisition; prevention of patient and temporal overlap; comprehensive evaluation of discrimination, calibration (including calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and calibration plots), and net benefit with confidence intervals; pre-specified subgroup and fairness audits; transparent labelling procedures and uncertainty analyses; principled sample-size calculations; and minimal, well-documented model updating (recalibration before revision). Finally, external validation should connect to post-deployment governance via drift detection, performance triggers, and change-control plans, complemented by site-specific local evaluation to ensure safety and reliability across diverse clinical environments. When executed to these standards, external validation transforms promising prototypes into dependable clinical tools, clarifying where a model performs, where it fails, and what adaptations are necessary for safe, equitable, and sustainable use. This framework links statistical evaluation to clinical use, model updating, and post-deployment monitoring.

items.title: A rare cause of syncope
items.abstract: A 52-year-old woman presented with syncope 6 months earlier. Ambulatory electrocardiography revealed sinus arrest, leading to a diagnosis of sinus node dysfunction and implantation of a right atrial leadless pacemaker. Subsequently, she developed palpitations and transient visual disturbances. A right ventricular Aveir leadless pacemaker was implanted (Panel A; Supplementary S1), but symptoms persisted, predominantly after physical activity. Ambulatory electrocardiography showed a pacing burden of 0.23%, 3123 premature atrial contractions, and 40 premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) with two morphologies. Device interrogation revealed no malfunction. Echocardiography showed no significant structural disease or systolic dysfunction. Exercise electrocardiography documented non-sustained ventricular tachycardia coinciding with syncope (Panel B). At rest (heart rate, 72 beats/min; LVEF 60%), exercise stress echocardiography showed limited mobility of the atrial leadless pacemaker without definite tricuspid-valve interaction (Supplementary S2). With increasing workload and heart rate above 90 beats/min, excursion of the free end progressively increased. At peak exercise (heart rate, 131 beats/min; LVEF 72%), the free end intermittently contacted the septal tricuspid leaflet, coinciding with increased PVC frequency (Panels C and D; Supplementary S3).

Oral anticoagulation and cognitive outcomes in atrial fibrillation and Alzheimer’s disease
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Oral anticoagulants, cognition, and clinical outcomes in atrial fibrillation and Alzheimer’s disease: a Swedish nationwide study’, by N. Zhu et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag584 and the discussion piece ‘Oral anticoagulation and cognitive outcomes in atrial fibrillation and Alzheimer’s disease: considerations for longitudinal analyses’, by N. Zhu et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag930. Zhu et al.1 report that non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulant (NOAC) use was associated with modestly slower cognitive decline than warfarin or no anticoagulation among patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) and Alzheimer’s disease (AD).1 This potentially important observation, however, depends critically on how death was handled in the longitudinal cognitive analysis. The authors used inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW) for attrition due to both dropout and death, yet death is qualitatively different from an unobserved MMSE assessment: cognitive function after death is undefined rather than simply missing. Methodological work on longitudinal outcomes truncated by death emphasizes that the analytic approach should correspond to an explicitly defined estimand, particularly when survival may itself differ between exposure groups.2 This distinction is consequential here. Of 7308 participants, 4092 (56%) had only the baseline MMSE assessment and only 1240 (17%) had three or more measurements. Moreover, 2588 participants died within the 3-year clinical-outcome horizon.1 Against this substantial truncation, the estimated NOAC–warfarin difference in cognitive decline was only 0.21 MMSE points per year, translating into ∼0.8 points in the modelled 5-year MMSE means.1 Reweighting for death can address selection under strong assumptions, but it does not by itself resolve the conceptual problem that the cognitive outcome ceases to exist after death; the resulting slope therefore requires a more cautious interpretation than a treatment-associated slowing of AD progression. This caution is reinforced by randomized evidence. GIRAF and CAF found no meaningful cognitive advantage of dabigatran over well-managed warfarin during 2 years of follow-up, while the substantially larger BRAIN-AF trial was terminated for futility, although its younger, low-risk population limits direct extrapolation to AD.3–5 These trials do not invalidate the Swedish findings, but they increase the importance of excluding selection through mortality as an explanation for a comparatively small cognitive association. Could the authors report whether the NOAC–warfarin difference persists in a joint longitudinal–survival model or a partly conditional analysis estimating MMSE trajectories among patients alive at each time point? An analysis integrating death and cognition rather than treating death as conventional censoring would be particularly informative. Until robustness to this terminal event is demonstrated, these data strengthen the clinical case for NOACs on established thromboembolic and safety grounds, but should not yet be interpreted as evidence of a disease-modifying cognitive effect in AD. All authors declare no disclosure of interest for this contribution.

Prevalence-dependent thresholding and the safety of ruling out left main disease
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Standard clinical and stress ECG variables to exclude left main and left main-equivalent disease: the MASTER study’, by M. De Carlo et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag464 and the discussion piece ‘Prevalence-dependent thresholding and the safety of ruling out left main disease’, by M. De Carlo et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag860. De Carlo et al. report a clinical and exercise electrocardiographic model intended to defer coronary angiography or coronary computed tomography angiography in patients with suspected chronic coronary syndromes. At an assumed 5% prevalence of left main coronary artery disease (LMCAD) and a 1:100 misclassification cost ratio, the negative predictive value was 98.2%.1 Their Discussion further states that a lower LMCAD prevalence would increase both sensitivity and negative predictive value, making adoption more advantageous. That interpretation is not supported by the supplementary analyses: after prevalence-dependent threshold selection, the higher negative predictive value at 0.9% prevalence was accompanied by lower sensitivity. At 5% prevalence, optimism-adjusted sensitivity and negative predictive value were 85.3% and 98.2% at the 1:100 ratio and 74.4% and 97.7% at 1:50.1 At 0.9% prevalence, Supplementary Table 7 reported sensitivities of 64.5% and 63.0%, with a negative predictive value of 99.5% under both ratios.1 The Mayo Clinic validation showed the same pattern: sensitivity fell from 87.2% to 79.5% at 1:100 and from 84.6% to 69.2% at 1:50, despite higher negative predictive values.1 These estimates imply that the proportion of affected patients missed increased from 14.7% to 35.5% at 1:100 and from 25.6% to 37.0% at 1:50. A lower prevalence reduces the absolute number of false negatives per 1000 patients, but it does not reduce the probability of missing LMCAD among patients who have the disease.

items.title: An uncontainable ‘ball’ in the heart: a giant right sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
items.abstract: An ‘uncontainable ball’ was found swinging relentlessly within the heart of a 38-year-old previously healthy woman presenting with a three-day history of chest tightness. Auscultation identified a 3/6 blowing murmur over the aortic area. Laboratory tests revealed elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (43.4 pg/mL), NT-proBNP (4198.0 pg/mL), D-dimer (16 311 ng/mL), INR 1.7, and marked leukocytosis (WBC 20.82 × 109/L, neutrophil 84%). Hepatic and renal functions were severely impaired (ALT 1263 U/L, AST 1005 U/L, urea 10.20 mmol/L), with mildly elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (7.45 mg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography unveiled the culprit—a giant (5 × 3 cm), thin-walled, ball-like aneurysm of the right sinus of Valsalva (Panels A and B; Supplementary data online, Videos S1 and S2). With every heartbeat, this ‘ball’ tumbled unrestrictedly between the right atrium and right ventricle, hammering the tricuspid valve and generating severe tricuspid regurgitation. Aortic CTA confirmed a contrast-filled saccular structure adjacent to the right coronary sinus with an ill-defined superior margin (Panels C and D), alongside multiple pulmonary emboli in the left lower lobe pulmonary artery and its branches, bilateral pleural effusions, and massive ascites. Given the critical condition, emergent surgery was performed after informed consent. Preoperative transoesophageal echocardiography re-identified the same uncontainable ‘ball’ with a 0.8 cm neck, continuous blood filling, and a 0.9 cm rupture on the right atrial side (Panels E and F; Supplementary data online, Videos S3–S5). 3D transoesophageal echocardiography clearly shows the aneurysm and the rupture site at the right atrial side (Panel G). Intraoperative findings confirmed a thin-walled aneurysm communicating between the aortic sinus and the right atrium (Panels H and I; Supplementary data online, Video S6). The procedure was completed uneventfully.

items.title: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation vs surgical replacement in low-risk aortic stenosis: time-dependent late mortality in a pooled analysis of trials
items.abstract: The expansion of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) to low-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) has been driven by randomized trials reporting favourable early outcomes and non-inferiority to surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), through early and intermediate follow-up.1 However, longer-term assessment is essential for patients with a longer life expectancy, in whom durability, reintervention risk, and survival are central to treatment selection.2 Recently released extended follow-up data from pivotal lower-risk trials have raised concerns that the early advantages of TAVI may attenuate over time, with emerging signals related to late mortality, valve durability, and reintervention.3–5 However, these trials were underpowered to evaluate all-cause mortality as an individual endpoint. Moreover, conventional time-to-event analyses may obscure clinically important time-dependent differences between two treatment strategies exhibiting non-parallel patterns of early and late risk. We therefore conducted a pooled reconstructed time-to-event analysis of randomized low-risk trials with extended follow-up of up to 7 years.

items.title: Obesity, frail obesity, and outcomes after durable left ventricular assist device implantation: a pooled analysis of the MOMENTUM 3 trials
items.abstract: Background and Aims Obesity in patients supported by left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) is linked to excess mortality and haemocompatibility-related events. Whether this association persists with the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 (HM3) pump is unknown. This analysis tested outcomes with obesity and the additive influence of co-existing frailty (‘frail obesity’) in the contemporary era. Methods The study pooled 2200 HM3 recipients from the MOMENTUM 3 pivotal randomized trial (n = 515) and Continued Access Protocol (n = 1685). Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 and frailty by a 40-item Rockwood cumulative-deficit frailty index (FI), with clinically relevant frailty defined as FI ≥0.325 (moderate–severe frailty); BMI was excluded from the FI to avoid mathematical coupling. The primary endpoint was survival to transplant, recovery, or 24 months of support free of disabling stroke (modified Rankin score >3) or pump replacement reoperation. Results Obese patients (n = 887, 40.3%) were younger, less often with ischaemic aetiology, and more frequently women, but more often had diabetes and hypertension, than non-obese patients. Unadjusted 2-year outcomes were similar between groups (freedom from the primary endpoint: 75.1% vs 77.1%, log-rank P = .34; survival: 79.9% vs 81.2%, P = .57). After covariate adjustment, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (hazard ratio [HR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07–1.58) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.10–1.67), as well as heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia, but not stroke, bleeding, or early right heart failure. Frailty affected 67.3% of obese recipients (571/849) and was associated with a higher adjusted risk of the primary endpoint (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.09–2.10), overall mortality and non-haemocompatibilty-related morbidity endpoints. The obesity-by-frailty interaction was not significant for either the primary endpoint (P = .436) or mortality (P = .215), indicating additive rather than synergistic risk; frail–obese patients nonetheless carried the highest absolute risk of any subgroup. Frailty improved by at least one severity class by 6 months in 75.9% of frail–obese patients, and improvement was associated with better survival (adjusted HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07–0.26). Conclusions In the HM3 era, obese and non-obese recipients had similar unadjusted 2-year outcomes; however, after adjustment for baseline case-mix, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of both the primary endpoint and all-cause mortality, together with heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia. Frailty was independently associated with adverse outcomes across nearly all endpoints and was highly prevalent among obese recipients; the combination of obesity and frailty was additive but not synergistic, with frail–obese patients carrying the highest absolute risk. Frailty, however, proved substantially reversible after LVAD support, and its improvement was associated with markedly better survival. Obesity and frailty should therefore be assessed together, rather than through BMI thresholds alone, with recognition that frailty status is dynamic after implantation and that improvement in frailty is associated with markedly better survival.

items.title: Heart failure therapy in congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries: effect on right ventricular function and survival
items.abstract: Background and Aims The aim of the study was to assess the effect of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) on cardiac function, neurohormonal activation, and mortality in adults with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (cc-TGA) presenting with systemic right ventricular (RV) systolic dysfunction. The study hypothesis was that GDMT use (assessed using the GDMT score) was associated with improved cardiac function (higher RV free wall strain [RVFWS]), less neurohormonal activation (lower N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP] levels), and lower mortality. Methods GDMT score, RVFWS, and NT-proBNP levels were assessed at baseline and 1-year follow-up. GDMT uptitration was assessed using ΔGDMT (GDMT at 1-year minus GDMT at baseline). Improvements in RV systolic function and neurohormonal activation were defined as a relative increase in RVFWS of >20% and a relative decrease in NT-proBNP levels of >20%, respectively. Results Of 213 patients (age 43 ± 15 years; 54% male), baseline GDMT score was 1.97 ± 1.27, and ΔGDMT score was 0.74 ± 0.39. Baseline RVFWS was −18 ± 5%; 25% had improved RV systolic function. Baseline NT-proBNP was 369 (142, 1004) pg/mL; 56% had improved neurohormonal activation. Higher baseline GDMT score and ΔGDMT score were associated with improvement in RV systolic function and neurohormonal activation. Overall, 34 (16%) patients died, and higher baseline GDMT score and ΔGDMT score were associated with a lower risk of mortality and of the composite adverse event endpoint (heart failure hospitalization, death, and heart transplantation). Clinical benefits of GDMT use were observed only in patients with moderate/severe RV systolic dysfunction, and not in patients with mild RV systolic dysfunction. Conclusions GDMT use was associated with improved outcomes in patients with moderate/severe RV systolic dysfunction.

Alcohol and cardiovascular disease: inter-organ crosstalk, microvascular dysfunction, and cardiovascular ageing
items.abstract: Alcohol-related cardiovascular risk is being fundamentally reappraised. Observational associations suggesting cardioprotection with light-to-moderate drinking have been challenged by contemporary cohort analyses, Mendelian-randomization studies, biomarker-informed investigations, and updated public-health guidance. Uncertainty nevertheless persists at very low exposure levels and for selected coronary or all-cause outcomes. Alcohol is therefore best viewed as a dose-, pattern-, and host-dependent cardiovascular stressor. Acute or binge drinking, sustained heavy intake, chronic intake with episodic binges, and withdrawal produce overlapping but distinct phenotypes, including hypertension, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, sudden death, alcohol-associated cardiomyopathy, heart failure, stroke, and vascular disease. A systems–cardiology framework is presented in which direct myocardial injury, electrical instability, haemodynamic and autonomic stress, vascular and microvascular dysfunction, and disrupted inter-organ signalling interact. Ethanol and acetaldehyde toxicity, redox imbalance, microbial and inflammatory mediators, neurohumoral activation, and metabolic or electrolyte disturbances can impair endothelial signalling, mitochondrial energetics, excitation–contraction coupling, electrical stability, and repair. Pathway dominance varies across exposure patterns and susceptible hosts; coronary microvascular dysfunction may represent a convergence pathway rather than an obligatory mediator. Cumulative injury can diminish perfusion, contractile, electrical, autonomic, and exercise reserve. Alcohol-related cardiovascular ageing is proposed as a unifying cumulative phenotype encompassing mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrative stress, inflammageing, senescence, impaired repair, circadian and epigenetic dysregulation, fibrosis, and ventriculo-arterial uncoupling, although direct human evidence remains incomplete. Age, biological sex, genetics, comorbidities, sleep–circadian disruption, nutrition, medications, and polysubstance misuse may modify pathway dominance and reversibility. Structured exposure assessment and alcohol reduction or abstinence, when indicated, are actionable components of cardiovascular prevention and care.

items.title: Atherosclerotic plaque healing: mechanisms and clinical relevance
items.abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque healing is a dynamic biological mechanism that occurrs after plaque disruption and represents an endogenous reparative response within the atherosclerotic lesion. This process unfolds through three partially overlapping phases: endogenous thrombus lysis, granulation tissue formation, and re-endothelialization. Through the coordinated interaction of circulating cells, vascular wall components, and soluble mediators, plaque healing promotes fibrous repair and structural stabilization of the disrupted plaque. For many years, plaque healing remained primarily a histopathological observation described in post-mortem studies. The advent of high-resolution intracoronary imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography, has enabled in vivo visualization of the characteristic layered morphology of healed plaques, providing direct clinical confirmation of these early pathological findings. These observations have significantly improved our understanding of the clinical significance of plaque healing. Healed plaques are more frequently observed in patients with chronic coronary syndromes, supporting the concept that healing contributes to plaque stabilization. At the same time, recurrent cycles of plaque disruption followed by repair may lead to progressive luminal narrowing, thereby contributing to the long-term progression of coronary atherosclerosis. This review provided an updated overview of the clinical significance and implications of healed plaques in coronary artery disease, the mechanisms underlying plaque healing, and examines emerging intracoronary and non-invasive imaging modalities that allow their in vivo identification.

items.title: Correction to: Macrophage SBK2 suppresses inflammation and atherosclerosis by NLRP3 phosphorylation
Weekly Journal Scan: Less-than- OPTIMAl evidence for a shorter duration of dual antithrombotic therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention in patients with atrial fibrillation
items.abstract: Comment on the article ‘1-month versus 12-month dual antithrombotic therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention in patients with atrial fibrillation (OPTIMA-AF): a multicentre, open-label, hybrid non-inferiority and superiority, randomised, controlled trial’ published in The Lancet. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(26)00665-3. Oral anticoagulation is essential for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF), but concomitant antiplatelet therapy after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) substantially increases bleeding risk.1 Previous randomized controlled trials established dual antithrombotic therapy with a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) and a P2Y12 inhibitor as the preferred strategy over prolonged triple therapy, with oral anticoagulation alone being recommended thereafter in stable patients.2–4 More recently, AFIRE,5 EPIC-CAD,6 AQUATIC,7 and ADAPT AF-DES8 have consistently supported long-term oral anticoagulant monotherapy in patients with AF and stable coronary artery disease after PCI, showing no clear ischaemic benefit and greater bleeding risk with continued antiplatelet therapy (either aspirin or clopidogrel). Yet, these trials addressed the late, stable phase after PCI, leaving uncertainty about how early antiplatelet therapy may be safely withdrawn. Current European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of patients with chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) recommend a short course of triple therapy with oral anticoagulation, aspirin, and clopidogrel for 1–4 weeks after PCI, followed by oral anticoagulation plus clopidogrel for up to 6 months in patients without high ischaemic risk and up to 12 months in those at high ischaemic risk, before transition to oral anticoagulation alone.9 However, the optimal timing of P2Y12 inhibitor withdrawal during the first year after PCI remains uncertain.

Is local coronary inflammation truly superior after PCI, or is the comparison driven by revascularization endpoints?
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Local vs systemic inflammation and outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention’, by Z. Ye et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag731 and the discussion piece ‘Local and systemic inflammation after PCI: complementary risk signals beyond revascularization’, by Z. Ye and K. Dou, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag932. We read with great interest the study by Ye et al. evaluating the relative prognostic value of local coronary inflammation, assessed by the pericoronary fat attenuation index (FAI), and systemic inflammation, assessed by high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).1 We congratulate the authors on this large, carefully adjusted analysis. We believe, however, that the conclusion that local inflammation shows a stronger association than systemic inflammation requires two clarifications. First, the patient-level MACE endpoint was dominated by unplanned repeat revascularization (130 of 164 events, 79%), and the vessel-level VOCE endpoint was dominated by target-vessel revascularization (97 of 118 events, 82%). Revascularization events are influenced by the completeness of revascularization, residual disease burden, operator judgment, and follow-up practice, rather than by inflammatory biology alone.2,3 Indeed, in the sensitivity analysis excluding revascularization from MACE, isolated high FAI-MAX with low hs-CRP no longer carried a significantly higher risk than low FAI-MAX with high hs-CRP (hazard ratio 1.70, 95% CI .69–4.15 vs 1.79, 95% CI .67–4.79). Although the dual-high phenotype remained the highest-risk subgroup, the claimed superiority of local over systemic inflammation was no longer apparent. We would welcome event-specific analyses for death and myocardial infarction and a formal evaluation of whether the incremental predictive value of FAI over hs-CRP persists after exclusion of revascularization, using reclassification metrics rather than area under the curve alone.4

items.title: Not All PVR Reductions Are Created Equal: Lessons From the CADENCE Trial
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The CADENCE trial evaluated sotatercept in combined post- and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (CpcPH-HFpEF). We analyzed the pathophysiological implications of the observed pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) reduction.A hemodynamic comparison was conducted contrasting the mechanistic effects of sotaercept with conventional pulmonary vasodilators.In CADENCE, PVR and pressure reductions occurred without marked cardiac output augmentation, contrasting with flow-mediated recruitment typical of traditional vasodilators. Sotatercept-induced PVR reduction may reflect true vascular reverse remodeling rather than vasodilation, underscoring the need to discriminate resistance reduction mechanisms in CpcPHHFpEF.

items.title: Utility of donor-recipient human leukocyte antigen matching in heart transplantation in the era of extended donor organ preservation: A multi-institutional analysis
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Closer human leukocyte antigen (HLA) match between the donor and the recipient leads to better outcomes after kidney transplantation. Since extended donor preservation is now possible in heart transplantation (HT), we examined the possible impact of prioritization of HLA matching in HT. METHODS: We included single organ HT recipients reported to the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) transplanted in 2010-2019. Outcomes included survival, treated rejection and development of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) across 5 and 10 year follow-up after transplant. We examined associations between matches at A, B, DR, DPB, DQA, DQB and DPA loci and the outcomes in univariable and multivariable analyses. RESULTS: There were 5176 patients in the 5Y cohort with a median of 9 (IQR 8; 11) HLA mismatches and 9118 patients in the 10Y cohort with a median of 6 (IQR 5; 7) HLA mismatches. In adjusted analyses, there was no significant association between donor-recipient HLA match and mortality, treated rejection or CAV in the 5Y cohort. In the 10Y cohort, HLA mismatch was a risk factor for mortality (HR 1.06, CI 1; 1.12, p=0.047) and treated rejection (HR 1.13, CI 1.07;1.2, p<0.001) in adults. Among pediatric patients, HLA mismatch conferred a nominally higher risk of mortality (HR 1.14, CI 0.97; 1.34, p=0.121) and treated rejection (HR 1.08, CI 0.96;1.21, p=0.226). CONCLUSIONS: We show that the current impact of donor-recipient HLA match on post-HT outcomes is relatively small. While novel organ preservation techniques may make HLA matching feasible, our data do not support its adoption into future iterations of the HT allocation system.

items.title: On generative artificial intelligence in scientific writing
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Scientific communication - the dissemination of ideas, hypotheses, and discoveries - is fundamental to advancing human knowledge and to ensuring public access to new knowledge as it is generated. Growth in the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific communication has been explosive, likely driven by high uptake among an adept userbase with demanding schedules, making the efficiency gains attractive. The rapid uptake of AI is creating disruptive changes in the way scientific communication happens, affecting the methods by which abstracts, manuscripts, figures, presentations, and funding proposals are generated, and in many cases impacting the final product. In this perspective piece, we reflect on the rapidly changing landscape of AI use in scientific communication with attention to the potential immediate and long-term risks. The inherent unauthorized secondary use of the data used to train AI models raises questions about credit and plagiarism in academia. Fabricated references have proliferated in the scientific literature resulting from "hallucinations" by AI models. Meanwhile, each use of an AI model comes with an incremental risk to the environment at an already perilous time. More abstractly, AI use in scientific communication risks the process itself becoming iterative, prioritizing summation while diminishing insights that fuel the scientific engine. Finally, the friction that AI models remove from writing may risk removing an essential part of the process of scientific thinking, particularly for the next generation of scientists. While we acknowledge that AI is here to stay, we feel an element of caution is warranted in its implementation, to help preserve science and its dissemination as a fundamentally human endeavor.

items.title: Harnessing Lung-Kidney Crosstalk: A Novel Ex Vivo Platform for Donor Lung Rehabilitation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The lack of perfusate metabolic homeostasis during ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) may impair lung physiology or stability and limit the application of advanced donor lung therapies. There is evidence that additional organ support during EVLP can improve graft preservation and transplant outcomes. We hypothesized that incorporation of a kidney into an EVLP circuit would maintain perfusate homeostasis and improve lung preservation and metabolic activity. METHODS: A novel circuit was developed to allow simultaneous normothermic perfusion of lungs and kidney in parallel. Donor pig lungs underwent 12 hours of cellular EVLP (EVLP, n=5) or combined cellular ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion (EVLKP, n=5). Lung function was assessed hourly and inflammatory cytokines, edema formation, hemolysis, histologic injury, and kidney performance were evaluated. RESULTS: Simultaneous lung and kidney perfusion achieved target pulmonary and renal perfusion parameters with stable hemodynamics. EVLKP demonstrated trends of higher compliance, lower inspiratory pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance. Perfusate lactate concentration in EVLKP was markedly lower (P<0.0001), glucose concentrations were higher (P=0.0102), and pH shifted towards physiologic levels (P=0.0009) compared to EVLP. Oxygenation capacity was comparable between groups. Kidney perfusion remained stable throughout EVLKP. CONCLUSIONS: Combined ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion is safe and feasible in a large-animal model for prolonged lung perfusion. EVLKP improved perfusate homeostasis compared with EVLP alone, which is associated with trends of improvement in lung physiologic parameters. These findings suggest that kidney-derived metabolic and biological support may provide benefits beyond perfusate filtration and highlight the potential importance of organ-organ crosstalk during ex vivo perfusion.

items.title: Treatment of children and young adults with a Fontan circulation and cardiovascular dysfunction. 2026 Consensus Statement from the European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN), endorsed by AHA, AEPC, EACTS, ISACHD, ISHLT and PICS
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The Fontan operation enables long term survival for many individuals born with single ventricle heart disease, but the resulting circulation imposes a lifelong hemodynamic burden and predisposes to cardiovascular dysfunction and multisystem morbidity. Evidence based guidance for assessment and management of Fontan specific cardiac and vascular dysfunction, however, remains limited. The European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN) convened an international, multidisciplinary executive writing group to review the available literature and develop consensus recommendations addressing cardiovascular dysfunction in children and young adults with a Fontan circulation. Recommendations were graded using established Class of Recommendation and Level of Evidence criteria adapted to the Fontan specific evidence base. The statement addresses cardiovascular assessment, pulmonary vascular disease and use of pulmonary vasodilator therapy, Fontan pathway obstruction, systemic venous and arterial abnormalities and collateral vessels, lymphatic dysfunction and intervention, myocardial dysfunction and heart failure therapy, and thromboembolic risk and antithrombotic therapy. The focus is on phenotype-guided management, hemodynamically informed treatment decisions, and medical, transcatheter, and surgical approaches tailored to Fontan circulation. Seven graded recommendation tables as well as a flowchart for considerations regarding pulmonary vasodilator therapy are provided to support clinical decision making. Fontan-specific evidence remains limited, so many recommendations necessarily represent expert opinion. This EPPVDN consensus statement, therefore, discusses knowledge gaps and priorities for collaborative research to improve outcomes for individuals living with a Fontan circulation.

items.title: Treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults. 2026 consensus statement from the European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN), endorsed by AHA, AEPC, EACTS, ESPR, PASCAR, PCS, and PICS
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN) is a registered, non-profit organization dedicated to advancing innovative diagnostic methods and treatment options for all forms of pediatric pulmonary vascular disease, including pulmonary hypertension (PH) related to congenital heart disease (CHD), PH associated with developmental lung disease (DEVLD-PH), persistent PH of the newborn (PPHN), postcapillary PH in left heart disease (PH-LHD), and associated cardiac dysfunction/heart failure. In the past, the EPPVDN has published consensus statements on the diagnosis and treatment of pediatric PH (2016, 2019), which have been endorsed by multiple societies. The executive writing group conducted comprehensive searches of the PubMed/MEDLINE bibliographic database (2000 to 2025) and engaged in multiple web-based and in-person meetings. Thirteen section task forces discussed and created consented recommendations. Prospective clinical studies, clinical trials, meta-analyses, expert consensus guidelines, and other articles with pediatric data were included in the search, using the terms 'pulmonary hypertension' and related keywords. Classes of recommendation (COR) and levels of evidence (LOE) were assigned based on AHA/ESC definitions, pediatric PH studies, adult studies including a minimum N number of 15 children, or studies involving adults with CHD. Classifications and definitions from the 7th World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) in 2024 were incorporated and discussed. We produced 6 graded recommendation tables (COR, LOE) and 3 algorithms for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children, and young adults. A total of 16 main and 17 supplemental display items cover a range of topics, including risk assessment, pharmacological therapy, transcatheter interventions and surgery, recommendations specific to PH subgroups/special populations and clinical settings. Adaptation of management recommendations for middle-to-low-income regions is provided. Together, these up-to-date guidelines provide a comprehensive, detailed, and practical framework for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults, aiming to improve outcomes and quality of life for affected patients.

items.title: Disruptions in U.S. Heart Transplantation: When Innovation Outpaces Evidence
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: For nearly four decades, heart transplantation was defined by a stable, predictable paradigm: brain-dead donors, ice-cooler transport, uniform three-drug immunosuppression, and biopsy-based surveillance. Within a few years, that paradigm has been upended. In this perspective, we examine the disruptions now reshaping heart transplantation in the United States. Some are desirable: new preservation platforms and the rapid growth of donation after circulatory death, which now accounts for nearly a quarter of U.S. heart transplants, have expanded the donor pool, and cardiac xenotransplantation has reached clinical testing. Others remain controversial: the 2018 allocation policy has altered listing and support practices, normothermic regional perfusion raises unresolved questions about the determination of death, and inconsistent definitions of ischemic intervals undermine comparisons across DCD studies. Still others are troubling: OPTN restructuring, uneven OPO performance, outsourced procurement, rising costs, and press reports of donors showing signs of life have strained public trust. Underlying all of these is a data gap: national registries capture few DCD procurement and preservation variables, and little about recipients' long-term health beyond survival. Innovation has outpaced our ability to evaluate its consequences. We propose a shared DCD clock built on fixed timestamps, national ethical standards for normothermic regional perfusion, transparency in procurement and its costs, longitudinal outcome reporting, and accountability shared by OPOs and transplant centers. The challenge facing the field is no longer simply how to transplant more hearts, but how to ensure that more transplantation becomes better transplantation.

items.title: Net Prolongation of Life with Ventricular Assist Device Support in Teenagers: Are We There Yet?
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Heart transplantation prolongs survival in children with end-stage heart disease, yet a single donor heart does not provide a normal lifespan. Contemporary graft survival for teenagers is approximately 15 years, the shortest of any pediatric age group, and re-transplantation remains uncommon. For most patients, the first allograft is the only allograft. Recent adult data demonstrating survival with durable mechanical circulatory support comparable to transplantation raise an important question for adolescents: could intentionally extending ventricular assist device (VAD) support through the teenage years, with transplantation deferred to adulthood, increase total life-years? This perspective examines that hypothesis for adolescents with dilated cardiomyopathy. We review the heightened risks of rejection, graft loss, and treatment nonadherence during adolescence; contemporary outcomes with dischargeable durable VADs in children; the potential for myocardial recovery during extended support; and organ allocation policies that may unintentionally discourage a prolonged-support strategy. We also examine patient and family perspectives and discuss unresolved questions regarding stroke risk, allosensitization, long-term quality of life, and optimal timing of transplantation. No prospective data currently support intentional long-term VAD support as a bridge to transplantation in teenagers, and this concept should be viewed as a hypothesis rather than a practice recommendation. However, for carefully selected adolescents who are clinically stable on durable VAD support, delayed transplantation may be a reasonable topic for shared decision-making discussions while acknowledging the substantial uncertainties that remain. As durable device technology continues to improve, evaluating whether prolonged VAD support can achieve net prolongation of life in teenagers warrants prospective investigation.

items.title: Measured Left Ventricular Mass Ratio for Size-Matching Identifies Graft Failure Risk in Obese Heart Transplantation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Optimal donor-recipient size-matching in heart transplantation with obese donors and/or recipients remains uncertain. We sought to validate the measured left ventricular mass (mLVM) ratio using local donor hospital echocardiograms, determine whether obesity modifies the association with 1-year graft failure compared to the predicted heart mass (PHM), and assess the clinical implications of discordance. METHODS: The Donor Heart Study prospectively collected echocardiograms from donation-after-brain-death donors. The associations of local mLVM ratio (donor measured LVM/recipient predicted LVM) and PHM ratio with 1-year graft failure (death or retransplantation) were assessed by adjusted Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic splines with obesity interaction terms. RESULTS: Among 2,036 heart transplants, size-matching ratios differed significantly by metric within and across obesity groups (all p<0.001). Obesity significantly modified the association between mLVM ratio and 1-year graft failure (interaction: p=0.009), but not PHM ratio. In obese transplants, the mLVM ratio demonstrated a U-shaped (nonlinear interaction: p=0.011) association with 1-year graft failure, with significant adjusted risk at low and high mLVM ratios; where the mLVM ratio captured a unique phenotype associated with graft failure when oversized (>1.20, aHR: 2.50 [95% CI: 1.30-4.82]). Reclassification from PHM to mLVM ratio improved risk classification by 10.4% and concordantly abnormal PHM and mLVM ratios more than doubled the risk of graft failure (aHR: 2.15 [95% CI: 1.10-4.22]) in obese transplantation. CONCLUSION: In obese transplants, locally derived mLVM ratio may identify high-risk donor-recipient mismatches not captured by the PHM ratio, with increased graft failure risk at both low and high mLVM ratios.
