items.title: Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Agonists or Tezepelumab for Obesity-Associated Asthma: A Cohort Study
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Obesity is associated with poor asthma outcomes. GLP-1 and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists induce weight loss and dampen airway inflammation independent of pathways currently targeted by biologics. Objective To compare differences in respiratory outcomes and weight loss between GLP-1-based medications and tezepelumab in asthma patients without diabetes. Methods A retrospective study was performed in a multi-institutional electronic health record database. Patients with specialist-treated, obesity-associated, moderate-to-severe asthma with at least one severe exacerbation in the prior year who initiated liraglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide, or tezepelumab between January 1, 2022 and December 31, 2025 were identified. Prevalent diabetes was excluded. Patients were followed for subsequent exacerbations, rescue inhaler prescriptions, respiratory-related healthcare encounters, and time to greater than 10% loss in body mass index. Overlap weighting accounted for imbalance in baseline asthma and obesity characteristics. Results 2779 patients were identified, of whom 133 initiated liraglutide, 1770 semaglutide, 472 tirzepatide, and 404 tezepelumab. In weighted estimates, patients starting tirzepatide experienced a lower hazard of severe exacerbation compared to tezepelumab (weighted hazard ratio [wHR] 0.41; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24-0.70); those starting semaglutide had a similar hazard (wHR 0.99; 95% CI 0.70-1.39). Tirzepatide and semaglutide initiators attained >10% reduction in BMI sooner, had less need for rescue inhalers, and had fewer subsequent respiratory-related encounters compared to tezepelumab. Conclusions GLP-1-based medications, and in particular dual-incretin GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists, may have comparable effectiveness to biologic therapy among patients with associated obesity without diabetes. Clinical trials are necessary to validate findings in this observational study.

items.title: Nocturnal intravenous gamma-hydroxybutyrate and sleep architecture in non-sedated intensive care unit patients: a polysomnographic experience
Enrichment using the Phoenix Sepsis Score in children: heterogeneous treatment effects in a hydrocortisone target trial emulation
items.abstract: Prognostic and predictive enrichment strategies could be used to address the heterogeneity of pediatric sepsis and identify subgroups of patients most likely to benefit from targeted therapies. Our aim was to determine if the use of the Phoenix Sepsis Score (PSS) can identify critically ill children with community-acquired sepsis who are most likely to benefit from early hydrocortisone therapy. This was an observational cohort study and target trial emulation in 15 pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) in the United States, including a development cohort and replication in a validation cohort. Patients < 18 years of age admitted to a PICU with confirmed or suspected community-acquired infection between 2010 and 2019 were included. Patients who were treated with systemic stress dose hydrocortisone in the first 24 h of PICU admission were compared with untreated patients across risk groups. There were 48,345 patients included in the main analysis. A PSS ≥ 4 points in the first 12 h of PICU admission had the best discrimination of outcomes, with a 10-fold higher mortality than those with a PSS < 4 in both the development and the validation cohorts. In the target trial emulation analysis, after adjusting for covariates associated with hydrocortisone use (age, malignancy, severity of illness, refractory shock status, and hospital), patients who received early hydrocortisone and were in the high-risk phenotype (PSS ≥ 4 in first 12 h) had a lower risk of in-hospital mortality (adjusted risk ratio [aRR] 0.72 [95% confidence interval [CI] 0.65–0.80]), while low-risk patients had increased risk (aRR 1.90 [95%CI 1.66–2.16], interaction p-value < 0.001) in the development cohort. The results were replicated in the validation cohort (aRR 0.79 [95%CI 0.68, 0.92] vs. aRR 2.95 [95%CI 2.43, 3.59], interaction p-value < 0.001). A highly generalizable risk stratification strategy using the easy-to-calculate PSS can be used for both prognostic and predictive enrichment in critically ill children with community-acquired sepsis. Further external and prospective validation of our results is warranted. Not applicable.

items.title: Differentiated effect of hypothermia versus normothermia after cardiac arrest by neurological status and clinical correlates of ischemic burden
items.abstract: Introduction The optimal temperature target after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains uncertain, as major randomized trials have not demonstrated a clear benefit of lower-target hypothermia compared with normothermia. Despite this, patients with differing degrees of ischemic burden or early neurological injury may hypothetically respond differently to temperature targets, raising the possibility of heterogeneous treatment effects. This study aimed to determine whether outcomes differ after OHCA with 33 °C versus controlled normothermia (36.0–37.7 °C) according to correlates of ischemic burden and neurological findings at hospital admission. Methods This secondary analysis of the TTM and TTM2 trials employed effect-based machine learning to probe for heterogeneous treatment effects. Causal forests and Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) estimated individualized treatment effects (ITE) based on ischemia duration, prehospital factors, and neurological examination findings at hospital admission. Treatment effect modifier variable importance parameter (TEM-VIP) analysis ranked the baseline variables most likely to modify effect. The primary outcome was six-month all-cause mortality, and the secondary outcome was poor functional outcome (modified Rankin scale score 4–6). Primary analyses evaluated potential heterogeneity within each trial, while secondary analyses pooled all participants. Measurements and main results All 2789 adult OHCA patients from the trials’ primary analyses were included (median age 65 years (IQR 56–73), 79.9% male). Death occurred in 49.4% of patients in the 33 °C group, and in 47.9% in the controlled normothermia group. Variation in six-month mortality ITEs estimated from ischemic burden correlates and initial neurological findings was minimal, and no significant heterogeneity of treatment effect was identified across all methods and analysis populations. In the pooled analysis, estimated conditional mean mortality risk difference ranged from − 1.2% to 2.1% in causal forest ( p = 0.99), and from − 0.5% to 1.5% in BART, with posterior probabilities for hypothermia benefit ranging from 42% to 53%. Absolute subgroup estimates in TEM-VIP analysis were small and non-significant. Results were consistent for the six-month functional outcome. Conclusions Among TTM and TTM2 participants randomized to 33 °C versus controlled normothermia post-OHCA, no evidence of detectable heterogeneity of treatment effect based on available clinical correlates of ischemic burden or initial neurological findings was identified, with minimal estimated variation in treatment effect.

items.title: Concomitant assessment of immunosuppression and Herpesvirus reactivation in blood at Day 7 after ICU admission in a mixed population
ECMO for combat casualties: current evidence, special considerations, and future directions
items.abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has traditionally been used cautiously in trauma because of bleeding, coagulopathy, traumatic brain injury, and the need for repeated surgery. However, advances in venovenous ECMO (VV-ECMO), anticoagulation strategies, trauma critical care, and ECMO transport have broadened its potential role in selected trauma patients. Combat-related casualties represent a distinct subgroup: they are often young, previously healthy individuals with preserved cardiopulmonary reserve who may develop severe but potentially reversible respiratory or circulatory failure after penetrating, blast, thoracic, or polytraumatic injury. Current evidence supports ECMO as a feasible rescue strategy in selected trauma patients, particularly for refractory trauma-induced respiratory failure, although combat-specific data remain limited. In this review, we examine trauma-ECMO evidence and representative cases; patient selection; ECMO configuration; trauma-specific complications; care across military roles; contested evacuation; and resource allocation. Given the scarcity of combat-specific data, the proposed clinical and operational frameworks should be viewed as conceptual models rather than validated algorithms or consensus recommendations; ECMO should remain a highly selective, system-dependent rescue strategy rather than a routine battlefield therapy. Not applicable.

items.title: Lactate improves hemodynamics in chronic heart failure: a randomized crossover study
items.abstract: Lactate has traditionally been regarded as a harmful by-product of anaerobic metabolism, and elevated blood lactate concentrations are associated with adverse outcomes in acute heart failure and critical illness. However, emerging evidence identifies lactate as an important metabolic substrate and signaling molecule. The hemodynamic effects of lactate in patients with chronic heart failure remain unknown. To determine the acute hemodynamic effects of intravenous and oral lactate treatment in patients with heart failure. In a randomized, double-blind, crossover study, 12 patients with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction underwent intravenous sodium lactate and isovolumic saline placebo infusion on one study day and oral sodium lactate and isocaloric placebo on a separate day. Hemodynamics were assessed hourly using pulmonary artery catheterization and echocardiography. The trial was registered at Clinicaltrials.gov (NCT06121323) released September 20th 2023. Intravenous and oral lactate administration increased blood lactate concentrations compared with placebo by 2.3 mmol/L ( P < 0.001) and 0.9 mmol/L ( P < 0.001), respectively. Intravenous lactate increased cardiac output by 1.5 L/min ( P < 0.001), and oral lactate by 0.4 L/min ( P = 0.01). Stroke volume and heart rate increased during intravenous administration (both P < 0.001), and heart rate increased during oral administration ( P < 0.001). Systemic vascular resistance decreased during intravenous lactate infusion ( P < 0.001), whereas pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ( P = 0.02) and central venous pressure ( P = 0.004) decreased during oral administration. LVOT velocity–time integral increased during both routes of administration and global longitudinal strain improved following intravenous lactate. Indices of diastolic function improved during lactate administration. In patients with chronic heart failure, lactate administration improved systolic and diastolic function and reduced afterload and cardiac filling pressures.

items.title: CT-based radiomics for interpretable outcome prediction after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a multicenter cohort study
items.abstract: Prognostic assessment after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) mainly relies on clinical variables and computed tomography (CT) findings, but current models often lack biological interpretability. We developed and validated a clinical-radiomics prognostic model and subsequently performed exploratory cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomic characterization of model-defined risk phenotypes. This multicenter cohort from the PROSAH-MPC registry included 879 patients across four hospitals. Patients from the primary center were split into training ( n = 637) and internal validation ( n = 160) cohorts, while patients from three other centers formed an external validation cohort ( n = 82). Admission CT hemorrhagic lesions were automatically segmented using the validated BrainHemoAI platform, and radiomic features were extracted with PyRadiomics. Clinical, radiomics, and combined clinical-radiomics XGBoost models were developed and interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Risk scores from the clinical-radiomics model were applied to an independent prospective enrichment, gene setCSF​ proteomic cohort to define combined model-based high- and low-risk groups. Gene Ontology (GO)/ Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), and protein–protein interaction (PPI) analyses were performed. The combined model yielded AUCs of 0.892 and 0.820 in the internal test and external validation cohorts, respectively. Risk reclassification analyses suggested that radiomic features may provide complementary prognostic information. SHAP identified radiomic heterogeneity and key clinical variables as major predictors. Meanwhile, exploratory CSF proteomic analysis identified candidate differentially expressed proteins and associated pathway signals that differed between groups defined by high and low combined clinical-radiomics risk scores. This clinical-radiomics prognostic model enables accurate outcome prediction and provides exploratory biological insight into unfavorable recovery after aSAH, supporting refined risk stratification and potential targeted therapeutic development. PROSAH-MPC. NCT05738083. Registered 16 November 2022 – Retrospectively registered, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05738083 .

items.title: Estimating the costs of capnography within a complete nasogastric tube verification pathway
Lung recruitability in ARDS: from recruited volume to functional response
items.abstract: Lung recruitability in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is commonly characterized by the potential of nonaerated lung to become aerated when distending pressure is increased. However, the amount of lung that can be recruited does not establish whether achieving and maintaining that recruitment results in physiological benefit. This distinction explains why anatomical estimates of recruitability do not translate directly into decisions about recruitment-oriented interventions or positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP). This Perspective proposes a physiological approach that distinguishes recruitment potential, achieved recruitment, and the physiological response to recruitment. Anatomical recruitability describes the potential for previously nonaerated lung to become aerated during a defined change in distending pressure, whereas anatomical recruitment describes the aeration achieved by that intervention. Functional recruitability is an interpretative concept that considers the physiological benefit of achieved recruitment in relation to its mechanical and hemodynamic consequences; it is not a new physiological variable, measurement, threshold, or method for PEEP titration. Accordingly, the significance of recruitment cannot be inferred from aeration alone but requires integration with respiratory mechanics, gas exchange, and cardiovascular tolerance under the conditions in which recruitment is maintained. Because both recruitability and its physiological consequences can evolve over the course of ARDS, reassessment under comparable conditions can be informative when clinically warranted. When additional recruitment produces little or transient physiological benefit, or when that benefit is offset by the mechanical or hemodynamic burden required to achieve or maintain it, we describe the response as recruitment futility. This term refers to the physiological response to a recruitment-oriented intervention and should not be equated with low anatomical recruitability or medical futility. The physiological significance of lung recruitability can be interpreted along a sequence from recruitment potential to achieved recruitment and physiological response, extending beyond the amount of lung recruited alone. This approach supports a more physiologically informed interpretation of recruitment-oriented interventions and provides a rationale for prospectively evaluating anatomical recruitability as a stratification variable in physiology-enriched ARDS trials.

Expiratory muscle activity and the physiological response to PEEP in hypoxemic patients
items.abstract: Expiratory muscle activity raises end-expiratory pleural pressure and may oppose the effects of PEEP. Whether the regional response to PEEP differs between hypoxemic patients with and without active expiration is unclear. Secondary analysis of two randomized crossover physiological studies. Thirty-one hypoxemic patients (18 invasive ventilation, 13 noninvasive support) received low (2–5 cmH 2 O) and high (14–15 cmH 2 O) PEEP in randomized order at constant inspiratory assistance. Active expiration at high PEEP was identified by gastric manometry; inspiratory effort and transpulmonary pressure by esophageal manometry; tidal ventilation (arbitrary units, a.u.) and end-expiratory lung impedance (EELI) by electrical impedance tomography. All comparisons were exploratory and unadjusted for multiplicity. Active expiration was detected in 10 (32%) patients at low PEEP and 22 (71%) at high PEEP. The PEEP-induced increase in inspiratory effort was similar between groups ( p = 0.49), but was accompanied by a rise in transdiaphragmatic pressure only with passive expiration (+3 cmH 2 O [1–4], p = 0.01), whereas with active expiration it coincided with intensified expiratory gastric pressure swings (+3 cmH 2 O [1–5], p = 0.001). End-expiratory esophageal and transpulmonary pressures rose slightly more (+4 vs + 3 cmH₂O) and less (+6 vs + 7 cmH₂O) with active expiration, without significant between-group differences. The PEEP-induced increase in global EELI was smaller with active expiration (+941 a.u. [384–1712] vs + 2348 [1215–3402], p = 0.03). With passive expiration, PEEP increased both ventral and dorsal EELI ( p = 0.004 and p = 0.008); with active expiration, only ventral EELI increased ( p = 0.04; dorsal p = 0.30). With active expiration, PEEP redistributed tidal ventilation dorsally ( p = 0.001) through a greater tidal recruitment/derecruitment fraction (13% vs 6%, p = 0.004), increasing dorsal dynamic strain (from 0.85 [0.62–1.05] to 1.10 [0.85–1.40], p = 0.001), corrected minute ventilation ( p = 0.002) and PaO₂/FiO₂ ( p = 0.001). In hypoxemic patients receiving assisted support, active expiration was common and more frequent at high PEEP, possibly to assist tidal volume generation through pre-inspiratory abdominal relaxation. With active expiration, PEEP improved oxygenation despite a smaller gain in lung volume, attenuated in the dependent lung, dorsal tidal recruitment and higher regional strain, so that oxygenation may mask injurious regional mechanics. Esophageal and transpulmonary pressure changes were directionally consistent but non-significant, suggesting a regional, predominantly dorsal effect.

items.title: Controlling time-related biases in ECPR observational studies
items.limitations: In conclusion, observational comparisons between ECPR and CCPR face structural limitations that statistical adjustment alone cannot fully address. At prolonged low-flow durations, few clinically comparable CCPR patients remain, limiting causal inference. We propose a prioritized path forward. First, as a readily achievable step, registries could improve measurement by recording timestamps for the decision to proceed with ECPR, the start of cannulation, the establishment of ECMO flow, and termination of resuscitation, using standardized definitions, to allow accurate definition of time zero. Second, although more resource-intensive, a multicenter prospective observational study dedicated to collecting time-varying data would make it possible to quantify these biases directly.

items.title: A clinical framework for phenotype-guided angiotensin II therapy: rethinking RAAS dysregulation and angiotensin II deficiency in vasodilatory shock
items.abstract: Background Vasodilatory shock is a heterogeneous syndrome characterized by dysregulated vascular signaling pathways contributing to microvascular injury, circulatory failure, and increased morbidity and mortality risk. Despite recent advances, contemporary vasopressor strategies remain mostly empiric without accounting for pathophysiologic heterogeneity. More specifically, renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) dysregulation during critical illness may result in a relative angiotensin II (ATII) deficiency state and represents patients more likely to benefit from targeted ATII therapy. This narrative review aims to characterize enriched vasodilatory shock phenotypes associated with RAAS dysregulation and relative ATII deficiency as well as to propose a pragmatic clinical and functional phenotype-guided framework for targeted ATII utilization. Main body Critical illness may disrupt RAAS homeostasis through systemic inflammation, organ-specific injury, procedure-related exposures, and RAAS-modulating medications. Growing evidence suggests several vasodilatory shock clinical phenotypes, including severe acute kidney injury, cardiac surgery-associated vasoplegia, kidney transplantation, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and recent exposure to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, may be associated with RAAS dysregulation and relative ATII deficiency through distinct underlying mechanisms. Among several of these clinical phenotypes, administration of ATII demonstrated rapid restoration of mean arterial pressure and vasopressor-sparing effects with signals of improved clinical outcomes observed in selected populations. However, responsiveness may be attenuated following recent angiotensin receptor blocker exposure. More recently, the Angiotensin II Initial Mean Arterial Pressure Response Index of Treatment Effect (AIMRITE) study introduced a complementary functional phenotyping approach based on early hemodynamic responsiveness following ATII therapy initiation. Conclusions Clinical phenotypes associated with RAAS dysregulation may represent an enriched vasodilatory shock population for targeted ATII therapy. Integration of clinical phenotype recognition with early functional assessment of treatment responsiveness offers a pragmatic, individualized framework for vasopressor selection and stewardship. Further investigation is warranted to validate phenotype-guided ATII strategies and evaluate the impact on patient-centered outcomes.

items.title: Comparison of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for risk for delirium and neurotoxicity among patients hospitalized for acute infection: two target trial emulation studies
items.abstract: Cefepime, piperacillin–tazobactam, and meropenem are commonly used broad-spectrum β-lactam antibiotics for hospitalized patients with acute infection. Concerns persist regarding cefepime-associated neurotoxicity, but comparative real-world evidence is limited. The objective of the target trial emulations is to compare the risk of hospital-onset delirium and other neurotoxicity events among adults treated initially with cefepime versus piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem. Retrospective observational cohort study emulating 2 target trials using propensity score–matched analyses of electronic health record data (January 1, 2023 to December 31, 2024) from patients admitted to a fourteen-hospital integrated health system including academic, community, suburban, and rural hospitals. Adults (≥ 18 years) hospitalized with suspected or confirmed acute infection who received initial treatment with cefepime, piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem in the emergency department or within 12 h of ICU admission were included. The primary outcome was incident hospital-onset delirium or other neurotoxicity events identified using ICD-CM-10 codes with a “not present on admission” indicator. After matching, 4,447 patient pairs (cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam) and 1,262 pairs (cefepime versus meropenem) were analyzed. Cefepime was not associated with a higher risk of combined delirium or neurotoxicity versus piperacillin-tazobactam (relative risk, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.80–1.22; incidence rate difference [IRD] per 100 patient days, 0.00; 95% CI, − 0.13 to 0.13) or meropenem (relative risk, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.75–1.59; IRD per 100 patient days, 0.07; 95% CI, − 0.16 to 0.30). No difference between groups in either study was observed in mortality at 30 days or hospital length of stay. Secondary outcomes findings were consistent with the primary outcome result and robust across subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Cefepime was not associated with higher risk of delirium or neurotoxicity compared with piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem, suggesting neurotoxicity risk alone should not guide empiric antibiotic selection.

items.title: Ventilator-circuit configurations for noninvasive ventilation in infants with acute respiratory failure: a randomized crossover trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Patient-ventilator synchrony may differ across ventilator and circuit configurations during noninvasive ventilation (NIV) in infants. We compared an intentional-leak single-limb turbine configuration (SLC-turbine), a dual-limb turbine configuration with an active expiratory valve (DLC-turbine), and a dual-limb compressed-gas pediatric ICU configuration (DLC-PICU) in infants receiving NIV for acute respiratory failure METHODS: In this single-center randomized crossover physiological study, infants underwent three 30-minute NIV phases in randomized order with unchanged pressure support, PEEP, and FiO₂. Esophageal pressure was used to assess the asynchrony index (AI), individual asynchronies, and inspiratory effort. Primary and secondary endpoints were AI differences between DLC-PICU and SLC-turbine and between DLC-PICU and DLC-turbine, respectively RESULTS: Twenty infants entered stabilization, 13 were randomized, and 12 completed the protocol (age 10 [7-21] months; SpO₂/FiO₂ 185 [160-220]). AI differed across configurations: 8.6% [6.7-16.5] with SLC-turbine, 25.4% [16.3-35.0] with DLC-turbine, and 45.7% [30.5-63.8] with DLC-PICU (p=0.0023). AI was higher with DLC-PICU than with SLC-turbine (Hodges-Lehmann difference +32.0%, 95% CI +13.9 to +50.1; p=0.0015) and DLC-turbine (+18.4%, 95% CI +5.9 to +36.3; p=0.021). Auto-triggering showed the clearest configuration-dependent difference and was more frequent with DLC-PICU than with SLC-turbine (7.5 [0.6-11.4] vs 0 [0-2.5] events/min; difference +5.30 events/min; p=0.0039), without a significant difference between DLC-PICU and DLC-turbine. Ineffective efforts, double triggering, and premature cycling did not differ across configurations. All NIV configurations reduced inspiratory effort versus unassisted spontaneous breathing, with no significant differences among NIV configurations CONCLUSIONS: AI was lower with SLC-turbine and DLC-turbine than with DLC-PICU and lowest with SLC-turbine. Auto-triggering showed the clearest configuration-dependent difference. All configurations reduced inspiratory effort versus unassisted spontaneous breathing, without significant between-configuration differences. Because ventilator platform, circuit and expiratory architecture, and device-specific control functions differed, effects of individual components cannot be determined. These findings are specific to the ventilators and configurations evaluated. Further studies should determine whether these physiological differences translate into improved NIV tolerance or short- and long-term clinical outcomes TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04017780. Registered on 12 July 2019.

items.title: Clinical pharmacist services in adult intensive care units (PHARM-ICU): an ESICM-endorsed international survey
items.abstract: International data describing critical care pharmacist (CCP) services in adult intensive care units (ICUs) are limited. We aimed to provide a global assessment of CCP services, evaluating practice models, workforce characteristics, and scope of clinical activities. A European Society of Intensive Care Medicine (ESICM)-endorsed, multinational, cross-sectional, pilot-tested web-based survey of CCPs providing clinical pharmacy services to adult ICUs was conducted between April 28 and December 31, 2025. The survey was disseminated through ESICM, the Society of Critical Care Medicine, the United Kingdom Clinical Pharmacy Association, International Pharmaceutical Federation member organisations, and professional networks. The questionnaire assessed CCP characteristics, ICU practice settings, service models, workforce allocation, multiprofessional care team (MCT) participation, and extended clinical roles. A total of 848 CCPs from 67 countries participated. Most respondents practiced in North America ( n = 376, 44.3%), followed by Europe ( n = 245, 28.9%). CCPs participated in MCT clinical rounds a median of 5 (IQR, 2–5) days per week, 780 (92%) participated at least once weekly, with significant variation between continents ( p < 0.001). On a typical weekday, 414 (48.8%) CCPs personally covered 10–19 ICU beds, while 200 (23.6%) covered fewer than 10 beds. Variability was observed in clinical practice models, workforce characteristics, and service delivery. Direct patient care was the primary focus, with 479 (56.5%) allocating ≥ 50% of available weekly ICU time to this domain. Service cover outside routine working hours was variable with 225 (26.5%) reporting regular contact for ICU-related issues. Pharmacist prescribing authority differed geographically ( p < 0.001) and was held by 257 (30.3%) CCPs, while 305 (36%) were involved in ICU nutrition-related activities. CCP services and extended practice roles vary substantially across regions worldwide. These findings provide an international baseline to guide future evaluation and development of consensus-based recommendations for critical care pharmacy services. Not applicable.

items.title: Cardioversion and stroke volume index rather than heart rate alone define haemodynamic success of rate control in septic shock-associated atrial fibrillation
Predictive performance of bedside physiological parameters for the failure of prophylactic non-invasive ventilation after extubation
items.abstract: Background Extubation failure is associated with increased mortality. Whether bedside physiological variables can identify patients at risk of reintubation during prophylactic NIV after extubation is unknown. Methods In this post hoc analysis of a multicenter physiological study, 60 hypoxemic adults at high risk of extubation failure underwent two 1-hour NIV sessions after planned extubation, with oronasal and full-face masks in randomized crossover order. We assessed the magnitude of airway occlusion pressure (Pocc), the esophageal pressure swing (ΔPes), SpO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, tidal volume, dynamic lung elastance (EL,dyn), ROX index [(SpO₂/FiO₂)/respiratory rate] and the pressure-oxygenation index (POX, SpO₂/FiO₂ divided by Pocc). Prophylactic NIV failure was reintubation for respiratory failure within 7 days. Discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis. Results Fourteen patients (23%) experienced NIV failure. Pocc yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.71–0.95) with the oronasal mask and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.72–0.95) with the full-face mask, showing greater discriminative performance than tidal volume (AUCs, 0.55 and 0.53), respiratory rate (0.54 and 0.38), SpO₂/FiO₂ (0.51 and 0.50), and the ROX index (0.54 and 0.38; all p < 0.05). By contrast, the discriminative performance of Pocc did not differ from that of EL,dyn (AUCs, 0.72 and 0.73; p = 0.08 and 0.11), POX (AUCs, 0.82 and 0.81; p = 0.68 and 0.29), or |ΔPes| (AUCs, 0.83 and 0.82; p = 1.00 and 0.64). Conclusions During prophylactic NIV, Pocc discriminated NIV failure better than conventional bedside variables, with no detectable difference from directly measured inspiratory effort. External validation is required.

Remote home-based rehabilitation for post-intensive care syndrome: a pilot randomized feasibility trial
items.abstract: Evidence for scalable interventions for post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) remains uncertain. This descriptive pilot randomized feasibility trial evaluated remote health coaching, home-based rehabilitation, and monitoring. Adult intensive care unit survivors with a Healthy Aging Brain Care Monitor-Self Report score of 12 or higher, 2–4 weeks after hospital discharge, were randomized 1:1 to a 12-week intervention or usual care. Feasibility outcomes included recruitment, retention, outcome completeness, intervention delivery, and safety; no success thresholds were prespecified. Clinical outcomes were exploratory. Analyses used outcome-specific complete cases by randomized group without imputation or multiplicity adjustment. Of 1039 patients contacted, 248 completed screening, 169 met the eligibility threshold, 65 consented, and 56 (5.4%) were randomized. Study completion was 20/28 (71.4%) with intervention and 22/28 (78.6%) with usual care. Core patient-reported outcomes were available for 42/56 (75.0%) and paired activity data for 25/56 (44.6%). Coaching completion was 218/336 protocol-specified sessions (64.9%) and 218/284 sessions scheduled while participants remained active (76.8%). No deaths, hospital or intensive care unit readmissions, urgent psychiatric referrals, or study-related injuries were recorded. Exploratory between-group differences in change were 0.10 for EQ-5D-5 L index (95% confidence interval [CI], -0.01 to 0.21) and − 2.08 for depressive symptoms (95% CI, -3.98 to -0.17). Remote rehabilitation was deliverable but requires refinement. Clinical findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish efficacy. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06184308; first posted 28 December 2023.

items.title: Impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on the occurrence of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia in trauma patients (antiVAP): a propensity score–weighted, retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis has been associated with a reduced risk of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in selected populations, particularly patients with acute brain injury. However, its role in severely injured trauma patients remains controversial. METHODS: This multicentre, retrospective cohort study, conducted in 15 French trauma centres, included severely injured adults who required mechanical ventilation initiated within 24 h of admission and continued for at least 48 h. Propensity score-based analyses assessed the association between early antibiotic prophylaxis (initiated within the first 24 h of management and continued for up to 72 h) and patient outcomes. The primary outcome was early-onset VAP; secondary outcomes included late-onset VAP, extrapulmonary infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 30-day mortality. RESULTS: A total of 1,321 trauma patients were included. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered to 746 patients (56%), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid used in more than 90% of cases. Early-onset VAP occurred in 240 of 746 patients (32%) who received antibiotic prophylaxis and in 195 of 575 (34%) who did not. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with early-onset VAP (weighted odds ratio [wOR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.22; p = 0.48). A cause-specific Cox model accounting for the competing risk of death before day 7 yielded similar results (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07; p = 0.19). Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with improve of secondary outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severely injured trauma patients was not associated with a reduced risk of early-onset VAP. CLINICALTRIALS: Gov ID NCT07059039 - Registration date: July, 10th 2025.

items.title: Prognostic relevance of protein prescriptions based on adjusted body weight in critically ill overweight or obese patients – analysis of a large international database
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: ESPEN currently recommends using adjusted body weight (aBW) to guide protein prescriptions for critically ill overweight or obese patients. The prognostic relevance of this concept is unknown. METHODS: We analyzed a subset of a large international point prevalence survey of nutritional practice in 785 intensive care units (ICUs) worldwide. Patients were included if they had been in the ICU for at least 96 h and had a BMI ≥ 25 kg/m². We modelled the association between early average protein intake (days 1-4 after ICU admission) and the cause-specific adjusted hazards of in-ICU death and ICU discharge alive within a competing risks framework. Intake was normalized to aBW, defined as ideal body weight plus 25% of the difference between actual and ideal body weight. RESULTS: 9,068 patients were analyzed. There was no evidence of an association between early protein intake and ICU discharge alive. In contrast, very low protein intake (below approximately 0.45 g/kg aBW/day) was associated with a higher hazard of in-ICU death. Above this threshold, there was no clear evidence of a further association between protein intake and the hazard of in-ICU death. The strongest association was observed at 0 g/kg aBW/day (adjusted hazard rate 1.41 i.e. an estimated 38% higher risk, 95% confidence interval 1.17-1.69). CONCLUSIONS: Early protein intake does not appear to be associated with time to ICU discharge among survivors. However, in critically ill patients with overweight or obesity, very low protein intake during the early acute phase may be associated with less favorable in-ICU outcomes.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of shenfu injection on sepsis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: The efficacy and safety of Shenfu Injection (SFI) as an adjunctive therapy for sepsis remain uncertain because the available randomized evidence is heterogeneous and generally of limited methodological quality. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy, safety, and certainty of the current evidence for SFI in patients with sepsis. Eight electronic databases were searched from inception to 18 October 2026 without language restrictions to identify randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing SFI plus conventional Western therapy (CWT) with CWT alone. The primary outcomes were 7-day and 28-day mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation (DMV), vasopressor duration, Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II) score, arterial lactate (Lac) levels, and adverse events (AEs). Random-effects or fixed-effect meta-analyses were performed as appropriate. Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) was used to assess the risk of random errors, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261329190). Fifty-six RCTs involving 4,362 participants were included. Compared with CWT alone, adjunctive SFI was associated with lower 7-day mortality (RR = 0.67, 95% CI: 0.52–0.86) and 28-day mortality (RR = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.65–0.78), shorter ICU length of stay and vasopressor duration, lower SOFA and APACHE II scores, and reduced lactate levels at 24 h, 3 days, and 7 days. No significant differences were observed for DMV or 6-hour lactate levels. Publication bias was detected for 28-day mortality, 7-day APACHE II score, and 3-day lactate levels. After trim-and-fill adjustment, the reduction in 28-day mortality remained statistically significant but was attenuated (adjusted RR = 0.87, 95% CI: 0.79–0.96), whereas the reduction in 3-day lactate levels was no longer statistically significant (adjusted MD = − 0.19, 95% CI: −0.49 to 0.10). The adjusted effect for 7-day APACHE II score remained statistically significant. Safety evidence was limited, with only 19 of 56 trials reporting adverse events. Although a possible increase in adverse events was observed (RR = 3.96, 95% CI: 1.57–9.97), this estimate was based on only 22 events, and TSA did not reach the required information size. Thus, the safety of SFI remains uncertain. According to GRADE, the certainty of evidence ranged from very low to high, with most efficacy outcomes rated as low or very low certainty because of methodological limitations, inconsistency, and publication bias. The available evidence suggests possible improvements in measures of hemodynamic support, organ dysfunction, and metabolic status with adjunctive SFI in patients with sepsis, while the mortality findings remain uncertain. Confidence in these findings is limited by the variable certainty of evidence (GRADE ratings ranging from high for vasopressor duration and moderate for 7‑day mortality to low or very low for most other outcomes), methodological limitations of the included trials, potential publication bias, limited and uncertain safety evidence, and the exclusive inclusion of studies conducted in China. Therefore, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and regarded as hypothesis‑generating rather than practice‑changing until confirmed by large, rigorously designed, multicenter randomized trials with standardized safety monitoring.

items.title: A comprehensive PROBAST-based assessment of mortality prediction models in adult intensive care units; an updated scoping review
items.abstract: Background Numerous mortality prediction models have been developed for general adult intensive care unit (ICU) populations, but concerns remain regarding their methodological quality, risk of bias, and validation. Previous reviews primarily identified available models and their predictors, without a comprehensive model-by-model risk-of-bias assessment. We therefore updated the existing evidence base and systematically assessed identified ICU mortality prediction models using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST), aiming to identify methodologically robust models warranting further validation. Methods and results We built on a systematic scoping review and its first update covering studies published up to February 8, 2023, and updated the search in PubMed (MEDLINE), Embase (Ovid), Web of Science, and CENTRAL through May 11, 2026. Eligible studies developed mortality prediction models for general adult critically ill populations. Data extraction and PROBAST assessment were performed independently by reviewer pairs using a standardized CHARMS- and PROBAST-based form. In total, 56 studies describing 84 mortality prediction models were included. Overall, 82/84 (98%) models were judged at high risk of bias, predominantly because of shortcomings in the analysis domain. Internal validation was absent in 21/84 (25%) models, while only 2/84 (2%) underwent external validation in the original publication. Only one model, ICNARC II, was judged at overall low risk of bias, while PREDICT was judged at unclear risk of bias. A prospective citation search identified no external validation studies for either model. Conclusion Nearly all identified ICU mortality prediction models were at high risk of bias, limiting confidence in their reported performance and practical implementation of their intended use. Rather than continuing to develop additional models, future research should prioritize rigorous external validation and, where necessary, updating of promising existing models while adhering to established methodological standards.

items.title: Premorbid hypertension modifies predicted optimal blood pressure targets for intracerebral hemorrhage
items.abstract: Background Prior trials found an inconsistent benefit of uniform, intensive blood pressure reduction after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Untreated hypertension impairs cerebral autoregulation, increasing vulnerability to cerebral hypoperfusion. We sought to determine whether premorbid hypertension treatment modifies systolic blood pressure (SBP) targets associated with optimal neurologic outcomes. Methods Using the Antihypertensive Treatment of Acute Cerebral Hemorrhage-2 trial, patients with premorbid hypertension were categorized as treated or untreated based on antihypertensive use within 30 days prior to ICH. The primary outcome was ninety-day poor functional outcome defined as modified Rankin Scale > 2. Multivariable mixed-effects regression using restricted cubic splines modeled the joint interaction between SBP achieved at 24 h and hypertension treatment. A secondary analysis assessed the interaction between hypertension treatment and SBP reduction intensity on early neurologic decline using Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) measured hourly during the initial 24 h. Results Among 732 participants, 299 had treated hypertension and 433 had untreated hypertension. Poor ninety-day outcome occurred in a total of 416 (57%) patients. The primary analysis demonstrated the association between achieved SBP and ninety-day outcome was modified by hypertension treatment (joint Wald interaction test χ²=20.45, p < 0.001). Spline models observed a J-shaped relationship among patients with untreated hypertension and a predicted optimal target of 130–140 mmHg. Patients with treated hypertension demonstrated continued reduction in the probability of poor outcome with lower SBP and a predicted optimal target of ≤ 120 mmHg. In the secondary analysis, hypertension treatment modified the relationship between SBP reduction and change in GCS, such that extreme SBP reduction was associated with GCS decline in those with untreated hypertension (joint Wald interaction test χ²=9.73, p = 0.008). Conclusion Premorbid hypertension treatment modifies the predicted optimal SBP targets after ICH. Personalized antihypertensive strategies that account for chronic hypertension warrant further study. Trial registration www.clinicaltrials.gov (Unique Identifier: NCT01176565). First submitted August 2010.

items.title: Weaning success and ventilation duration in PRiVENT: reply to Cheng
Drawing before counting: causal diagrams and g-methods in critical care evidence synthesis
Lower respiratory tract secretory IgA and 28-day mortality in severe pneumonia: a multicenter prospective cohort study
items.abstract: Secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA) contributes to mucosal defense in the lower airways. We investigated the clinical correlates of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) sIgA and its association with 28-day mortality in a prospective multicenter cohort of 465 patients, including 248 with paired samples. Hospital-stratified Cox models assessed associations with 28-day mortality. For baseline sIgA, the hazard ratio (HR) per log10 unit was 0.75 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.54–1.05; p = 0.093). In the 248-patient paired-sample cohort, with 84 deaths, greater change in log10 sIgA was associated with higher mortality (HR, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.11–2.98; nominal p = 0.018). Immunosuppression was associated with lower baseline sIgA, whereas circulating IgA, IgM and interleukin-1β correlated positively with BALF concentrations. These findings link lower-airway sIgA dynamics to mortality and support further investigation of mucosal immune responses in severe pneumonia.

items.title: The sepsis trial landscape: a domain-specific systematic review and meta-analysis of adult sepsis randomized controlled trials
items.abstract: Despite decades of sepsis randomized clinical trials (RCTs), few therapeutic interventions have demonstrated reproducible mortality benefit. Whether this phenomenon reflects failure of individual therapies or broader limitations in sepsis RCT design remains unclear. We hypothesized that examining clinically distinct treatment domains would reveal differences in mortality effect estimates while identifying recurrent trial-design limitations shared across domains. Therefore, we performed a domain-specific meta-analysis of adult sepsis RCTs and evaluated the distribution of mortality effect estimates across treatment domains using a complementary landscape analysis framework and structured trial-design analysis. We conducted a meta-analysis of adult sepsis and septic shock RCTs published between 2000 and 2025 (PROSPERO CRD420261289221). Using PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL, two reviewers screened studies and extracted data. Trials were grouped into six treatment domains: initial resuscitation interventions, intravenous fluid quantity, intravenous fluid type, vasopressors, corticosteroids, and vitamin C–based therapies. Separate random-effects meta-analyses estimated pooled risk ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). We also performed a complementary landscape analysis using Python to evaluate the distribution of mortality effect estimates relative to study sample size, as well as a structured thematic analysis to identify recurrent trial design constraints across treatment domains. Across 62 RCTs ( n = 36,739), pooled mortality effects demonstrated no mortality benefit across each of the six treatment domains: resuscitation interventions (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.77–1.01), intravenous fluid quantity (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88–1.05), intravenous fluid type (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.89–1.01), vasopressors (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.88–1.07), corticosteroids (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.84–1.00), and vitamin C-based therapies (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.83–1.09). A landscape analysis showed wider dispersion of mortality effect estimates among smaller trials, whereas larger trial estimates generally clustered near the null. A structured thematic analysis using a prespecified trial-constraint framework identified recurrent design limitations across treatment domains, including delayed intervention timing, biologic and clinical heterogeneity, treatment contamination, and trial design and infrastructure constraints. Across the six prespecified treatment domains in sepsis, RCTs have not demonstrated consistent reductions in mortality. Recurrent trial-design limitations were common across treatment domains and may inform interpretation and future trial design.

items.title: Evaluation of kidney function at ICU discharge using iohexol clearance in patients with normal serum creatinine after acute kidney injury
items.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common complication in critically ill patients and is associated with high rates of mortality or progression to chronic kidney disease, even when serum creatinine returns to normal at ICU discharge. This study aims to evaluate the frequency of non-resolving kidney dysfunction at ICU discharge despite normal serum creatinine levels following AKI, and to assess its association with chronic kidney disease at 6 months. This multicenter, observational study included patients who experienced AKI (KDIGO stage 2 or 3) during their ICU stay and had serum creatinine < 130 µmol/L (men) or <110 µmol/L (women) at discharge. Iohexol clearance and serum and urinary creatinine were measured at ICU discharge, once other organ failures had resolved. Serum creatinine was also assessed at 6 months. Non-resolving kidney dysfunction was defined as iohexol clearance < 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . Among 137 patients, 70 (51%) had non-resolving kidney dysfunction at ICU discharge. Among these 70 patients, urine creatinine clearance and CKD-EPI-based estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) were < 60 mL/min/1.73 m 2 in 69% and 19% of cases, respectively. In multivariable analysis, risk factors for non-resolving dysfunction included older age, longer ICU stay, presence of malignancy, and higher baseline and admission serum creatinine. Patients with non-resolving kidney dysfunction had significantly lower CKD-EPI GFR at 6 months compared to those with resolving dysfunction. Non-resolving kidney dysfunction was present in approximately half of patients who had experienced severe AKI despite normal serum creatinine at ICU discharge, highlighting the limitations of serum creatinine in assessing renal recovery in critically ill patients. Non-resolving dysfunction was associated with lower CKD-EPI GFR at 6 months. ClinicalTrials.gov, identifier: NCT02961478. Registered on November 11, 2016.

items.title: A supervised, biologically informed Innate Immunity Score reflecting immune activation shows prognostic value and potential for treatment stratification in sepsis
items.abstract: Background Most sepsis subtyping strategies have been developed using unsupervised methods and were not specifically designed to quantify immune activation. Moreover, they often rely on categorical classifications, while a continuous representation may better capture sepsis immunobiology. Methods By integrating plasma cytokine response data with monocyte RNA sequencing profiles of 110 healthy volunteers who were intravenously challenged with 1 ng/kg lipopolysaccharide, we derived a continuous Innate Immunity Score (IIS), which we applied to five independent clinical cohorts of patients with sepsis ( n = 1267). We intersected the IIS with unsupervised established subtyping strategies (Mars, SRS, CTS, ARDS hyper/hypoinflammatory) and continuous sepsis scores (SRSq, lymphoid, and myeloid dysregulation scores). Furthermore, we performed an in-silico drug prediction analysis to explore potential therapeutics that reverse the transcriptomic signature associated with a high IIS, and explored heterogeneity of treatment effect (HTE) in sepsis for hydrocortisone using the IIS. A parsimonious classifier model was developed to support potential clinical applicability. Results The IIS was calculated based on the weighted expression of 46 genes that discriminated best between a high versus low plasma cytokine response to LPS administration in healthy volunteers. The IIS was associated with markers of immune activation, disease severity, organ dysfunction, and mortality in patients with sepsis. Several molecular pathways were uniquely upregulated (e.g. innate immune system) or downregulated (e.g. downstream Tcr signaling, generation of second messenger molecules, regulation of T-cell activation by CD28 family) in patients with a high IIS compared with established hyperinflammatory subtypes. A range of candidate drugs were predicted to reverse the transcriptional state associated with a high IIS, including corticosteroids, methotrexate, tyrosine kinase and mTOR inhibitors, and simvastatin. HTE was observed for hydrocortisone, suggesting harm for patients with a low IIS (≤ 0.66, 69% of patients) and benefit for those with a high IIS (> 0.66, 31%, p = 0.039). HTE could not be established using the SRSq ( p = 0.660), myeloid ( p = 0.648), or lymphoid ( p = 0.385) dysregulation scores. Finally, the three-gen​e ratio log 2 [(​​ GPR84 , PIM1) : SLC27A1 ​] accurately determined the IIS ( r = 0.91, p < 2.2 × 10 − 16 ; RMSE = 0.07). Conclusions A supervised, biologically informed continuous stratification approach reflecting immune activation in sepsis shows prognostic value and potential for treatment stratification. Therefore, it may provide a framework for exploring targeted immunomodulatory strategies. Trial registration CMO Arnhem-Nijmegen; reference no. NL68166.091.18 (registration date: 04-02-2019). Registered at Overview of Medical Research in the Netherlands (OMON) reference no. NL-OMON48466. Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov; reference no. NCT06801873.

items.title: Discordant evidence on corticosteroids in sepsis: a meta-research study
items.abstract: Background Despite an extensive evidence base of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews (SRs), current sepsis guidelines provide only weak recommendations for corticosteroid therapy, while available SRs report conflicting mortality conclusions. We aimed to characterize the evidence landscape of SRs evaluating corticosteroids for sepsis, including their clinical scope, underlying RCT evidence bases, mortality conclusions, and to explore potential sources of discordance. Methods Meta-research study of SRs on corticosteroids in sepsis published between 2015 and 2025. Study-pool overlap was assessed using a SR×RCT inclusion matrix, Jaccard similarity (J), and hierarchical clustering. SRs and RCTs were classified according to standardized Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (PICO) profiles. We explored discordance in short-term mortality conclusions among clinically comparable SRs and potential associations with study-pool composition, target populations, and methodological characteristics. Results Forty-two SRs including 121 unique RCTs were identified. More than half of pairwise SR comparisons shared no RCTs, and only three pairs showed high overlap (J > 0.8). SRs addressing similar intervention and target population profiles frequently relied on different study pools. Among 38 SRs with short-term mortality meta-analyses, 15 (39%) reported benefit and 23 (61%) no evidence of effect. Discordance occurred exclusively among SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies; conclusions were consistent for hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone (benefit) and hydrocortisone, ascorbic acid, and thiamine (no evidence of effect). SRs including adult sepsis ± shock populations more frequently reported benefit than those restricted to septic shock (62% vs 22%), although this comparison was based on only 22 SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies and estimates were imprecise. No single methodological or clinical factor consistently explained discordance. Conclusions SRs addressing apparently similar clinical questions frequently synthesized different underlying evidence bases and reported discordant conclusions. When selecting SRs to inform clinical decisions and recommendations for sepsis management, clinicians and guideline developers should consider not only methodological quality and reported PICO, but also whether the included RCTs adequately represent the intended clinical question.

items.title: Twice-yearly depemokimab: beyond dosing convenience

Long-term safety and efficacy of twice-yearly depemokimab in type 2 asthma with an eosinophilic phenotype: 2-year integrated analysis of the phase 3a SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 studies and AGILE open-label extension
items.abstract: Background Depemokimab is the first ultra-long-acting biologic, with enhanced interleukin-5 binding affinity, high potency, and extended half-life, enabling twice-yearly dosing. The double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3a SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 studies demonstrated depemokimab efficacy and safety over 52 weeks in patients with asthma with type 2 inflammation and an eosinophilic phenotype. Here, we present long-term safety and efficacy outcomes over the 52-week, phase 3a open-label extension (OLE) of SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 (AGILE) alongside an integrated post-hoc analysis of the 104-week SWIFT and AGILE period. Methods In SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2, patients (aged ≥12 years) with asthma with type 2 inflammation, an eosinophilic phenotype (≥150 cells/μL at screening or ≥300 cells/μL during the previous 12 months), and a history of at least two exacerbations in the previous 12 months despite receiving medium-dose or high-dose inhaled corticosteroids were randomly assigned (2:1) to subcutaneous depemokimab 100 mg or placebo every 26 weeks in addition to standard of care for 52 weeks. Patients who completed SWIFT-1 or SWIFT-2 could join the single-arm, 52-week AGILE OLE study, conducted at 156 centres across 14 countries. Patients continued depemokimab (depemokimab-depemokimab group) or switched to depemokimab from placebo (placebo-depemokimab group). The primary endpoints for the 52-week AGILE OLE period were the incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events, and immunogenicity as measured by the presence of anti-drug antibodies and neutralising antibodies. Secondary efficacy outcomes, including exacerbation rate, St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ) total score, Asthma Control Questionnaire-5 (ACQ-5) score, and pre-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ), were also assessed. Additional post-hoc analyses were carried out to assess safety and efficacy over the 104-week integrated SWIFT and AGILE analysis period. AGILE OLE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05243680. The SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 trials are registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04719832 and NCT04718103. Findings Between March 1, 2022, and May 19, 2025, 629 patients were included in the AGILE OLE study (419 patients in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 210 patients in the placebo-depemokimab group). During the 52-week AGILE OLE period, adverse events occurred in 297 (71%) of 419 patients in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 146 (70%) of 210 patients in the placebo-depemokimab group; serious adverse events were infrequent (37 [9%] of 419 in the depemokimab-depemokimab group and 19 [9%] of 210 in the placebo-depemokimab group), with no treatment-related or fatal serious adverse events reported. In the depemokimab-depemokimab group, the reduced annualised exacerbation rate was sustained over 2 years (0·51 [95% CI 0·43-0·61] in the 52-week SWIFT-1 and SWIFT-2 period and 0·56 [0·47-0·66] in the AGILE OLE). Improvements in SGRQ total score, ACQ-5 score, and FEV 1 were maintained over 2 years. In the placebo-depemokimab group, improvements in clinical outcomes were observed after the switch to depemokimab during the AGILE OLE. Interpretation Twice-yearly depemokimab was well tolerated and demonstrated sustained efficacy over the 2-year SWIFT and AGILE period, supporting its long-term therapeutic benefit and safety profile. Funding GSK.

The present and future of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease prevention, diagnosis, and management in China: a Lancet Respiratory Medicine Commission

items.title: From coverage to equitable reach: addressing social inequalities in COPD in China
Breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management in adults: evidence update on behalf of The Dyspnoea Society
items.abstract: Breathlessness affects an estimated 40% of adults living with chronic disease, with substantial consequences for individuals, carers, and health-care systems. This Dyspnoea Society Research Statement, developed for researchers, clinicians, and adults living with or caring for someone with breathlessness, provides a state-of-the-art synthesis of recent advances in chronic breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management, and outlines a research agenda for the next decade. Key advancements include establishment of neural respiratory drive as a mechanistic contributor to exertional breathlessness; neuroimaging evidence that breathlessness arises from integration of peripheral and central processes within a dynamic brain network involving sensorimotor and cognitive-affective regions, supporting behavioural and psychosocial interventions; and improved measurement through responsive multidimensional instruments and approaches to quantify symptom abnormality relative to physical activity. Evidence supports early use of low-risk, non-pharmacological interventions for management of breathlessness, whereas evidence for pharmacological therapies is limited in most situations. Health-care redesign, including symptom-focused diagnostic pathways, integrated care models, and disease-agnostic breathlessness services, might help to improve patient outcomes while reducing health-care costs.

items.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea: an overlooked challenge in the current NHS Strategy
items.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is common, frequently symptomatic, and closely associated with conditions already prioritised by the UK National Health Service (NHS), including obesity, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, cardiovascular disease, and stroke. Previous estimates suggest that approximately 8 million UK adults aged 30-69 years could have OSA, although the proportion remaining undiagnosed is uncertain. Evidence supports treatment benefits for daytime sleepiness, symptom burden, quality of life, driving safety, and blood pressure in some patients, but not a consistent reduction in major cardiovascular events. UK data indicate long diagnostic waits, regional variation, and gaps in follow-up. A proportionate NHS response should prioritise targeted case-finding within existing chronic-disease pathways, access to validated home-based diagnostics, specialist capacity for complex disease, and sustained treatment support. Implementation should be phased and evaluated prospectively for clinical outcomes, equity, workforce requirements, affordability, and budget impact.

items.title: Laennec beyond the stethoscope
Defining residual lung disease with CFTR modulators
Ending the global neglect of pneumonia: from awareness to accountability
Longitudinal change in FEV1 in adults with cystic fibrosis treated with elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor in France: a prospective observational study
items.abstract: Background Without cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulators, cystic fibrosis is associated with an accelerated decline in percent predicted FEV 1 (ppFEV 1 ) of approximately 1·5% per year. Although treatment with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) initially increases ppFEV 1 , little is known about its subsequent effect on ppFEV 1 decline. Recent analyses of the extension phases of the phase 3 ETI pivotal studies found no evidence of ppFEV 1 decline over 4 years in patients aged 12 years and older who were treated with ETI. The objective of this study was to examine the decline in ppFEV 1 in a large, real-world cohort of adults with cystic fibrosis. Methods Data from adults (aged ≥18 years) with cystic fibrosis and at least one F508del CFTR variant who initiated treatment with ETI between Dec 24, 2019, and Dec 23, 2023, at 31 cystic fibrosis centres included in the French prospective national observational ETI study in adults were analysed over 3 years. Eligible participants were those with at least three measures of ppFEV 1 taken within 3 months following ETI initiation and the end of follow-up. The reference ppFEV 1 was the highest ppFEV 1 reached during the first 3 months of ETI treatment, after which subsequent decline in ppFEV 1 was analysed by use of a linear mixed-effects model with random effects to estimate each participant's variation from the population mean. Findings Data from 2321 adults with cystic fibrosis were included in this analysis. 1262 (54·4%) participants were male and 1059 (45·6%) were female. Median age was 29·2 years (IQR 23·1-36·7) and the pre-ETI initiation ppFEV 1 was 59·7% (IQR 39·8-79·1). Within the first 3 months following ETI initiation, ppFEV 1 increased by a median of 14·5 percentage points (IQR 7·9-22·7). The subsequent mean decline in ppFEV 1 was 0·70% (95% CI 0·57-0·83) per year. Importantly, the decline in ppFEV 1 was heterogeneous, with 1583 (68·2%) of 2321 participants showing no or limited decline (less than or equal to 1·5% per year). The remaining 738 (31·8%) participants showed a decline of greater than 1·5% per year, with 342 (46·3%) of these participants having a decline of greater than 3·0% per year. In multivariable analyses, the decline in ppFEV 1 was greater in participants with a higher ppFEV 1 at 3 months after ETI initiation. Treatment with oral azithromycin at 1 year after ETI initiation was associated with a lower risk of having a decline greater than 1·5% per year (relative risk 0·78 [95% CI 0·68-0·90]; p Interpretation These results suggest that approximately a third of adults with cystic fibrosis who are treated with ETI had a persistent decline in ppFEV 1 . These data emphasise the importance of regular ppFEV 1 monitoring and highlight the need to improve current therapeutic strategies to prevent ppFEV 1 decline. Proposed strategies could include use of newer CFTR modulators to restore CFTR function more effectively, as well as mucoactive, anti-infective, and anti-inflammatory therapies. Funding Association Vaincre la Mucoviscidose, Société Française de la Mucoviscidose, and Filière Maladies Rares MUCO-CFTR.

items.title: Consensus on the definition, components, and grading of composite postoperative pulmonary complication outcomes (PrECiSIOn): insights from an international Delphi expert panel
items.abstract: Postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) are common after surgery and contribute substantially to morbidity, mortality, and health-care burden, and are frequently used as endpoints in clinical studies. However, absence of standardised definitions and heterogeneity in component selection limit comparability across studies and might bias estimates of treatment effects. The Postoperative Pulmonary Complications-Evaluation for Consensus on Standardised Outcomes (PrECiSIOn) study was an international, mixed-method consensus study using a Delphi process to establish a standardised definition of PPCs, determine severity-based ranking of individual components, and define approaches for their assessment. A multidisciplinary panel of experts in PPCs was recruited and candidate PPC components were identified through a focused literature review, structured into domains, and evaluated across iterative Delphi rounds using a seven-point Likert scale, with consensus predefined as ≥75% agreement. Patient and patient care representative perspectives were incorporated through interviews and surveys, and panellists assigned severity weights to components reaching consensus. Input from 44 panellists and five patients and patient representatives informed the prioritisation of clinically meaningful outcomes. Consensus was achieved on a standardised PPC construct comprising components grouped into four domains: symptoms, diagnoses, therapies, and outcomes. Panellists supported the use of routinely collected clinical data and a standardised in-hospital monitoring approach but did not reach consensus on the optimal follow-up period or need for post-discharge surveillance. Severity-based rank ordering enabled hierarchical organisation of PPC components according to their clinical importance, supporting the development of ordinal composite outcomes that account for differences in severity between individual complications. This international consensus-based framework provides a standardised definition of PPCs incorporating severity-based rank ordering, addresses important limitations of existing composite outcomes, and might facilitate more consistent and clinically meaningful evaluation of perioperative interventions. Further work should focus on external validation, implementation in clinical trial analyses, and assessment of applicability across diverse patient populations and health-care settings.

items.title: RSV multidose vaccine puts Africa's RSV burden in focus
Children are not small adults: CAD for childhood tuberculosis
Closing the logic gap—expanding who we consider for tuberculosis treatment
How to measure first responders’ arrival time in a smartphone alerting system? An observational study
Wearable-based automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting: a systematic review
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with survival strongly dependent on rapid recognition and timely emergency care. Wearables capable of automated cardiac arrest detection and alerting may reduce delays to treatment, particularly in unwitnessed arrests. Therefore, this review aims to systematically evaluate the existing evidence on the performance of wearable sensors and algorithms designed for OHCA detection. METHODS: A systematic search was performed using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, the Cochrane Libraries, forward citation and backward citation to identify all eligible studies up to 22 September 2026. Studies describing non-invasive, intended wearable systems designed to detect OHCA and reporting on their detection performance were included. The methodology and report of the present review are based on recommendations of the PRISMA statement and Cochrane Collaboration. Primary outcome is the sensitivity for cardiac arrest detection. Secondary outcomes include false positives cardiac arrest alerts and specificity. Studies were evaluated using the QUADAS-2 tool. RESULTS: From 6,344 records screened, 13 publications were included with the number of participants ranging from 18 to 1,423. Wristbands were the most prevalent device type (n = 9). Nine studies used photoplethysmography as primary sensor type, with accelerometry as additive sensor modality (n = 2). Other sensors used were mechanical plethysmography (n = 1), electrocardiography (n = 1), sound-based (n = 1) and a nonlinear resonant circuit (n = 1). Sensitivity ranged between 43.8 and 100%, with ten studies reporting a sensitivity of ≥90%. False positives ranged between multiple per day and one per twenty-one user-years. DISCUSSION: Wearable devices have demonstrated promising sensitivity for detecting cardiac arrest. However, (external) validation and real-life data are scarce, and the sensitivity-false alarm trade-off requires further investigation. REGISTRATION: OSF, https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AEPF8.

items.title: AEDs in hospitals: more than just pushing a button
Post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation and coronary angiographic phenotypes in angiography-evaluable survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest
items.abstract: Background The clinical meaning of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with suspected coronary etiology remains uncertain. We aimed to describe coronary angiographic phenotypes and clinical outcomes according to post-resuscitation ST-segment findings in an angiography-evaluable subset of OHCA survivors with presumed coronary lesion-related arrest. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 149 successfully resuscitated OHCA patients admitted to our institution between January 2015 and December 2023, who underwent post-resuscitation coronary angiography and had presumed culprit lesions, defined by integrating angiographic findings with electrocardiographic, echocardiographic, and biomarker data in the clinical context. Patients were classified according to the presence or absence of post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation. Results ST-segment elevation was associated with a more acute occlusive coronary phenotype, with more impaired culprit-vessel flow and greater myocardial injury. In contrast, patients without ST-segment elevation more frequently had multivessel disease and chronic total occlusion, suggesting more complex coronary artery disease. Favorable neurological outcome was less frequent with ST-segment elevation in unadjusted analyses, but this association was not independent of pre-hospital factors. Conclusions In this selected OHCA subset, post-resuscitation ST-segment elevation was associated with an acute occlusive coronary phenotype and greater myocardial injury, as in non-arrest acute coronary syndromes. However, the absence of ST-segment elevation did not exclude a coronary culprit lesion, so comprehensive coronary assessment is essential. ST-segment elevation was not independently associated with clinical outcomes after adjustment for pre-hospital factors. These findings should be interpreted considering substantial selection inherent to the study population.

items.title: Long-term survival following extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation: a two-center five-year analysis
items.abstract: Randomized trials have shown short-term benefit of extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but the long-term durability of survival and neurological recovery after hospital discharge remains poorly defined. We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory VT/VF OHCA from two academic centers (University of Minnesota, USA, and Charles University, Prague) from January 2013 through December 2022. The primary outcome was 5-year survival. Secondary outcomes included neurological status by Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) and associations of age and discharge disposition with long-term outcomes. Among 728 patients treated with ECPR, 211 (29.0%) survived to discharge; 138 from Minnesota and 73 from Prague. Median follow-up was 3.9 years; 68 patients (32%) completed 5 years. No patients were lost to follow-up. Among hospital survivors, 76.9% and 67.2% were alive at 1 and 5 years, respectively, with most deaths occurring within 90 days of discharge. CPC 1-2 was present in 78.7% at discharge and remained high among survivors beyond 1 year (93.4-94.2%). Five-year survival declined by age from 91.6% for those between 18-39 years and 52.9% for >70 years. Discharge disposition also strongly stratified long-term prognosis. Among patients discharged alive after ECPR for refractory OHCA, long-term survival was substantial, with approximately two-thirds alive at 5 years with favorable CPC in most. Younger age and discharge home or to acute rehabilitation identified subgroups with particularly favorable prognosis. These findings support the long-term durability of benefit among selected patients treated within established ECPR systems of care.

items.abstract: This is the annual summary of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations; a comprehensive review was completed in 2025. This latest summary addresses the most recent published resuscitation evidence reviewed by International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation task forces, including Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid. Members from these 6 task forces assessed the certainty of the evidence using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria, and their statements include consensus treatment recommendations. Highlights from task force discussions and insights into how decisions regarding treatment recommendations were made are provided in the Justification and Evidence-to-Decision Framework Highlights sections. The task forces also listed priority knowledge gaps for further research.
